HENRY CORBIN

# Within Iranian Islam

## Spiritual and Philosophical Aspects

**VOLUME I**

### Twelver Shiism

## Prologue

This book does not attempt to tell the whole history of Iran's philosophical and spiritual thought. That would have made an already substantial work even longer. It would also have required a level of completeness that the current state of research simply does not allow.

Some important subjects are therefore bound to be missing. Ismailism, for example, appears here only in passing or for comparison. Yet it is the other major branch of Shiism, and it was certainly among the leading forces in Islamic metaphysics and *gnosis*—the search for spiritual knowledge. We have discussed it elsewhere and hope to return to it in greater detail.[^EII1-1]

Another major absence is the enormous poem by Jalal al-Din Rumi known as the *Mathnawi*, often called the *Qor'an-e farsi*, or “Persian Qur'an.” But Western readers already have a way into that work. Even those whose Persian is still limited can study it line by line, thanks to R. A. Nicholson's complete and faithful English translation.[^EII1-2] Our main purpose here is to explore much less familiar ground: places where, over the centuries, the spiritual life of Iran has produced its harvest.

The *Mathnawi* can fairly be seen as a characteristic expression of Persian-language Sufism, a tradition that also flourished for centuries in Anatolia. And Western scholars have long tended to treat Sufism as though it alone represented the mystical life of Islam. But both views give us only part of the picture.

Above all, I want to draw attention to a particular gift of Iranian thought. Some will call it the genius of Iran; others, the enduring calling of the Iranian soul. It is the ability to build a philosophical understanding of the world without ever losing sight of what that understanding must become in a person's own spiritual life. Unless philosophical reflection bears fruit in personal transformation, philosophy becomes an empty exercise of the mind.

Iranian thought has a remarkable ability to unite philosophical inquiry with mystical experience. Refusing to separate the two gives each of them a distinctive character. That is why it is so regrettable that Iranian and Iranian-Islamic philosophy has been largely absent from our histories of philosophy. The omission has left our understanding of humanity poorer and incomplete.

For more than a thousand years, and particularly during the last four centuries, Iran's philosophers and spiritual writers have produced an extraordinary body of work. They wrestle with many of the same questions as Western philosophers, but often approach them from directions—and offer answers—that the course of Western intellectual disputes has pushed aside.

Yet their voice has scarcely been heard beyond Iran. Even Iranians themselves are not always aware of what their inherited culture might have to say to people today, still less of how to bring that message to life in the present.

This union of philosophy and mystical experience also asks us to rethink two common Western assumptions about Sufism. First, Sufism is often presented as something that can simply dispense with philosophy. This misses the fact that Iranian philosophers, by reflecting on the very act of knowing, have undergone what is traditionally called *unio mystica*, or mystical union.

Second, Sufism is often treated as the sole home of mystical life in Islam. Yet some of Iran's great spiritual teachers use the language of Sufism without belonging to a Sufi order (*tariqat*) or even calling themselves Sufis.

For reasons we will explore later, many of these teachers have, for roughly four centuries, preferred the words *irfan* and *irfani*—inner spiritual knowledge and the people who seek it—to the terms *tasawwuf* (Sufism) and *Sufi*. A researcher educated in the West may have learned that Shiism has little sympathy for Sufism and concluded that Shiism has no deeply inward spiritual life of its own. To see the mistake, the researcher need only begin studying someone like Haydar Amoli, a fourteenth-century teacher who argued that a true Sufi is also a true Shiite. For a Shiite, then, what matters is to be truly Shiite in this inward, spiritual sense.

Alongside Shiite Sufi orders, the researcher will discover great Shiite mystics who do not describe themselves as Sufis. At the traditional theological centre in Qom, for example, one can speak freely about *irfan* and *irfani* and have a lively, comfortable discussion. But mention *tasawwuf* or *Sufi*, and a shadow may pass over the faces of those listening. It may take years to understand why.

The researcher must set aside a familiar picture of Islamic intellectual life. In that picture, there are the theologians of *kalam*, who defend religious beliefs through argument; there are the philosophers influenced by Greek thought, known as the *falasifa*; and somewhere between them stand the Sufis, with little affection for either group. Reality is more complicated.

A saying that has become almost a motto points to a different arrangement. It goes back to the spiritual transformation brought about by Suhrawardi in the twelfth century—the subject of the whole of Book II. The saying proposes that Sufism stands in relation to *kalam* theology as Suhrawardi's philosophy of light (*ishraq*) stands in relation to the philosophy of the *falasifa*. These four approaches reveal Iranian Islam in a very different light. We cannot understand it by simply applying categories developed for the rest of the Islamic world.

That difference becomes clearer when we realise how little most of the thinkers and spiritual teachers discussed in this work are known in the West. Many of their writings still exist only as manuscripts. I hope the aspects brought to light here will interest philosophers and students of religion alike. There is no point pretending that these ideas fit comfortably with the fashionable ideologies of our day. Perhaps they will be all the more valuable for that: they may remind us of things we have forgotten amid the noise of our fiercely competing convictions.

There is no point hiding, either, the awkward position—and the many difficulties—of a philosopher working with Asian and Islamic sources. Because so little groundwork has been done, such a philosopher must first take on the job of a scholar who prepares old texts for publication. Often, before discussing a work, one must first establish a reliable edition of it. A philosopher who can work with texts already edited, perhaps even written in their own language, should consider the difference.

There is another difficulty: nobody quite knows where to place this kind of scholar. They are rather like an orphan. Scholars of Asian languages and cultures are not necessarily concerned with metaphysics and may regard the philosopher among them as a wandering knight who has strayed into the wrong company. Philosophers, for their part, are ready enough to consider the questions, but unfamiliar names and new technical terms soon leave them bewildered.

We will return to these odd difficulties, partly to encourage younger researchers to overcome them. It will fall to them to make Iranian philosophy, and Islamic philosophy more broadly, part of the shared intellectual inheritance of philosophers everywhere.

It should therefore come as no surprise that the research gathered in these four volumes took more than twenty years. It depended on repeated and extended stays in Iran and on friendships there that have remained dear to me. Alongside this work, I continued teaching in Paris and, for several years, also in Tehran. I hope all those who attended those classes know how much their attention encouraged me.

It is rare for a researcher to have the chance, during their lifetime, to explain what they set out to do, and why and how they tried to do it. Rarer still is the chance to write something that serves at once as a statement of purpose and a personal testament. I was given just such an opportunity not long ago, when the Religious Sciences Section of the École pratique des Hautes-Études at the Sorbonne published a centenary volume. I refer the reader to my contribution because the present work both illustrates and expands upon what I said there.[^EII1-3]

I must also mention another undertaking, pursued at the same time with our distinguished colleague Professor Sayyed Jalal al-Din Ashtiyani of the Faculty of Theology and Islamic Sciences at Mashhad University: an *Anthology of Iranian Philosophers from the Seventeenth Century to the Present*. The first volume is already complete.[^EII1-4] May we be able to bring the whole undertaking to completion. As planned, it will fill five substantial volumes and introduce around fifty Iranian thinkers from the last four centuries, almost all previously unknown in the West. Many of their works still survive only in manuscript. Several are studied in the present book.

Bringing these thinkers into view will challenge some of our most established categories, beginning with the way we divide the history of philosophy into periods. Are these philosophers medieval or modern? By date they do not belong to what we call the Middle Ages.

Yet the questions that concern them connect at every point with the period Western historians call medieval. They are “modern” in the calendar sense, but their picture of the world does not quite match what the West usually calls modern. And there are striking similarities between the Persian Platonists, such as Mulla Sadra of Shiraz, and their contemporaries among the Cambridge Platonists. Our familiar division into Antiquity, the Middle Ages, and Modern Times may no longer serve us, because it was made to fit specifically Western history. We will need some other way, beyond dates, to recognise that these Iranian and Western philosophers were thinking at the same time.

That is just one difficulty. There are others, of a different kind. We will see not only that Shiite Islam is almost unknown in the West, but that this unfamiliarity often leads to serious misunderstandings about its nature, and sometimes to reluctance or outright hostility. Our Iranian friends find such reactions especially painful because they cannot understand what has caused them. In this respect, the 1968 conference on Imami Shiism at the University of Strasbourg was a welcome sign that scholarship is beginning to change.[^EII1-5] Shiism amounts to far more than cursing the first three caliphs or following a fifth school of Islamic law alongside the four officially recognised in Sunni Islam. As this volume will try to show, Shiism is a vital home for Islam's inner spiritual teachings.

The very word *esoteric*, which refers to such inner teachings, brings its own misunderstandings. So do *gnosis* and *theosophy*. We must use these words because they are the closest available translations of important Arabic and Persian terms. But I know that many serious readers meet them with suspicion, even irritation. I cannot resolve all the misunderstandings in a few lines. Those who read the whole work will see what I mean. For now, we need to establish how I am using these words.

For a long time, Western movements claiming secret knowledge have made the words *esoteric* and *esotericism* suspect. I would ask readers to return to their basic meanings. The Greek expression *ta exō* refers to what is outward, or *exoteric*; its companion refers to what is inward, or *esoteric*. Could we instead speak of “inwardness” and “thinkers of the inner life”? Those expressions would be accurate in one sense.

But today they might suggest that the inner world exists only as a matter of private feeling or psychology. That is not at all what these thinkers mean.

For them, the inner worlds are spiritual worlds. They have a reality of their own, just as rigorously understood as the reality of the physical world, though different from what we ordinarily call objective reality. The Arabic words *zahir* and *batin* express the same contrast—and connection—as outward and inward, visible and hidden, appearance and what lies behind appearance. The question is how deeply we can enter into reality itself.

Of course, the human condition is such that not everyone can enter the inner meaning in the same way. This is not something accessible simply because a large crowd wants it. In traditional settings, that limit is accepted as part of human nature. Ruzbihan will speak of those who know the inner meaning as “the eyes through which God still looks upon the world.” In that setting, *batin* does not evoke the small, secretive circles that have rightly made some Western forms of supposed esotericism suspect. Still, I would like to repeat a contemporary writer's thought: it does not matter if the chapels are small, provided great saints are honoured there.

The word *gnosis* causes even greater confusion, partly because it is so closely linked with this poorly understood idea of inner knowledge. Scholars increasingly stress that *Gnosticism*, the name given to certain religious systems of the early Christian centuries, does not cover everything that can be called gnosis. We should not expect every form of gnosis to match those early systems. There are Jewish, Christian, Islamic, and Buddhist forms of spiritual knowledge that can all be described in this way.

People who know little about the subject sometimes dismiss gnosis as mythology. They do so because they have no sense of the world that our philosophers will introduce as the *mundus imaginalis*: the imaginal world, a real world of images that is neither the physical world nor mere fantasy. Others treat gnosis as a body of ideas that replaces faith with intellectual argument. But gnosis goes far beyond the familiar opposition between believing and knowing.

Gnosis is knowledge that saves or transforms the person who receives it. It is saving knowledge *because* it is knowledge, and it is knowledge *because* it brings salvation. It becomes real only through a new birth: a spiritual birth. In this sense, the very act of knowing has a sacred character. Gnosis cannot be separated from mystical knowledge, known in Arabic and Persian as *ma'rifat* or *irfan*. We will see this in Shiite gnosis (*irfan-e shi'i*) and in Suhrawardi's philosophy of illumination (*ishraq*).

Seen from this perspective, rejecting gnosis, however devout the motive, risks leading to agnosticism. By *agnostic*, I do not simply mean someone who refuses to profess a particular religion. I mean someone who cuts thought off from being itself and, in doing so, shuts both themselves and others out of the worlds that gnosis opens. Those worlds are first encountered inwardly—in the esoteric dimension of experience. This distinction is essential if we are to understand the thinkers we will meet.

*Theosophy* is another word that arouses suspicion. Once again, I ask readers to consider its original meaning. The Arabic expression *hikmat ilahiya* means exactly what the Greek *theosophia* means: divine wisdom. Such wisdom is concerned not only with the question of what it means for anything to exist, but also with the spiritual worlds opened by gnosis. It does not rely on ordinary sense perception or on reasoning alone. It involves a third activity of the soul: direct inward insight and the experience of spiritual vision, called *kashf* and *moshahadat*.

We cannot dispense with a word for this kind of wisdom, nor can we detach it from philosophy. Suhrawardi himself demands serious philosophical training from students before they attempt to advance any further along the path of divine wisdom.

A few other words need explaining. At times I will argue against *historicism*, the habit of making a thought entirely dependent on the historical period in which it arose. I may even suggest something like “anti-history.” This should not be mistaken for a rejection of historical research. Quite the opposite. A humanity that abandoned history would suffer from a kind of collective loss of memory. That danger may already be growing. Always demanding something “new,” and claiming to care only about what is “new,” can be a sign of forgetfulness so deep that we can no longer see how alive our own past remains. Bringing neglected manuscripts into the light is, after all, genuine historical work. But that is not the issue here.

What I cannot accept, if I am to do justice to these writers, is the narrow idea that a thought can be understood only by placing it at a particular point on a timeline. From that standpoint, a thinker is explained by “the age they lived in,” or reduced to earlier influences. It then seems obvious that their ideas must be out of date now. I have tried instead to understand *lived time*: the time a person actually inhabits through their choices and experience. From a philosopher's point of view, the demand to “belong to one's time” can sound absurd if it means nothing more than living during a particular stretch of calendar time. A date on a calendar cannot tell us what position a thinker takes towards the age around them.

A philosopher must, in a deeper sense, be their own time. That is where their true place in history lies. Mulla Sadra's philosophy of existence helps us understand that a living tradition survives only through decisions made anew, again and again. A tradition understood in this way is the very opposite of a funeral procession. It requires continual rebirth. And this is what I mean by gnosis.

I have therefore been guided by the conviction that the past, and death itself, reside not in things but in souls. Everything depends on the choice we make when we discover an unexpected connection with something handed down to us. We may decide that it is neither dead nor confined to the past. On the contrary, we may sense that *we ourselves are its future*.

This is the exact opposite of thinking that the period we happen to inhabit must define us merely because chronology has placed us there. Once our outlook changes, so does our relation to the past. What once seemed to belong to a finished age can now find its future in us. Only through such a change can we understand what Suhrawardi achieved when he brought the divine wisdom of ancient Persia back to life. What use, then, is the word “irreversible,” so freely applied to the passage of history today? It is we who give life or death to what we inherit. In doing so, we discover that our true contemporaries need not be people who happen to share our dates.

By contrast, the frantic race to keep up with history—and to defeat everything supposedly “outdated”—is a hopeless struggle. We are really fleeing a distorted image of an unrecognised part of ourselves. People often say that philosophy of history is in decline while theology of history is gaining ground. In fact, theology of history is hardly new. Within Islam, Shiite and Ismaili thinkers made an important contribution to it through their philosophy of prophecy.

Unfortunately, some present-day Christian theology seems to be looking for adventures in history precisely because it has lost touch with its *Logos*—the divine meaning or Word at its centre. That really would be something new, and a sign of such deep confusion that it is more urgent, and harder, to overcome than any supposedly outdated past. By seeking salvation in history and trying not to fall behind the direction that others claim history must take, theology begins competing with a secular view that partly grew out of theology itself. In the process, it forgets that its own horizon is the fulfilment of all things, beyond history's end.

Neither a theology nor a philosophy of history is possible without an image of the world as a whole—one that comes before, and reaches beyond, all the separate facts we can observe. Such a vision belongs to a being who is not merely caught inside history but also has a life beyond its limits.

Later, we will return to the Arabic-Persian word *hikayat*. It offers endless possibilities for reflection because it can suggest both *telling a story* and *imitation*, in the sense of the Greek *mimesis*. Every outward story reflects, imitates, or retells an inward story: the story of the soul and the worlds of the Soul. That inward story is not a record of events arranged by date. Rather, it allows us to understand why certain patterns return, and how events can disclose deeper meanings.

If we look only at outward facts, we are left holding an empty shell. Yet many philosophies of history have treated just such a shell as the source of historical causes. By the standards of the thinkers we are studying, this is precisely the misunderstanding I have associated with agnosticism. My task, then, has not been to force Iranian-Islamic philosophy into some outside theory about how history develops. I have tried to understand its inward history, the history it calls *esoteric*.

The same necessity shapes the world in which I have tried to meet these thinkers and, as far as possible, live alongside them. Their true surroundings were the spiritual worlds they knew and explored through metaphysical thought. As for their social environment, we often know perfectly well what they thought of it. Their fundamental attitude was one of *tajrid*: a deliberate withdrawal or separation. To people today who understand human beings mainly as members of a collective, that separation may seem scandalous. But it is a fact of their lives.

It would therefore be a strange contradiction to explain these thinkers by the very things from which they wished to distance themselves—the “alien” world of which the gnostics spoke—or to claim that their thought was produced by what they explicitly rejected. That would confuse philosophy with the sociology of philosophy, as happens all too often. The confusion loses sight of the very thing metaphysics seeks to understand. And it loses sight of it because it quietly assumes that this object does not exist. Once again we encounter the agnostic attitude: without something social to point to, a person imagines there is nothing left but “pure thought,” because they have already separated thought from existence itself. I do not believe that is the best way to understand gnostics.

Such an approach would also quietly erase the boundary between the sacred and the secular—a boundary some theologians today are happy to dismiss as false. But *how* is the boundary to be overcome? One possibility is to make every activity of life sacred, turning the human being into someone whose whole life becomes an act of worship. In Christianity today, Eastern Orthodox spirituality alone has preserved a living sense of that ideal. In Islam, it was expressed through *fotowwat*, spiritual chivalry, to which we will return at the end of the book.

The other possibility is simply to strip the sacred of its sacred character. That is where the present-day “betrayal of the intellectuals,” as it has been called, is leading. The Iranian philosophers and spiritual teachers discussed here took no part in that betrayal.

I will, however, often use the word *phenomenology*. I do not mean to align myself with any particular school of philosophy that uses this name. I take it in the original sense of the Greek expression *sōzein ta phainomena*: “save the appearances,” or preserve what reveals itself. To do so is to encounter something where it actually takes place. In the study of religion, that means meeting a religious experience in the life of the believer, rather than only in critical scholarship or accounts of the surrounding circumstances. We must allow what appeared to the believer to show itself to us. That is the religious reality we are trying to understand.

The believer may be an ordinary person of simple faith or a mystic with the deepest experience of divine wisdom. Mulla Sadra himself said that someone concerned with inner meaning may feel much closer to the ordinary believer than to the theologian who explains everything through reason. The person who understands the inner meaning can preserve the outward meaning (*zahir*) in which the ordinary believer trusts, without dismissing it as mere allegory. From this standpoint, we can distinguish what is *true to the experience as lived* from what is *historically true* by the standards of modern historical criticism.

It is surprisingly difficult to translate *phenomenology* directly into Arabic or Persian if we begin with dictionaries. But what is the method really trying to do? Is it not to preserve what appears by uncovering the hidden meaning and purpose beneath it? This brings us close to the Arabic expression *kashf al-mahjub*, a title found in many works of philosophy and mysticism. It means “unveiling,” or “bringing into the open what was hidden,” and describes exactly the approach we call phenomenology.

We can now see how the relationship between *zahir* and *batin*—the outward and the hidden, the outer form and the inner meaning—is bound up with the phenomenology practised here. Ultimately, this is nothing other than *ta'wil*, the interpretation practised by our Iranian thinkers. The term means “leading something back to its source.”

This approach to inner meaning, this interpretation or *ta'wil*, will focus chiefly on preserving the meaning of two phenomena. The first is what we call the “phenomenon of the Holy Book”: a book brought by a prophet sent by God and speaking on God's behalf. This is something shared by all three branches of the Abrahamic tradition: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. As we follow our Iranian spiritual thinkers in their interpretation of hidden meaning, we begin to see how these traditions might come together. Their only unshakable common ground would be this inner meaning, or *batin*. All those whom the Qur'an calls the *Ahl al-Kitab*, the “People of the Book,” have been given the same problem and the same task by their scriptures.

This shared Abrahamic task of interpretation is entirely different from what is usually, and often wrongly, called “syncretism”—the blending of different religions. Theologians readily use that label to evade a question that unsettles them. Today, this easy dismissal seems to arise from a contempt for religion shared by those who want Christianity to be something other than a religion and those who set metaphysics against religion. Both the contempt and the opposition seem artificial when interpretation holds outer form and inner meaning together as inseparable partners: *zahir* and *batin*, religion in its outward, established form (*shariat*) and the truth discovered through spiritual knowledge (*haqiqat*), the symbol and what it symbolises.

By keeping these two sides in balance—the visible institution and the prophetic Spirit—Shiite and Ismaili thought could glimpse a unity rooted in the inner meaning of religion. Could mystical Byzantium be an image of the heavenly Jerusalem unless it brought together at least all the spiritual seekers among the People of the Book? Readers should therefore not be surprised if we turn more than once to the Russian philosopher Berdyaev.

The second phenomenon will recur throughout these pages, because it embraces almost everything discussed here. We will call it the “phenomenon of the mirror.” In this way of seeing the world, we face an image appearing in a mirror, instead of what we take to be the brute, solid reality of everyday experience—a reality we would violate in order to exploit.

We do not come closer to the image by breaking the mirror. As a way of understanding what is real, this idea finds its fullest expression in the intermediate world known as the *mundus imaginalis*, or imaginal world.

It offers a contrast, even an antidote, to the obsession with “incarnation”—with spirit becoming flesh—that preoccupies so many religious thinkers today. From this obsession to historical materialism is only a short step.

Our Shiite thinkers, however, strictly avoid thinking in terms of “incarnation,” even where their teaching about the Imams faces the same problems as Christian teaching about Christ. Their favoured terms include *mazhar*, a form in which something appears or becomes manifest, and *mazhariya*, the function of making it manifest.

This is certainly “docetism”—a spiritual appearance rather than a physical incarnation. But it goes hand in hand with their “spiritual realism,” which transfigures rather than incarnates. The early Christian phrase *caro spiritualis*—“spiritual flesh”—is the right one here.

This way of seeing is so deeply rooted that we cannot understand certain characteristic forms of Iranian art without knowing the philosophy behind them. A few examples may help. Some time ago, I was struck by the art of cutting a shape out of a material to leave an empty silhouette: a vase, for instance, or a human figure.

At the back of that empty space lies a coloured surface that holds the viewer's attention. It reveals the form freed from matter, without filling the empty space. Reaching a hand into the opening would not mean “touching” the form.

This is something like an “epiphany of beings without bodies”—a way for them to appear. Byzantine art excelled at suggesting this by quite different means. What is suggested is an appearance in the *quarta dimensio*, the fourth dimension: the only one in which the Invisible Ones can appear.

Figures like these, whose forms do not reside in matter because the matter has been removed, can be seen in the music room of the Ali Qapu palace in Isfahan. One technical explanation is that they acted as sound boxes, helping the room resonate.

The legend offers something better: they preserved the vibrations of the music. When the sovereign came to the room alone to sit in quiet reflection, he heard the concert a second time. Perhaps the only trace left by an appearance of the Invisible Ones is an incantation in sound, heard only by the ear of the heart.

The same search is suggested by the central pool in a traditional Iranian garden—a “paradise”—or in a mosque. Think, for example, of the pool in the great courtyard of the royal mosque in Isfahan. Its shimmering water gathers together the reflections of the vast surfaces of blue glazed tile, or *kashi*, that surround it. At night, they give way to a gathering of stars.

Diving into the pool to “touch” the image would be as useless as breaking a mirror. The shining surface is where the image appears—the *mazhar*, or place of manifestation—but the image itself is not there. Compare what we said earlier about *hikayat*: all these ideas belong together.

Consider another example. In Shiite art, both wall paintings and manuscript illustrations show the figures of the Holy Family, especially the five known as the “People of the Cloak”: the Prophet Muhammad, his daughter Fatima, and the first three Imams.

Yet their faces remain veiled. Each person looking at the image is free to experience an inner appearance shaped by their own longing. They might then make their own the words of a visionary account in the *Acts of Peter*: *Talem eum vidi qualem capere potui*—“I saw him as I was able to perceive him.” A vision can never be imprisoned in a fixed object. The shimmering colours of a Persian miniature seem to flow outward, towards the edges and beyond the space of the picture. Even when enlarged to the dimensions of a painting, a miniature remains a miniature.

This may also help answer a question that often comes up in conversations in Iran: why did classical Persian literature not produce novels in the sense in which we use that word? The answer is that one cannot write that kind of novel while seeing the world “in a mirror.” The story that interests the Iranian seeker of spiritual knowledge is a story of initiation, of a person's inward journey. And that interest brought about a crucial development in Iran's spiritual culture: the movement from heroic epic to mystical epic. We will see the beginnings of it in Suhrawardi's work.

These are only passing glimpses, but they suggest how much remains to be said—how much still needs to be allowed to reveal itself. A prologue is not meant to summarise a whole book. Its task is to introduce the themes that explain how the book is arranged. That is what I have tried to do.

The four volumes that make up this work contain seven books. Book I, in Volume I, examines the main aspects of Imami, or Twelver, Shiism. It draws on the teachings handed down from the Imams themselves, while also showing how the great interpreters of the Safavid period, in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, developed those teachings. It explores points of contact between Shiite and Christian ways of reading sacred texts for their inner meaning, and between the problems raised by the spiritual role of the Imams and those raised by Christian teachings about Christ.

Book II, which fills Volume II, is devoted to Suhrawardi's great act of revival in the twelfth century: his philosophy of light. Its connections with medieval Western philosophies of light, such as that of Robert Grosseteste, still call for much more study.

Book III, in Volume III, deals entirely with Ruzbihan Baqli of Shiraz and leads us to questions familiar to the “Faithful of Love,” in Dante's world and before it. Book IV explores some of the highest reaches of Shiite and Sufi metaphysics, especially in the work of Haydar Amoli and Semnani in the fourteenth century.

Book V, in Volume IV, introduces some of the outstanding figures of the School of Isfahan. Book VI examines the meaning of the Shaykhi school, which developed in the nineteenth century. Finally, Book VII is devoted to the Twelfth Imam as the spiritual centre of Shiite devotion, culminating in the ideal of spiritual chivalry (*fotowwat* or *javanmardi*). Here the connections with Western traditions of chivalry, and with the tradition inspired by Joachim of Fiore, will become clear.

I have deliberately pointed out these connections and comparisons again and again. The purpose of this work is to share my conviction that Iran's spiritual culture can no longer be left outside the world's shared cultural life. These pages should make clear what we would lose by continuing to leave it there.

Yet I cannot pretend that the task is easy. To master the texts and find words that make their ideas accessible in Western languages requires a lifetime of work. What I have attempted here is only a small part of what remains to be done.

And to the reader willing to accompany me through all seven books, I will say this: I am inviting you on a series of Iranian pilgrimages that are also pilgrimages of the soul. They demand a great adventure of the spirit—the adventure of all those who, because they loved, were called to build the “House of Seven Pillars.”

*February 1971 — H. C.*

## Note on Transcription

Technical and financial limits have forced us to abandon letters with special pronunciation marks. As a result, the emphatic sounds of the Arabic alphabet—*s*, *t*, *d*, and *z*—are not distinguished here from their ordinary counterparts. For Arabic terms commonly used in Persian, our spellings follow actual Persian pronunciation as closely as possible.

For example, the emphatic Arabic consonants *dad* and *za* are both represented simply by *z*. We use an ordinary apostrophe for both the Arabic letters *ayn* and *hamza*. I apologise to fellow scholars of Eastern languages, though these unavoidable simplifications should cause them little difficulty.

For readers unfamiliar with these languages, a few explanations may help. The letter *h* always represents an audible breath sound. The spelling *ck* corresponds to French *tch*, which sounds like English *ch* in *church*. The letter *j* is pronounced like English *j*. The spelling *kh* represents the sound of German *ch* in *Bach* or the Spanish *j*. A similar sound is used in certain words from the Avesta, the sacred texts of Zoroastrianism. The *s* is always pronounced as a clear, voiceless *s*, as in *see*, rather than *z*. The letter *w*, pronounced in Arabic much as it is in English, is pronounced *v* by Iranians, in Persian and in Arabic loanwords alike.

A circumflex over a vowel marks its full, long form. The letter *û* is pronounced like *oo* in English *moon*. The letters *o* and *e* represent their normal Persian sounds. For words of Iranian origin and names commonly used in Persian, the vowel called *kesra* (originally represented by *i*) is written *e*. In words of Arabic origin, I have kept the usual *i* spelling, even though Persian speakers may pronounce it differently. Thus a form written *hatin* is pronounced approximately *hatene*, as are other words of the same kind.

It is worth remembering that *Imam* ends with an *m*, not an *n*. In Arabic, the word *iman* means “faith” and is an entirely different word. In Arabic, *Imam* is pronounced with a final *m* sound, while in Persian its vowels are pronounced somewhat differently. The title should be capitalised when it refers to one of the Twelve Imams of Shiism, to distinguish these figures from an ordinary leader of prayers at a mosque.

There is no reason to put the Arabic article *al-* before Persian personal names, since Persian has no equivalent article. I therefore write *Suhrawardi*, not *al-Suhrawardi*. The latter is an unnecessary Arabic alteration, rather as the name Descartes was Latinised to *Cartesius*.

Some Arabic nouns end in a form known as *ta marbuta*. When such nouns have entered Persian, I have written them according to their Persian pronunciation and spelling. That way, a term does not need to be respelled whenever we move from an Arabic to a Persian context. Examples are *hikmat*, *nobowwat*, and *walayat*.

Another example is the title for the lord or “Angel of a species.” My form *Rabb al-Nu'*, pronounced in Persian approximately *Rabb on-no*, reflects the Persian form of the Arabic *Rabb al-naw'*. Qur'anic references follow the kind of edition most commonly used in Iran. Verse numbers follow Flügel's edition.

Finally, I have generally written Greek terms in a form that readers can pronounce, since unfortunately more and more readers cannot read the Greek alphabet.

## Outline of Books I and II

The Islamic world is not a single, uniform whole. Islam as a religion cannot be equated with the Arab world as a political or cultural entity. There is an Iranian Islam, just as there is a Turkish, Indian, Indonesian, Malaysian, and other forms of Islam.

Readers who want to learn about the archaeology and art of Iran, before and after the coming of Islam, have a great many books to choose from. But there are far fewer books for someone asking a different question: what ideas, spiritual needs, and ways of seeing the world moved Iranian people to create those works?

From the beginning of Islam, the Iranian world formed a distinct part of the wider Muslim community. Its character and calling can be understood only if we see Iran's spiritual world as a whole, both before and after Islam. Islamic Iran became a particularly rich home for the great philosophers and mystics of Islam. For them, philosophical thinking was never detached from what it should bring about in a person's life. Nor were its effects limited to what we now call the social environment. They extended to the whole spiritual world that a person helps to form through their own being—a world reaching beyond the boundaries of earthly life.

This conviction has guided the author in building the seven-book work presented here. It draws on more than twenty years of research in Iran itself, both in libraries and among close Iranian friends, together with years of teaching in Paris and Tehran.

The approach is chiefly what the author calls *phenomenological*, though it does not belong to any one school of phenomenology. Its purpose is to meet religious experience as it shows itself to the people who have it. That is why the subtitle, *Spiritual and Philosophical Aspects*, matters so much. Every aspect is something seen by someone. But here the observer—the person studying the experience—must become a guest within the spiritual world of those to whom it is revealed, and share with them the responsibility of taking it seriously.

Historical questions must therefore be considered from within that religious world, not by forcing an outside system of categories onto it, whether a theory of historical conflict or anything else. Only then can the connections drawn throughout this work be seen together, as different expressions of one underlying spiritual reality.

The first two volumes contain Books I and II.

Book I introduces essential aspects of Twelver, or Imami, Shiism. It had deep roots in Iran from early times and became the state's official religion in the sixteenth century. The study begins with something the author has called the “phenomenon of the Revealed Book”: the experience of receiving and understanding scripture among the *Ahl al-Kitab*, the “People of the Book.” In the Qur'an, this name refers to the communities associated with divine scriptures; here the author considers Judaism, Christianity, and Islam together.

Across the traditions that look back to Abraham, readers and interpreters of the Bible and Qur'an have faced the same fundamental question: what is the *true meaning* of the sacred Book? For both, that true meaning is the spiritual meaning hidden beneath the literal words. Their efforts to discover it led to similar ways of uncovering the inward meaning of revelation. The existence of a revealed Book gives rise to *hermeneutics*—the art of understanding and interpreting a text. Those who have sought the hidden meanings of the Bible and Qur'an may still have much to teach present-day philosophers, who are so concerned with questions of interpretation.

The technical word for uncovering the Qur'an's inner meaning is *ta'wil*. It means bringing something back to its origin, or to the original pattern from which it comes. Shiite metaphysics centres on two closely connected ideas. One is that God, in God's deepest reality, cannot be known, reached, or even named. The other is that God becomes manifest through a complete company of fourteen beings of light, who appeared on earth as the “Fourteen Immaculate Ones”: the Prophet Muhammad, his daughter Fatima, and the Twelve Imams.

The inner meaning that Shiite *ta'wil* draws from the Qur'an is concerned above all with these fourteen figures. This gives us a distinctively Shiite understanding of prophecy—one that refuses to place the whole future of religious life in the past. In the contrast Corbin draws here, the majority Sunni understanding is that the coming of the final Prophet closed the possibility of any new prophetic message. Shiism, however, keeps the future open. Even after the “Seal of the Prophets,” something is still awaited: the full unveiling of the spiritual meaning of what the great prophets have revealed.

The holy Imams were entrusted with this work of interpretation, and their teachings fill many volumes. Yet spiritual understanding will not be complete until the end of our present age, when the Twelfth Imam—now hidden, and understood as the mystical centre of this world—returns and reveals himself.

This way of reading scripture carries with it a particular understanding of time. History is divided into a period when prophets bring revelation and a period when people are led into its spiritual meaning. Here Shiite teachings about prophecy meet the hopes of the Western movement inspired by Joachim of Fiore, with its announcement of an approaching age of the Spirit.

But this is already more than an ordinary division of historical time. It belongs to a vision of what lies beyond history, because its ultimate fulfilment brings history itself to an end.

Similarly, Shiite teachings about the Imams presented Shiite thinkers with problems much like those Christian thinkers faced when trying to understand Christ. Yet Shiite thinkers generally sought answers along lines that official Christian teaching rejected. Perhaps this is one reason why Shiite gnosis avoided being turned into a purely worldly form of social messianism.

Shiite metaphysics and Shiite spiritual life are inseparable. Because the West has learned so much more about majority Sunni Islam, it has too often assumed that Sufism and the spiritual dimension of Islam are the same thing. In reality, Shiite spirituality extends beyond Sufism. There are certainly Shiite Sufi orders, and many Sufi orders trace their line of teachers back to an Imam.

But someone seeking the inner meaning of Shiism is already, by that very commitment, on the spiritual Path—the *tariqat*—without having to join a Sufi order. At the summit of a mystical Sinai, knowledge of the Imam as one's own spiritual guide leads to self-knowledge.

Volume II, appearing at the same time as this one, contains Book II: *Suhrawardi and the Platonists of Persia*.

Volume III, now in preparation for publication, will contain Book III, *The Faithful of Love*, and Book IV, *Shiism and Sufism*.

Volume IV will contain Book V, *The School of Isfahan*; Book VI, *The Shaykhi School*; and Book VII, *The Twelfth Imam and Spiritual Chivalry*, together with a general index.

# Book One

## Aspects of Twelver Shiism

### Chapter One

#### Shiism and Iran

##### 1. The Difficulties of the Inquiry

Suppose someone asks me to explain a particular point in Plato's theory of Ideas. I can reasonably assume that my listener already knows something about philosophy. I won't have to tell Plato's life story or explain what Greece is, what philosophy is, or what makes Greek philosophy distinct. The same is true of philosophers and subjects that feature regularly in our courses. We have a shared background that makes it easier to talk.

But suppose that same person wants to move beyond the limits of their own culture and asks me what Twelver Shiism is, admitting that they know almost nothing about it. I immediately find myself in a difficult position. I fear I may have to explain one unfamiliar thing by introducing something even less familiar.

I might begin with the word *Shiism* itself. Its French form is a strange mixture: a Greek-derived ending attached to a word of Arabic origin. The Arabic word *shia* comes from a verb associated with following or accompanying someone. It can describe any group of supporters or followers, or a school of thought. One could even speak of the *shia* of Plato, meaning Plato's followers. But when Muslims use the term on its own, it refers to those who see themselves as followers of Islam in its complete and authentic form because they follow the Twelve Imams.

Of course, I would then have to explain what an *Imam* is. The word means “someone who stands in front” or “someone who guides.” In ordinary religious practice, an imam leads the congregation in ritual prayer, and the worshippers follow his movements. In Sunni Islam, the word therefore commonly refers to the person who leads prayers in a mosque. In Shiism, however, *Imam* has a much deeper and more specific meaning. It refers to twelve figures descended from the Prophet Muhammad, beginning with Ali ibn Abi Talib, the husband of the Prophet's daughter Fatima al-Zahra—Fatima “radiant as flowers”—and ending with the Twelfth Imam, who has been known for nearly eleven centuries as the Hidden Imam.

Together, the Twelve Imams form a complete circle of spiritual guides. They are both the treasures of divine revelation and its guardians: the ones who guide us towards its true meaning. Understanding revelation therefore requires an act of interpretation, traditionally called *hermeneutics*, which means discovering and helping others discover the meanings hidden beneath the outward, literal words of a sacred text. These hidden meanings are also called *esoteric*, meaning “inner.”

That would bring me to another idea: *walayat*. It is the special favour and closeness to God that makes the holy Imams God's friends or those nearest to God (*awliya Allah*). I would have to explain why Shiite thought sees *walayat* as the essential partner of prophecy (*nobowwat*).

Indeed, for the Prophet himself, it is understood as the source of his prophetic mission—the inner dimension of prophecy (*batin al-nobowwat*). And I would have to clear up a basic misunderstanding from the start: to be a prophet does not primarily mean to predict the future. It means to speak a word received from God.

But after explaining all that, I would still have to introduce the Islamic understanding of revelation. I would need to explain what the Qur'an means as a holy book revealed from heaven, what the Prophet's mission involved, how it relates to the missions of earlier prophets, and why Shiism believes that prophecy necessarily calls for its complement: the Imamate, or spiritual guidance of the Imams. I would then have to explain why Twelver Shiism understands the line of Imams to be complete with twelve, no more, and how this differs from Seven-Imam Shiism, or Ismailism, whose thought is organised around a recurring pattern of seven Imams.

Finally, I might explain that Twelver Shiism has been Iran's official religion for nearly five centuries, although numerous sources show an Iranian attraction to this form of Islam from the earliest days of Islam's arrival in the country. I might also suggest that the Shiite idea of the Twelfth Imam—the Hidden Imam, the Imam whose return is awaited—has a remarkable affinity with the *Saoshyant*, the saving figure of ancient Zoroastrian Persia. By this point, my kindly listener might be lost in thought or full of doubts. Yet I would still have done little more than outline an answer, and its details would threaten to become overwhelming.

Every reference I make risks being obscure; every explanation calls for another; and the person I am addressing has no familiar point of reference to rely on. Once we leave the debates of the Christian and post-Christian world, the questions raised by religious philosophy seem to come from another planet. Yet the questions raised and lived through in Islam should feel especially close to us. Islam, too, is a prophetic religion centred on a revealed book. Indeed, the term *Qur'an*, “the Book,” means, in this respect, what our word *Bible* means.

Perhaps the real difficulty is that we are afraid these questions might come too close. They could force us to rethink the very terms in which we normally ask our own questions. A meeting free from any wish to defend one religion against another would be immensely fruitful. Unfortunately, post-Christian ideologies have already done so much damage in large areas of Islamic consciousness that such a meeting may still be far away. A pessimist might say that the opportunity has already passed.

I do not believe that it has. Still, if I try to give my listener a brief introduction, I can point to only a handful of books dealing with the theological and philosophical questions I have raised. Such books are rare. There is no shortage of research and scholarship, but much of it does not even begin to address the question that matters to us. What concerns us throughout this book is, above all, Shiite spirituality: Shiism as it is lived by the spiritual person.

To approach it this way, we must accept that spiritual worlds can have a lasting reality, that they continue to question us and invite us to respond. For many Westerners today, this means overcoming an almost automatic impulse to dismiss what cannot be known by ordinary observation. If we do not overcome that impulse, we end up mistaking philosophy for the sociology of philosophy—that is, the study of philosophers as a social group and of the circumstances around their ideas. There is an enormous difference between these two pursuits. Yet many well-meaning conferences miss the essential questions precisely because they fail to see that difference.

I take the view that the spiritual traditions of East and West have a meaning that endures. Their meaning is still taking shape within us. We can make those traditions part of our own present, and it is in this sense that they have a history. Their historical meaning does not consist in confining them to a closed, superseded past or explaining them away through social and political circumstances, whether those circumstances have disappeared or still exist. Everywhere and always, these traditions have sought to free human beings from precisely such limits.

When I speak of *spiritual facts*, I mean real facts. But their reality is not the same as that of outward historical events, because it does not depend on dates. To make a spiritual truth depend on the moment when it was first spoken in the world is an approach generally called *historicism*. It confuses the “time of the soul” with the “time that has fallen into history”—a distinction the thinkers we shall study will help us understand. The West may already have suffered a shipwreck through historicism, dragging more than one traditional civilisation down with it.

These are the difficulties on our side. Would overcoming them make everything easy? Not at all. Entering the spiritual world of Shiism presents difficulties of its own. For a start, one cannot simply turn up, notebook and questionnaire in hand, and begin interrogating people. If you immediately question a Shiite about their religion—even, or especially, someone who knows it thoroughly—you may find that they politely close themselves to every further question. Or they may get rid of the questioner with harmless, fanciful answers.

There are several reasons for this. One might see it as a habit inherited from centuries of persecution, but that explains only part of the situation. The deeper reason is the obligation of *taqiya* or *ketman*: discretion, or the disciplined keeping of spiritual secrets. The holy Imams themselves required this, not simply as a way of protecting oneself, but out of complete respect for teachings held to be sacred. Only those capable of hearing and understanding a truth are entitled to receive it. To do otherwise is to hand a treasure entrusted to you to someone unworthy of it—and so to commit, almost casually, a serious spiritual betrayal.

The result is an extraordinary reserve about religious matters. That reserve begins to ease only when someone becomes convinced that the person speaking with them approaches these matters with genuine sympathy and understanding. I saw this repeatedly when I took part in a Shiite study circle in Tehran, to which I will return later. The shaykh at the heart of the group would not begin to speak until he had recognised and identified everyone present. In Shiite Iran, I believe I came to understand what a living esoteric religion really is.

The same discretion helps explain the general absence of missionary zeal and attempts to win converts in Iranian Shiism. In that very circle, I recently heard a young mullah, about thirty years old, say with deep conviction that Shiism addresses everyone, but that only a spiritual minority can truly accept it, and that its task is to bring such people to light. The Imams themselves, he said, had understood this perfectly. How often I also heard it said: “If the Imam himself has not led you to these things, if the ability to understand them is not already within you, everything people tell you from the outside will fall on deaf ears.” We shall see that the idea of the Imam as an inward guide runs through the whole of Shiite spirituality.

Such an approach, founded on the spirit of initiation, is hardly designed to make scholarly research easy. Shiite literature is immense, in both Arabic and Persian, and includes printed books as well as vast stores of manuscripts. Demanding a complete reading list at the outset is not necessarily the best way to find your way through it. Books reveal themselves gradually: not only through long visits to libraries, whose catalogues are improving considerably, but also through friendly conversations and unexpected encounters. The same may happen with a celebrated pilgrimage site that you somehow never knew existed. Ask why no one told you about a particular book or place earlier, and the answer is almost always the same: only now was the time for you to discover it. Nothing happens by chance.

In short, perhaps even more than with other religious worlds, entering the spirit of Shiism and living within it requires becoming its *spiritual guest*. To be a guest in a spiritual world, however, you must first make room for it inside yourself. You can live in the Shiite spiritual world, and understand what it is like to live there, only if that world also lives within you.[^EII1-6] Without this inner participation, you can speak only from the outside, probably misunderstanding what you describe. No one can give a proper account of a building they have never entered.

The philosophers of illumination who follow Suhrawardi, known as the *Ishraqiyun*, insist that philosophy and spiritual life cannot be separated. In this they give Iranian Islamic thought one of its distinctive features.

But they also challenge the researcher to undertake a long spiritual journey. The guest they welcome cannot be a weekend visitor. They must become a long-term resident, and eventually something like an adopted member of the family, accepting the duties that come with belonging to the household. They may even be the first to recognise and describe a danger that threatens it. If so, they have a responsibility to help their new brothers and sisters face that danger, so that the house can continue to shelter everyone who comes to it for refuge.

It is, of course, an “esoteric” house. I know that the word *esoteric* is often misused in the West, and that Western readers have good reason to find it irritating when it is used to dress up thoroughly ordinary interests or social vanity. Here, though, I use it in a precise sense, to translate Arabic terms such as *batin* and *ghayb*. They describe a spiritual world inaccessible to ordinary sense perception or abstract reasoning. It is the inner, invisible world of the soul, the only world in which souls can truly offer one another hospitality. Spiritual traditions called esoteric bear witness, in their different ways, to the same hidden, inward realities that transcend our everyday world.

These traditions are forms of divine wisdom—what the Greek roots of *theosophia* literally mean. They converge on the goal of the same quest. The home of Wisdom, *Domus Sapientiae*, stands at the summit of the soul, wherever that summit is reached, just as the centre is present wherever one truly reaches the centre.

As the researcher goes deeper, the difficulties encountered on the Shiite side may be resolved through the energy of the search itself, when that search genuinely comes from the heart. I am less certain that the problems awaiting the researcher on the Western side will be so easily settled. Simplified explanations accepted long ago and repeated without question can prevent us from asking the new questions needed to enter this spiritual world. Sometimes it seems there is a strange determination to play down the meaning and importance of Shiite religious experience, as though recognising its spiritual foundations might threaten established academic or religious positions.

The researcher will also have to confront the effects of Western influence on a traditional civilisation—effects suffered first of all by their Shiite friends. There is a mysterious law: “Only the weapon that caused the wound can heal it.” Perhaps, if the West has produced the poison, it can also produce the antidote. But I am not sure it has yet recognised that responsibility. These difficulties deserve a closer look.

##### 2. Understanding a Spiritual World

Religious experience—the perception of a religious reality—is a primary phenomenon (what German thinkers call an *Urphänomen*), like hearing a sound or seeing a colour. A primary experience is not something we explain by reducing it to something else. It is our starting point, something that helps us explain many other things. The weakness of philosophies that call themselves “positive,” and of approaches that hover around philosophy without really practising it, is that they try to derive religion from something else. They explain it through politics, society, ethnicity, economics, geography, or other circumstances, and in doing so miss what is uniquely religious about it.

We can pile up as many circumstances as we like, but they will never produce a particular religious experience unless there is first a consciousness that perceives it, that allows the religious reality to appear to itself. If a religion exists, its most basic reason for existing is that there are people who live and profess it. We achieve nothing by telling them, “You can disappear now. We've explained you.” Religious reality has a way of appearing again, freely and without warning: the Spirit blows where it wills. Its perception does not need to be justified by something outside itself.

The study of how things appear to consciousness, and of what we can know through that experience, is called *phenomenology*. It asks what something means when consciousness encounters it and gives it its place in the world. Yet considerable effort has been spent trying to explain—or rather reconstruct—Shiite religious experience by appealing to the assumptions of our modern Western view of life. Those assumptions may be completely foreign to religion as it is experienced.

I will return to this point. We have too often forgotten the primary fact of religious experience. We have forgotten that human beings shape their world and surroundings in response to their sense, however dim, of where they come from and where their lives are going. Instead, we take the reverse process for granted, assuming that their surroundings produce their deepest spiritual concerns. But it is the original religious experience that can explain those surroundings. How could someone see this, though, if they have lost the very ability to see it?

What we need to see is precisely what these explanations fail to reach. They gather all sorts of information already known from elsewhere and use it to “reconstruct” a religious reality that was there from the beginning. But no analysis could ever give us that reality if a consciousness had not first experienced it. We must try to see what the philosophers and spiritual teachers saw when they raised their questions and debated them.

How can we do that if we are not, in our own way, philosophers and spiritual seekers? What if we have forgotten what philosophical vision means, or surrendered philosophy's enduring right to ask its own questions, whatever the period in which we live? We make precisely that surrender when we mistake philosophy for the sociology of philosophy. Behind it lies a choice, stated openly or simply assumed, not to believe that the object of metaphysical inquiry exists at all. Metaphysics is treated as an illusion belonging to an outdated age. What interests us “scientifically,” so the argument goes, is people's social behaviour and the political circumstances that might explain why humanity spent so long pursuing the supposed illusion of religious and metaphysical truth.

But is it really scientific to explain to people who see something why they see it, when you yourself cannot see what they see? What can you know about the object of their vision if you cannot perceive it? For you, the object is simply nonexistent. How, then, can social circumstances explain that supposed nothing? When such explanations are applied to the intricate details of metaphysical systems—details often unknown to the people who dismiss them in advance—the results can be almost comical. Unfortunately, that does not stop the damage they cause.

In the West, we have tended to turn religious realities into social realities, driven by something like an urge to make them “incarnate” in visible, worldly forms. We prefer to study the historical answers people have given to a problem rather than reach the problem itself. We would rather explain religion as something other than itself than allow it to speak in its own terms. For all these reasons, and more, we have forgotten something basic about Islam: before anything else, it is a religion. Its source is a prophetic inspiration, and its Prophet experienced anew the scriptural revelations that came before his own.

Instead, some have tried to explain Islam in racial terms, identifying it with the Arab people and forgetting both the reach of Islam beyond the Arabic-speaking world and the devotion of non-Arab Muslims. Political ambition alone cannot turn an ethnic identity into the universal calling of a religion. Here and elsewhere, I have tried to clear up this confusion by explaining why we should speak of *Islamic philosophy* rather than *Arab philosophy*.[^EII1-7] This does not diminish the true greatness of the Arab contribution. On the contrary, it allows us to see it in relation to the Arab Prophet, as a prophetic greatness rising far above the limited ambitions of rulers and conquerors. It belongs to the divine realm, not to anything human beings can claim as their possession.

We can then recognise, without hesitation, the many Iranian thinkers who have shaped the history of Islamic philosophy and spirituality—not only in its first centuries, but from the seventeenth century right up to our own day. Its great works are written not just in classical Arabic but also in Persian. What emerges from this Iranian contribution is a spiritual world with a character of its own: Iranian Islam, with its Shiism, its philosophy of illumination (*Ishraq*), and its Sufi traditions.

But if we are serious about respecting religious experience, we must once again refuse an explanation based on ethnicity, as though mysterious “racial genes” somehow produced this spiritual world. Such an explanation would be no more convincing than an attempt to derive the form of Sunni Islam from an Arab “race.” In the end, what would any of this tell us about humanity's spiritual life?

This sort of explanation would leave us within the same fundamental refusal to recognise spiritual realities that I have already criticised. It would remain utterly foreign to the experience it claimed to explain. A simple example may help. In French, it seems perfectly natural to identify one part of Islam by adding a national label. The title of this book speaks of “Iranian Islam,” and I will also use the phrase “Iranian Shiism.” These categories seem obvious to us.

But translated literally into Persian, they would sound awkward, even offensive. Adding a national label in this way can seem to turn something sacred into something merely worldly. Iranian friends have pointed this out to me many times: a literal translation would sound strange and jarring. Perhaps what seems self-evident to us, with our focus on observable and practical categories, is alien to the spirit of these traditions. Are we not at risk of distorting something essential?

Rather than build explanations out of external causes, then, let us attend to spiritual experiences as they present themselves. Let us discover what religious life shows us, and what it can explain. In this case, the first thing we see is the extraordinary, wholehearted devotion of the Iranian soul to the Shiite idea, which it has made its own in a special way.

But when you give yourself entirely to something, it is truer to say that it has taken hold of you than that you possess it. Spiritual reality contains and surrounds us more than we contain it. Once we reverse our ordinary way of looking at the relationship between inner life and the world, the bond between Iran and Shiism takes on a meaning unlike any other—a lasting significance that cannot simply be taken away.

We must therefore try to understand what Iran's philosophers and spiritual teachers committed themselves to. What was the spiritual cause they had already embraced before Islam's prophetic message reached them, and how did that earlier commitment shape their reception and understanding of Islam? Shiism directs philosophical reflection above all towards the reality of the prophetic message. This “prophetic philosophy” includes an understanding of the human being that takes the Prophet and the Twelve Imams as its principal examples. *Ishraq*, the philosophy of illumination, is a new emergence of ancient Persia's philosophy of Light.

As the book unfolds, we shall see that the spiritual character of Islamic Iran is shaped especially by Shiism and Ishraq. Because so little of this world has been properly understood until now, it also shows us how much we still have to learn from Iranian philosophers and spiritual teachers—and what work we may need to undertake today and tomorrow, with them and for them.

I have just spoken of “prophetic philosophy.” It is striking that Persian has words of Iranian origin for both a prophet and the prophetic mission: *vakhshvar*, *vakhshur*, and *payghambor*, alongside the Arabic *nabi* and *rasul*. Such words already have counterparts in the *Avesta*, the sacred book of Zoroastrian Persia. Through Suhrawardi's Ishraq, the prophetic message of ancient Iran becomes part of the same line as the great Semitic prophets. Earlier still, Ismaili spiritual interpretation had placed Zarathustra, or Zoroaster, among the spiritual dignitaries of the age of Moses.

One could argue that this way of linking traditions does not belong to critical history. Yet it is itself a spiritual fact—one that helps explain a great deal. Above all, it illuminates what matters to us here: the Iranian search for the True Prophet and the continuing pursuit of a prophetic philosophy, a recurring form taken by Iranian spiritual consciousness.

When an Iranian teenager studies the country's pre-Islamic past at school, they are not introduced to an age of ignorance, darkness, and “idolatry”—the period known in Arabic as *jahiliya*. They learn instead about the legendary heroes and their deeds in Ferdowsi's *Shahnameh*, the *Book of Kings*. We shall meet some of those figures later in this book, especially in Book Two. The student also learns the name of a prophet: Zarathustra, whom we in the West call Zoroaster, following the Greeks. His name entered Western philosophical writing through figures such as Kleuker, Nietzsche, and G. T. Fechner.

Zarathustra is the earliest name that appears on the horizon of Iran's religious past, whether we place him in the tenth or the seventh century before our era. A prophet is someone who brings a divine revelation to humanity. That is how his own community traditionally understood him. It is also how he was understood within Islam by the school of Illuminationists that followed Suhrawardi. This traditional understanding has a claim to be heard in its own right; newer interpretations based on ethnology do not automatically cancel it.

Yet this book will not be about that remarkable ancient past. In an earlier work, I tried to identify certain enduring features of the Iranian vision of the world, a vision that transforms the very meaning of the earth and its landscapes. From the beginning, Iranian religious thought was guided by its clear vision of the final events that would bring the cosmic struggle to an end—a struggle set in motion by the invasion of the forces of Ahriman, the power of evil. It was the first to formulate, and continued to develop, what we may call a “philosophy of Resurrection.” I shall not return here to those enduring themes that lead “from Zoroastrian Iran to Shiite Iran.”[^EII1-8]

What we must do instead is choose a few passages from the enormous body of *hadith*: traditions preserving what the Shiite Imams taught their closest disciples. These teachings are deeply religious and spiritual, far removed from political claims to power. For reasons that remain mysterious, the Abbasid caliph Ma'mun (died 218 AH / 833 CE), son of Harun al-Rashid, decided to name the Eighth Imam, Ali Reza (died 203 AH / 818 CE), as his successor. This provoked furious protests from hostile members of the Hashimite family, and the Imam himself had to struggle inwardly to accept an appointment he had no power to refuse.

But the Imam died unexpectedly a year later, in circumstances that Corbin does not regard as accidental, and the extraordinary plan came to an end.

As we shall see, even well-intentioned talk of the Imams' political “legitimacy,” as descendants of Ali, turns a spiritual question into a worldly one and misses the point entirely. The closed line of Twelve Imams, whose last member remains invisibly present in this world until the end of our age, is not competing with any political dynasty. They do not even occupy the same field. We might compare them to the secret line of guardians of the Grail in Western traditions. Those guardians do not compete with any earthly royal house or even with the Church's official hierarchy and apostolic succession. They stand beyond them. The Imams, like the guardians of the Grail, belong to another world, one that cannot be reduced to social institutions or events in political history.

A teaching repeated by one Imam after another declares: “Our cause is difficult and demanding. None can bear it except an angel of the highest rank, a prophet sent by God, or a faithful believer whose heart God has tested for faith.”

We shall return to that saying, as we shall to these words of the Sixth Imam, Ja'far al-Sadiq (died 148 AH / 765 CE): “Islam began as a stranger, and it will become a stranger again, just as it was in the beginning. Blessed are the strangers among the community of Muhammad!” These “strangers” are those who leave the crowd behind to follow the Imam in spiritual worship.

Some people hear this challenge and answer yes. Their answer cannot be explained by anything other than who they are. It reflects a choice made at a level deeper than their life in this world, whose ultimate reasons escape our deductions. That assent is the living reality of Shiism. It is also the hidden message of Islam as generations of Iranian spiritual seekers have understood it, and to which they have devoted themselves with passionate faith.

##### 3. Some Prejudices Against Shiism

Why is it, then, that when we draw attention to Shiism and its place in Islamic philosophy and spiritual life, some people whose work and calling are devoted to religion—and especially to Islam—seem surprised, even alarmed, before quickly rejecting the subject? Their first response may be that Shiism is, after all, only a “marginal Islam.” Because they prefer what seems practically effective, they announce their preference for the majority view and those who represent it.

We could answer that anyone who has lived with Shiism in Iran for several years will never have felt they were on the margins of Islam. Quite the opposite: they will have felt themselves at the heart of an intensely living spiritual reality.

But what troubles me most about this rejection is its preference for numerical majorities. It reduces spiritual reality—already so delicate and fragile among people today—to a matter of power and numbers, as though everything had to be justified by statistics. I am inclined to see this as a grave offence against the spirit itself. Sometimes it even leads to systematically negative decisions that, I can say from experience, leave our Iranian Shiite friends deeply hurt and bewildered.

It is as though outsiders had arbitrarily decided to reduce Islam to a religion of law alone: the *sharia*, the religious law and its outward obligations. If you point out that Islam in its fullness depends on two inseparable sides—*sharia*, the law, and *haqiqa*, the inner spiritual truth and reality—you are told that this is no longer Islam.

Yet if there is a division *within* Islam between the *fuqaha*, the scholars of religious law, and the *urafa* or *hukama*, the spiritual sages and thinkers devoted to divine wisdom, someone standing outside Islam has no right to declare that the latter do not belong to it.

Still, the answer comes back, ready-made. If you explain that the *walayat* of the Imams is the inner dimension of prophecy, and that Shiite *irfan*—Shiite spiritual knowledge—is, in a special sense, the inner knowledge of Islam itself, these same critics take fright at the very word *gnosis*, or direct spiritual knowledge. Their idea of what that word means is far removed from the thing itself. They then think they are entitled to push Shiism to the margins.

But in making that sweeping judgment, they would be placing the Twelve Imams, along with the countless witnesses to spiritual truth, outside Islam. We should say plainly what is at stake: spiritual Islam itself would be denied the right to be Islam.

Is that, ultimately, what these critics want? To confine Islam within the boundaries of religious law so tightly that anyone drawn to its spiritual depths has no choice but to leave it?

That would ignore the fact that the *urafa* and *hukama* found the spiritual path they sought precisely *within* Islam, in its inner dimension. This is what Shiism represents for those who follow the teachings of the holy Imams. Inevitably, we must now consider the relationship between Shiism and Sufism. The question will return throughout this book, including in the terms used by thinkers who were both Shiites and Sufis—above all Haydar Amoli, who lived in the eighth Islamic century, the fourteenth century of the common era.

Unfortunately, although Western scholars have studied Sufism quite extensively, and many Westerners know something about it—and people who feel spiritually lost may be drawn to it, sometimes in genuine forms and sometimes in less genuine ones—the same cannot be said of Shiism. Our understanding of Sufism is therefore incomplete and sometimes distorted. This makes it harder to grasp what the relationship between Shiism and Sufism actually involves, or why many Shiites who are themselves deeply mystical have serious reservations about Sufism.

Western readers generally know Sufism through its Sunni setting. As a result, they often see it as the only alternative to a religion built on law. Shiism, meanwhile, is explained as an attachment to the political rights of a particular family, with little thought given to what “political” might mean in different contexts. Even less effort is made to distinguish the spiritual circles around the Imams, in which the specifically religious idea of Shiism took shape—the only aspect that concerns us here—from political activists or agitators who may have used it for their own purposes, as happens with other religious ideas.

Shiism is consequently reduced, almost, to a fifth school of religious law alongside the four recognised in Sunni Islam: the Hanbali, Hanafi, Maliki, and Shafi'i schools. A similar tendency has appeared in attempts at unity within some Sunni circles. The result is a mistaken conclusion: if Shiites object to Sufism, their reasons must be the same as those of Sunni religious authorities. That is how the question gets distorted before the discussion has even begun.

The picture becomes harder still when we find Shiite spiritual thinkers such as Haydar Amoli and Mulla Sadra Shirazi having to defend themselves on two fronts. On one side stands a certain kind of Sufism; on the other, a certain kind of Shiism that is so afraid of Sufism that it retreats into a narrow legalism, forgetting what makes Shiism itself.
