This paradox shows us where the doctrine of the Imams, together with the whole teaching about the primordial Muhammadan Reality, stands in relation to what remains unrevealed. It points to the level before existence itself is revealed—the level the Imam calls “the secret still wrapped in secret.”

The first *maqam* is therefore not yet the place where the prophetic message appears. Rather, it is the source of every prophetic mission, just as the active command is the source that brings its own first effect into being: the first reality to flow from it, the primordial Muhammadan Reality.

**2. The second *maqam*** is the second level of divine wisdom, called “the secret of the secret.” The first *maqam* is the absolute Secret, forever hidden within itself: the completely concealed inner reality. The secret *of* that secret is the act by which the primordial divine Essence reveals itself in the very thing that conceals it. It is hidden in its manifestation and manifest in its hiddenness. This is “a secret upon a secret,” which is why the second *maqam* is also called “the inner meaning of the inner.”

Here we encounter the mystery of the first manifestation of God within the Muhammadan Reality, the complete company of the Fourteen Pure Ones. This is the level of the *ma'ani*: the meanings through which we understand the divine, and through which the divine makes itself known to us. They are, so to speak, our ways of understanding (*modi intelligendi*).

In a conversation with Jabir al-Ju'fi, the Fourth Imam says:

> O Jabir! To fulfil *tawhid* is to know (*ma'rifa*) the God of eternal sovereignty, whom no eyes can see although He sees all eyes. He is the Subtle One, the All-Knowing, the hidden Mystery (*ghayb batin*), as He Himself says. As for the *ma'ani*, it is we [the Imams, the Fourteen Pure Ones] who are His *ma'ani*—the meanings of Him that are revealed to you (*zahiruhu fikum*). He created us from the light of His essence.

Here we should recall the mystery of the heavenly *Anthropos*, the primordial Human Being, familiar from many traditions of spiritual knowledge. In Shiite thought, the Fourteen Pure Ones, united in their deepest being, fulfil the role of this heavenly Human Being: they are the form in which God first becomes manifest. In other words, human beings cannot speak meaningfully of God, and God cannot reveal Himself to human beings, without some form in which the divine can be understood in human terms.

But this takes place “in Heaven,” in a reality beyond the senses. It does **not** require an incarnation in the Christian meaning of the word (see Chapter VII below). We may think here of the visionary traditions surrounding Enoch or the ascent of Isaiah.

This first manifestation “in Heaven” lies at the very foundation of the Shiite understanding of the Imams. It gives that understanding a role comparable to the Christian teaching about Christ as the divine Word, or *Logos*. It also makes *tawhid* possible. Without the teaching about the Imams, a person's attempt to affirm God's oneness would risk becoming a kind of spiritual idolatry: treating an idea of God as though it were God Himself. The teaching protects us from two opposite mistakes.

One is *ta'til*: leaving God so completely beyond our knowledge that nothing meaningful can be said of Him. The Imams prevent that by giving the *ma'ani*, the divine qualities and meanings, a firm place in reality. The other mistake is *tashbih*: treating God as though He resembled created things. The Imams prevent that too, because these qualities are not the divine Essence itself; they always point beyond themselves.

Shaykh Ahmad returns to his example of Zayd. When we speak of Zayd standing or sitting, moving or resting, acting generously, or showing some other quality, we are naming different aspects of him—different meanings through which we can know him. In the same way, when the Imam says, “We are His *ma'ani*,” these meanings are the ways in which God, as revealed to humanity (*Deus revelatus*), appears to us and can be understood by us.

We will return to them in Chapter VII. In relation to the divine Essence, without which they would have no reality, they are that Essence understood “in this or that way.” In relation to the concrete traces they leave behind, they are the names of personal beings who carry these qualities and make them visible. They are their forms of manifestation (*mazahir*).

This is how we should read the many sayings that call the Fourteen Pure Ones the Attributes of God, the Names of God, the Mercy of God, the divine Face that remains when everything else has passed away,[^EII1-160] or the Face of God turned towards the world of human beings. They are the goal (*maqsad*) towards which anyone seeking God turns; the ways God is made known at every level of existence, and in every meaning (*ma'na*) through which human beings conceive of Him. They are the signs revealed “on the horizons and within souls”—in the outer world and in our inner lives (Qur'an 41:53).

In short, the Fourteen Pure Ones are the original spiritual beings (*arwah*) who possess life within themselves and give life to others. They are the holy souls who form the “Fourteen Temples of primordial *tawhid*,”[^EII1-161] all sharing one and the same essence. They are the place from which the calling into existence proceeds, as well as the place from which the prophets receive their mission.

An entire family of symbols points to this mystery: the letter *Nun* at the opening of Qur'an 68:1; the primordial Book; the “keys to the unseen” (*mafatih al-ghayb*); the barren Earth (compare Qur'an 33:27) and the first Water that makes it fertile; the primordial Inkwell from which the Pen—the Intelligence of the universe—draws; and the oil that is “almost ready to shine, even though no fire has touched it” (Qur'an 34:35).

**3. The third *maqam*** is the level of the “thresholds” or “gates” (*abwab*). It is the “secret that only another secret can teach”: the inner meaning of what appears outwardly. Within the primordial Muhammadan Reality (*Haqiqat Muhammadiya*), this is where Intelligence—the Muhammadan *Logos*, the Prophet in his existence before the created world—emerges eternally.

We can express this only through the images already introduced. The primordial Water falls upon barren Earth (32:27), upon a land that has no life yet (35:10). Oil bursts into flame when fire touches it (24:35). The meaning of the creative Word reaches an idea that was still lifeless, and suddenly the earth puts forth perfect growth: the lamp shines, and meaning itself comes alive. All these images lead us to the Name through which heaven and earth receive their light.

For the Neoplatonic Illuminationists, that Name is the Intelligence of the universe (*'aql al-kull*). For Shiite thinkers, it is the Pen, the Muhammadan Intelligence, the Muhammadan Spirit, or the Muhammadan Light (*'aql*, *ruh*, *nur Muhammadi*). These three descriptions correspond to the three forms of a saying attributed to the Prophet: “The first thing God created was my Intelligence,” or “my Spirit,” or “my Light.”

The Merciful One establishes Himself within this first Muhammadan Intelligence. He places within it, and brings forth from it, the unseen realities of all things: the subtle forms of creatures before they appear in the world we know. Intelligence is therefore the Gate (*bab*) through which God's gifts reach created beings. And because created beings receive everything through it and turn back towards God by way of it, Intelligence is also the Gate through which creatures approach God.

This is what the saying of Imam Ja'far means by “a secret that only a secret can teach.” The prophetic Word eternally stands between God and creation as the one that reveals and interprets. Because revelation continually emerges within the primordial Muhammadan Reality, the Imams themselves are “the place of the eternal prophetic message.” At the first *maqam*, they remain enclosed within the mystery of what has never been revealed. Here, by contrast, they are the place where revelation happens: where its light descends and its stars come to rest.

At the second *maqam*, they are the inner meaning of the inner. At the third, they are the inner meaning of the outward: the hidden meaning of what the Muhammadan Word reveals. They guard the law brought by the Prophet. They are at once the keepers of the treasure and the treasure itself, the secret that must be passed on and the secret that alone can pass it on to the beings below them.

**4. The fourth *maqam*** is identified directly with the Imamate. It is the level of the outward meaning (*zahir*).[^EII1-162] This does not mean that the Imamate is merely outward. On the contrary, the eternal Imamate, as understood at the second and third levels, is precisely the secret that hides and remains hidden beneath the outward form of prophetic revelation: the “secret that remains secret.”

The Twelve Imams share a single essence and are “the place of the prophetic message” because the teachings entrusted to God's Messenger are preserved within them. While the outward form of religion governs life, they guard those teachings' hidden meaning.

At this level, then, the Imam is God's guarantor and witness, the one who answers for God before humanity: His Face turned towards the Earth, the eye through which He looks upon human beings. The Imam opens fortified castles and abandoned wells; he offers shelter to those who have been cast out, safety to those who are afraid, and help to believers. He remains God's unseen representative (*caliph*) in this world throughout the Great Occultation, until the present great age—the present *Aeon*—reaches its end.

We can now see, with Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i, that these levels are already summed up in a conversation between the Fourth Imam and Jabir al-Ju'fi, quoted earlier (pp. 121 and following):

> Do you know, Jabir, what *gnosis* is—what it means to possess true spiritual knowledge (*ma'rifa*)? It is: (1) the fulfilment of *tawhid*, affirming God's oneness at the level where we can speak of God only by denying all comparisons; (2) knowledge of the *ma'ani*, the divine qualities and positive meanings that human beings can understand; (3) knowledge of the “Gates” (*abwab*), the thresholds where the prophetic mission of each prophet comes into view; (4) knowledge of the Imam; (5) knowledge of the “Pillars,” the four immortal Living Ones; (6) knowledge of the *Nuqaba*; and (7) knowledge of the *Nujaba*.

We have already seen that the last two groups are the spiritual “chiefs” and “nobles” who form a hidden hierarchy, with the Imam at its centre or pole (*Qutb*). In the present age, when religion's outward form prevails and the Imam is hidden from public sight, these figures too remain concealed.

We must recognise that they exist, but we cannot point them out or identify them by name. Their names belong to the Imam's secret.[^EII1-163] The first three points in the saying correspond, one by one, to the first three *maqams* we have just described. Points four through seven together belong to the fourth.

We have had to compress a great deal into this brief explanation of the four *maqams* described in the two versions of Imam Ja'far's saying. Even so, what we have seen should help us understand his allusions. The prophetic Word appears through a succession of levels, each one a further descent or manifestation (*tanazzulat*) of revelation. At every level, the revelation has a special dwelling place, a secret preserved at its heart: the Imamate of the Twelve Imams, which is the inner meaning of revelation at every stage.

From this idea grow the general Shiite teachings about prophecy and the Imams (see Chapter VI below). It also opens up the many levels of spiritual interpretation discussed earlier: the different depths at which we can discover the outward and inner meanings of the Qur'an. Each level at which the prophetic Word is revealed is also a new manifestation of the eternal Qur'an as it descends from the original pattern of the Book (*Umm al-Kitab*), beginning at the level of “the secret still wrapped in secret.”

##### 2. *The Descent of the Sacred Book Through the Levels of Reality*

How is the eternal divine Word related to the Book that gives that Word a material form in the world we experience (*'alam al-shahada*)? This is one of the central questions facing any philosophy of prophecy that grows out of a religion founded on revelation. Mulla Sadra Shirazi sums up that approach particularly well:

> The Word that comes down from God is Word in one sense and Book in another. Because the Word belongs to the world of the divine Command (*'alam al-amr*), it differs from the Book, which belongs to the world of created things [...].

> Since the Word belongs to the world of the Command, its dwelling place is in people's hearts: “It is in the hearts of believers, and only those who have been given knowledge can perceive it” (Qur'an 29:48), and “only those who know can understand it” (29:42). The Book, by contrast, belongs to the created world (*'alam al-khalq*). Its dwelling place is in written tablets that have a physical form and can be seen by anyone—for example, the tablets of Moses.

> But as for the Word, “none may touch it except the Pure Ones” (56:78). It is a “sublime Qur'an” (56:76), of exalted rank, upon a “secret tablet” (*Tabula secreta*; the Preserved Tablet, *Lawh mahfuz*, 85:22), “which none may touch except the Pure Ones, a revelation from the Lord of the worlds” (56:78–79).

The Book is precisely this revelation from the Lord of the worlds as it *descends* (*tanzil*) into a form accessible to us.[^EII1-164]

The distinction between the world of the divine Command (*'alam al-amr*) and the created world (*'alam al-khalq*) is fundamental to Islamic esoteric thought. Broadly speaking, the world of the Command receives its existence directly and eternally from God's command “Be!” (*Esto*, KN). The created world, by contrast, comes into being through the world of the Command, which stands between it and that first creative act.

We have already seen how Shiite thinkers explain this distinction while avoiding confusion about the unity of being (*wahdat al-wujud*)—the idea that *being* has one and the same meaning wherever it is found. In the account given above, that unity begins only at the second spiritual level, or *maqam*. There we are already dealing with *being brought into existence*. The act that *brings* something into existence—the active divine Command (*amr fi'li*)—remains beyond being itself, beyond the very existence it commands into being. That existence is the *receiving* side of the Command, what Latin philosophers called its *significatio passiva*.

For the Illuminationist philosophers, the world of pure Intelligences is the world of the Command. Our Shiite thinkers agree, but with an important qualification: this is the Command *as received and brought into effect* (*amr maf'uli*). In that sense, the Intelligences are already created beings.

Yet they do not belong to the created world called *'alam al-khalq*. Their creation is eternal; it does not enter ordinary chronological time. Their time is not ours, but the “subtle time” discussed earlier by Qazi Sa'id Qummi. The pure Intelligences receive the eternal Command directly and embody its effect, just as iron placed in fire receives its heat and becomes hot. This is why they can be called the world of the Command, even though they are the Command in its received, or activated, form.[^EII1-165]

Beneath this difficult vocabulary lies a philosophical decision with far-reaching consequences. The world of Intelligence is often called the First Emanation of the Light of Lights.

But we have also seen that, for Shiite spiritual philosophy, the First Emanation is the Light of Lights *itself*. It comes directly from the mystery of the Command—the “secret still wrapped in the secret.” This Light of Lights (*Nur al-anwar*) is the primordial Muhammadan Reality. From it, as the image of the Throne and its four lights suggests, the many levels of spiritual worlds unfold, all the way down to the world we can perceive with our senses.

The way these worlds unfold mirrors the spiritual levels (*maqamat*) described earlier. Each level marks a successive place where the prophetic Word, or *Logos*, appears. As the Word passes from one world to the next, it takes on new forms until it becomes the revealed Book in our visible world. For Shiite thinkers, this process already contains the beginnings of both the teaching about prophecy and the teaching about the Imams. That is because the primordial Muhammadan Reality (*Haqiqat Muhammadiya*) is both what descends and what makes the descent possible.

The Prophet's and the Imams' sayings about hidden meaning all invite us to explore this theme. One famous saying of the Prophet speaks of seven depths of inner meaning; we shall examine a fourteenth-century spiritual writer's treatment of it later (Book IV, Chapter II). Semnani's reading of the “seven prophets of your being” rests on a related insight (see also Book IV, Chapter IV).

To keep our discussion manageable, I shall draw mainly on Sayyed Kazem Reshti's great, unfinished commentary on the Verse of the Throne (*Ayat al-Kursi*, Qur'an 2:256). Its introduction also uses the two-part saying of Imam Ja'far that we examined in the previous section.[^EII1-166]

Shiite esoteric thought seeks the *true meaning* of divine revelations—the hidden meaning within the words. To say what that meaning is, therefore, is also to give some account of how it comes into existence. That brings us back to the successive appearances of the divine Word in different worlds. It also brings us to prophecy and the Imams. The “eternal Imam”—not any individual Imam considered simply as a historical person—holds the secret of the prophetic revelation in every world, because in a profound sense *he is that secret*. This is extremely difficult to put into words.

Yet it is precisely what the idea of the primordial Muhammadan Reality is meant to express.

We should keep one thing firmly in mind. At every level at which we consider this primordial Reality—the complete spiritual company of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones—the Imams exist before earthly history as the “place of the prophetic message.” That, as we saw, is how the *Ziyarat al-jami'a* first greets them. They are the place where the prophetic Word appears.

At the level of the “secret still wrapped in the secret,” they are the “secret of that secret”: the inner meaning of the inner meaning, concealed within the first manifestation of God. At the next level, they are the “hidden secret” within the appearance of the Muhammadan Word: the inner meaning of its outward form. This is the “secret that only a secret can teach.” The meaning is that no one knows the secret of prophetic revelation unless the Imam shares it with them—and the Imam is himself that secret.

Finally, it is the secret concealed within the visible, literal text of the Book as it appears in our world.

This means that the prophetic Word, the “Messenger of God,” appears across a series of worlds arranged in levels. Every new appearance also involves a concealment, as when the first level gives way to the second. What was outwardly visible at one level becomes hidden at the level below it. The secret underlying these appearances therefore has a distinct way of existing at each level.

From the very beginning, every appearance of the Prophet is inseparable from the Imam and the Imam's secret. Muhammad himself is reported to have said of Ali—that is, of the Imam—“He was sent secretly with every prophet, but with me he was sent openly.” This is why one branch of Shiite interpretation asks how the Imams exist at the different levels where the prophetic Word appears, in worlds that precede our material world. There the Word is still pure speech, before it becomes the Book and takes on the Book's outward, written form. This is also among the hardest questions in Shiite spiritual philosophy, and its thinkers usually address it with great reserve.

What are these different worlds? And how are they represented through the successive levels of the primordial Muhammadan Reality? The answer comes in symbols, especially the image of the Throne (*'arsh*) in Shiite accounts of creation. Philosophers speak of four fundamental realities: Intelligence (*'aql*), Spirit (*ruh*), Soul (*nafs*), and Nature (*tabi'at*). Here all four belong to the primordial Muhammadan Reality, the first being brought into existence and the Light of Lights.[^EII1-167] Four archangels, or four Lights, shine out from this Light of Lights. Each becomes the source of an entire world, which in turn contains other worlds.

The *Intelligence* of the Muhammadan Reality is the source of every intelligence. Its symbol is **white light**, the upper pillar on the right side of the Throne, and it is called the “Spirit proceeding from the divine Command.” Its *Spirit* is the source of all spirits, represented by **yellow light**, the lower pillar on the right. Its *Soul* is the source of all souls, represented by **green light**, the upper pillar on the left. Its *Nature* is the source of all natures, represented by **red light**, the lower pillar on the left.[^EII1-168]

The worlds are thus arranged in five levels:

1. **The world of Divinity (*lahut*)**, or the “world of secrets” (*'alam al-asrar*): the Unrevealed, the realm of the active divine Command (*amr fi'li*).
2. **The world of Lights**, or pure Intelligences (*'alam al-anwar*): the world of *jabarut*, represented by white light.
3. **The world of Spirits** (*'alam al-arwah*): the higher *malakut*, represented by yellow light.
4. **The world of Souls**: the lower *malakut*, represented by green light. The imaginal world (*'alam al-mithal*, *mundus imaginalis*) is the world of Images belonging to the whole *malakut*.
5. **The world of material bodies**, or Nature, represented by red light.

The four lights that first shine from the Light of Lights—the primordial Muhammadan Reality—are also the archangels who did not have to bow before Adam (see Qur'an 2:32). They did not bow because they *were* the lights before which the other angels bowed when they bowed before Adam. Some texts also speak of fourteen higher archangelic lights shining from the Light of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. These, too, did not bow to Adam: together they formed the luminous being of the heavenly Human. Earlier (p. 55), we suggested a possible comparison with the fourteen Aeons of light mentioned in certain Coptic Gnostic texts.[^EII1-169]

What does this image of the Throne mean for a living person? In Shiite spirituality, the faithful believer, one who follows the path fully (*mu'min*), has a spiritual being made up of rays from the Throne's four lights. Every individual existence receives the very act of *existing* from the reality symbolized by white light; its distinct *identity* from yellow; its *particular form and measure* from green; and its *original matter* from red.[^EII1-170][^EII1-171]

A saying expresses this mystery of the Muhammadan Reality as the source of all realities and essences: “I am the Essence of essences (*dhat al-dhawat*). I am the Essence of everything that has an essence” (of all the ways Essence takes form, *al-dhawat li'l-dhat*). This is also what Shiite thinkers such as Mulla Sadra explain when commenting on the Throne.

Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i sums up the overall structure of existence in this way. The first existence, brought directly into being by the divine Command and receiving that Command within itself (*amr maf'uli*), is the primordial body of the Light of Lights. It is one Light with fourteen flames: the “fourteen temples of God's oneness” (*tawhid*). Together they form one primordial essence.[^EII1-172] From it radiates the light of the cherubic Intelligences, the “Angels of the Veil,” and the light from which the prophets were created. The beings of faithful believers were in turn created from the light radiating from the prophets, and so on down to the earth itself.

He writes: “Nothing is created from an essence lower than itself. Every lower reality is created from the light radiating from a higher reality. A higher reality is, for example, the sun itself; a lower reality is the sunlight that falls upon the surface of the earth. Every reality possesses its true nature (*haqiqat*) at its own level and in relation to what stands below it. But in relation to what stands above it, it is a symbol and image (*majaz*), something brought into effect.”[^EII1-173]

Here two ways of understanding the Book come together: the Book of the World (*Liber mundi*), the cosmic Qur'an, and the Book of Revelation (*Liber revelatus*). At the same time, the whole complex practice of *ta'wil*—reading symbols to discover their inner meaning—becomes rooted in the very process by which things come into existence.

For in each of the worlds described above, worlds that can only be indicated by symbols (and here we should be quite clear about the difference between a symbol and an allegory), the prophetic Word passes through another stage of its descent. The Word gradually takes on a more definite form until it becomes the written Book. These are the successive ways in which the eternal Qur'an appears as it passes from world to world.

At the level of *lahut*, the realm of Divinity and the Unrevealed, the “world of secrets” (*'alam al-asrar*), there is not yet any Word (*kalam*), any Name, or any description. This is the first spiritual level described earlier as the “secret still wrapped in the secret.” Shiite interpretation connects it with this verse: “You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was.

“Yet We made it a light by which We guide whom We please” (42:52). It is the unfathomable depth from which the command that brings being into existence arises eternally. The being called forth by this Command is the Muhammadan Reality itself. Its Intelligence, the primordial Intelligence, is the prophetic Word: the Prophet's Word existing before time. Hence the saying, “The first thing God created was my Intelligence.”

This Word is both God's knowledge of creation and God's knowledge of himself in that Word.[^EII1-174] That knowledge is the eternal original of the Book (*Umm al-Kitab*): the Qur'an in all its appearances, levels, descents, and meanings. “We communicated to you a Spirit proceeding from Our Command. You did not know what the Book was...” (42:52). The same idea is expressed in another way: “The Qur'an is a secret sign (*ramz*), a message in code, between the Friend and the Beloved. No one but those two knows the true reality (*haqiqat*) of what it says.”[^EII1-175]

Divine revelation through the prophetic Word therefore begins below the level of the “secret forever wrapped in the secret,” in the *world of Lights* radiating from the Muhammadan Reality. This world of Lights, or pure Intelligences, is the first world to which the Prophet, in his existence before time, is sent on his mission. It marks his first “descent.” In keeping with the symbolism just described, the Qur'an is **white light** in this world, shining like the “White Pearl.”

As the act of creation moves from one world to the next, the prophetic Word is sent to the inhabitants of each higher world in turn, to announce the message to them. The eternal Qur'an “descends” (*tanazzul*) with him: to the world of Spirits, where it is **yellow light**; to the world of Souls, where it is **green light**, like an emerald, and where the covenant with earthly humanity takes place in the sacred history before time (Qur'an 7:171);[^EII1-176] and finally to the world of bodies, where it is **red light**.

One basic law governs these successive manifestations. As the Word descends from one world to the next, what was openly visible—the outward meaning (*zahir*)—to the beings of the higher world becomes hidden, the inner meaning (*batin*), for those of the world immediately below. At every step, a new covering or veil, symbolized by that world's colour, encloses the one before it. What was directly visible to the beings of the higher world is now a “hidden secret” in the next.

Prophetic revelation as we know it on earth—with its outward and inner meanings, and with prophecy and the Imams as its two inseparable sides—has had this same structure from the very beginning of the worlds through which it passes. We know, too, that the inner meaning of prophetic revelation in every world is the inner reality of the primordial Muhammadan Reality: the complete spiritual company of the Twelve Imams, the “place of the prophetic message.”[^EII1-177]

The beings of the world of Lights have their own powers of perception and understanding (*masha'ir*), formed from the light overflowing from the Muhammadan Reality.

Yet even they do not understand the Qur'an as the Prophet-Word understands it at that level beyond time. Likewise, what the beings of the world of Souls understand as a hidden meaning is only an outward covering, a *husk* (*qishr*), compared with what the beings of the world of Spirits know.

What is hidden knowledge in the world of Spirits is still only a husk beside what the pure Intelligences of the world of Lights know. And even those Intelligences grasp no more than a husk compared with the knowledge of the Prophet-Word.

So the hidden meaning reached by the beings of the world of Souls is only a “husk of a husk” beside the Prophet-Word's knowledge of the original Qur'an, the Muhammadan Reality itself. At the lowest level, those in our world who read only the literal words reach merely the outer husk of what readers seeking the inner meaning can perceive. This is why, for these thinkers, the *haqiqat* discovered through inner interpretation is not an *allegorical* truth. It is a spiritual truth that is *literally real at its own level*: spiritual because it belongs to a higher world, and literal because it matches the way things exist and are perceived in that world.

When sayings speak of an inner meaning known only to prophets and Imams, they mean the innermost meaning in its absolute reality. What counts as hidden for us on earth is still outward and visible to beings above us. But the absolute inner meaning, which is not and can never become an outward meaning, belongs to the Fourteen Immaculate Ones alone.

When this descent of the Qur'an reaches our earthly world, the world of things perceived by the senses, it begins the *cycle of prophecy*. That cycle starts with Adam and continues from prophet to prophet until the Muhammadan Light appears in full in the “Seal of the Prophets,” the last prophet to bring a divine law. Each earlier prophet had been a partial appearance of that Light. With Muhammad's revelation, the cycle of prophecy closes and the *cycle of walayat*—the spiritual guardianship of the Imams—begins (see Chapter VI). It starts with the First Imam and will end with the return of the Twelfth Imam, bringing our age to its close (see Book VII).

As we have just seen, the way the Word passes from one world to another requires the presence of the Imams on earth once the Word has become a Book. Imam and Book belong together. A saying often repeated in Shiite circles puts it neatly: “The Qur'an is the silent Imam. The Imam is the speaking Qur'an.” At the end of its descent, the Word has become a Book made of written words, accounts, and stories—*hikayat*.

As we noted earlier, this Arabic term suggests something important: the events of a story told on earth do not contain their full meaning in themselves. They *resemble*, or correspond to, events that have taken place or are still taking place in higher worlds, and those higher events give them meaning. This is what I mean by *sacred history*—a history whose meaning lies beyond ordinary earthly events.[^EII1-178]

To understand it is to practise *ta'wil*. Revelation has completed its descent (*tanzil*); now we must lead the Book back to its source, its original form. The whole movement has two arcs: an *arc of descent* (*nuzul*, *tanzil*), representing the prophetic mission that brings revelation down, and an *arc of return* (*su'ud*), the arc of the Imams, which carries out *ta'wil* by retracing the path of descent in the opposite direction.

This vision of existence helps us understand statements by these writers that would otherwise be puzzling. They say that the books revealed to earlier prophets—the Torah, Psalms, and Gospel—are all versions of the Qur'an, different states in which it appears; the Qur'an is their secret, their living core, and their deepest meaning is contained within it. That is why the Imam of the Resurrection (*Qa'im al-Qiyamat*) will reveal the secret of every divine revelation through complete *ta'wil*.

They also say that the Qur'an contains knowledge of the “world of Mysteries” beyond the senses: events that took place in other worlds or will take place in ours; teachings that reached us and teachings that did not; truths kept hidden among the prophets, the Near Angels, the Cherubim, and the highest angels;[^EII1-179] and all the intimate prayers and psalms (*munajat*) spoken by a prophet, an Imam, or an angel.

Looking out over this immense horizon, Sayyed Kazem Reshti writes:

> My brother, read the Qur'an, and never abandon it. It is more precious to you than anything else. If you persevere, you will see the secret of what I have just said. When you understand these things, you will have gained a certain measure of knowledge of the Qur'an.

> But you will also understand that you cannot read it as it truly is. That is beyond us, whether as Muslims (*muslimin*) or as believers (*mu'minin*). Only the prophets and the Imams can read it in that way [...].
>
> Do not let the little understanding you possess mislead you into claiming that you know the Qur'an. So do not turn against someone who makes a claim and supports it from the Qur'an in a way different from your own understanding, provided you find nothing in that person's reading that is ruled out or contradicted by the sayings of the Imams and the agreement of the true School, the Imami tradition [...].
>
> Once you understand that the Qur'an's true meaning, its spiritual reality (*haqiqat*), is a coded message (*ramz*) understood only by God Most High, the Prophet, and the members of his Household—the Twelve Imams—and that the members of that Household share it with those who make their home among them, you will understand something else. We hear the Qur'an from the Prophet in many worlds, and at last we understand, as far as we are able, what has filtered through to this world. These many worlds differ in their subtlety and obscurity, their height and density, their freedom from matter and their materiality.

> We must therefore recognize that our understanding varies with the different powers by which we understand.[^EII1-180]

Starting from the lowest level of manifestation, where the Qur'an appears as a Book, we can trace these different depths. When we understand it only after its descent to the world of bodies, symbolized by red light, and perceive no more than its outermost husk, we are dealing with its *outward meaning* (*zahir*).

What we understand of it in the *imaginal world* (*mundus imaginalis*)—the world of the “emerald cities,” Jabalqa, Jabarsa, and Hurqalya, the world of Images within the *malakut*—is called its *inner meaning* (*batin*). What we understand in the *malakut*, the world of Souls symbolized by green light, is the *inner meaning of the inner meaning* (*batin al-batin*). In the world of Spirits, represented by yellow light, we reach the *inner meaning of the inner meaning of the inner meaning*. And in the world of pure Lights, represented by white light, we reach a fourth depth of inner meaning.

Divine mercy comes closer to us as it lifts us to higher knowledge. In the words of a sacred saying (*hadith qudsi*), “My love has no limit and no end.”

Yet our author reminds us that everything we can understand is still only an outward meaning, a husk, compared with the first spiritual realities from which our own existence proceeds. In other words, even what we perceive as the deepest inner meaning is outward and visible compared with the being and understanding of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. Our intelligence—the subtlest part of ourselves—is to their being what a body is to a spirit.

If our own speech can be expressed on the levels of Intelligence, Spirit, Soul, Image, and body, we can begin to imagine what a different order of speech belongs to *them* at each level or “dwelling place” through which they appear as they descend from world to world.

This is simply the same law of manifestation applied to ourselves. As we have seen, what is outwardly manifest at a higher level becomes hidden at the level below, as though successive veils were being added. Or we may think of existence becoming increasingly receptive to, and dependent upon, the Command that brings it into being, until that Command makes it a being in this world—and makes the Word a Book. The levels at which we interpret the revealed Book match the levels at which being itself is revealed, as the cosmic Qur'an, from the first Command.

The two-part saying of the Sixth Imam quoted at the beginning of this chapter can therefore be understood in both directions. Earlier we explained it by tracing the *descent* of the primordial Muhammadan Reality.

We can now understand it through the hierarchy of worlds and the corresponding levels of Qur'anic interpretation, following the *return* upwards, in the opposite direction. In the descending order, the inner meaning is first the “secret still wrapped in the secret,” compared with what appears in the world of pure Lights. It is next the “secret beyond a secret”: the secret of the first manifestation of God as the Muhammadan Reality, which encloses the secret of the Unrevealed, compared with what appears in the world of Spirits. It is then the secret hidden beneath the outward appearance in the imaginal world, “the secret that only a secret can teach,” for the world of Souls.

Finally, it is the secret concealed beneath the outward forms perceived by human beings in the earthly world. These are the four spiritual levels (*maqamat*) described earlier.

Knowing the Qur'an, in this sense, means coming to know the secret of God's oneness (*tawhid*) as it appears through the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. It is an immense and demanding undertaking. This is why the Imams repeatedly said: “Our cause is difficult and demands great effort. Only an Angel brought close to God, a prophet sent with a mission (*nabi mursal*), or a believer whose heart God has tested in faith can bear it.”

##### 3. Reading the Qur'an for Its Hidden Meaning

We cannot go into every method used in this highest form of interpretation. Let us recall the distinction between two terms. By *hermeneutics* I mean the way understanding works: how someone understands something according to their own way of existing, and how they can make that understanding clear to someone else. *Exegesis* refers more specifically to the detailed work of explaining a text—the practical methods through which interpretation is carried out. The treatises that discuss these questions systematically are extremely complex. They offer several overlapping arrangements of levels of meaning. One day these should be compared with the methods of Jewish Kabbalah and Christian esoteric thinkers.[^EII1-181]

In general, the distinction between outward meaning (*zahir*) and inner meaning (*batin*) corresponds to the distinction between *tafsir* and *ta'wil*. *Tafsir* explains the Qur'an as its words appear in their direct, literal sense. It follows the rules of Arabic grammar, uses the meanings recorded in dictionaries, and allows figurative meanings when the passage requires them. It draws on history, law, language, and poetry to resolve difficulties in the written text.

Great works of *tafsir* have been produced in classical Arabic and Persian by commentators known as *mufassirun*. Those who seek the inner meaning have never denied the value of this work at the level where it belongs: the level of understanding the text as it appears to ordinary reading. Unfortunately, we cannot say that every commentator has shown the same openness towards the possibility of another way of reading. There is no need to reopen that argument here.

We have already noted that *ta'wil* means literally to *bring something back to its origin*, to its original pattern or source (*asl*). For example, it leads each *hikayat*, each story, back to the event beyond ordinary history that it reflects and expresses in historical form. In its broadest sense, *ta'wil* can describe every form and level of interpretation that seeks an inner meaning, including all the successive depths of *batin* we have just described.

But the practice varies considerably. The differences depend on what a thinker believes about being and the beings that exist, and therefore on what that thinker understands *revelation* to mean. Averroes does not practise *ta'wil* in the same way as the Ismailis, Twelver Shiites, Illuminationist philosophers, or Sufis such as Ruzbihan. These different approaches need not contradict each other. Their levels of interpretation are not opposing sides in a contest.[^EII1-182]

Sometimes *tafsir* itself is used in such a broad sense that it includes *ta'wil*. For example, Mulla Sadra Shirazi's monumental work is called a *Tafsir*, although it is really an exercise in *ta'wil*. The reverse also happens. As Sayyed Kazem points out, *ta'wil* can have a narrower meaning than the one just described. In that case it names a kind of interpretation lying between the outward meaning (*zahir*) and the higher levels of inner meaning (*batin*).

Used in this narrower sense, *ta'wil* connects the Qur'anic text either with the *small world within us*—the human being understood as a miniature universe, where Qur'anic teachings illuminate our inner life, as in Semnani's interpretation discussed later—or with the alchemical process and all its spiritual implications. The latter concerns the *intermediate human being* (*al-insan al-awsat*), between the natural person and the Perfect Human, or what Arabic writers call *al-mawlud al-falsafi*, the being the Latin alchemists called the *Filius philosophorum*, the “child of the philosophers.” Here *ta'wil* brings the Qur'an to life at the level of earthly human existence and the changes a person undergoes inwardly.

Going beyond this, into the higher levels belonging to worlds beyond the senses—the spiritual stages described earlier, and the ways the Fourteen Immaculate Ones or the Muhammadan Reality exist at different levels of manifestation—is called *tafhīm batini*, a higher form of inner interpretation.[^EII1-183][^EII1-184][^EII1-185]

Has anyone actually carried out this kind of interpretation systematically for the entire Qur'an? As far as I know, not completely. Many scholars have attempted it, however, and some have achieved part of the task. A complete treatment would exceed the strength and lifespan of one person. It would take a team of scholars, or several lifetimes of work, and the result would fill several library shelves.[^EII1-186] Its starting point must remain the sayings and teachings (*hadith*) of the Shiite Imams, who themselves set out the principles behind the Qur'an's many levels of meaning.

We should not be surprised that Twelver Shiites, who often had to keep their beliefs and activities hidden during Islam's early centuries, were already fully occupied with preserving as many of the Imams' teachings as they could.[^EII1-187] Only later could scholars begin to organize those teachings into a larger system.

Today we have substantial commentaries called *tafsir*—though many are really works of *ta'wil*—that collect, beside each Qur'anic verse, the sayings in which an Imam explains or refers to that verse. Some have been published; other major works remain unfinished or unpublished. The Shaykhi school has produced exemplary commentaries on several chapters of the Qur'an.[^EII1-188]

Ismaili thinkers, for their part, have generally preferred to weave their interpretations into large works that set out a complete system of thought.[^EII1-189] Nor could we study this subject properly without the commentaries of Sufi spiritual thinkers such as Ruzbihan—who draws on earlier Sufi commentaries—Ibn Arabi, and Semnani. Their approaches often meet or overlap. Taken together, these works open up the wide horizons of spiritual interpretation that we discussed earlier (Chapter IV).

For Shiite spiritual thinkers, reading the Qur'an alongside the teachings given by the Imams to their close companions and disciples is the central practice of meditation. This is why a Western reader who knows the Qur'an only through a grammatically accurate, literal translation into a European language cannot begin to imagine everything that a spiritually trained Muslim reader finds there. Such a reader cannot fully understand Sayyed Kazem Reshti's appeal quoted above (p. 209), or the many similar appeals. In the West we have never had the opportunity to read the Qur'an as these sages (*hukama*) and seekers of spiritual knowledge (*'urafa*) read it. A translation that tried to communicate their experience would require immense labour and would become a very large work indeed.

Someone will object that what we need instead is sound, evidence-based historical criticism. That is a legitimate approach, and we have already discussed it.

But our concern here is with a fact of spiritual life that cannot be denied: the way leading Muslim spiritual thinkers have read and lived by the sacred Book for almost fourteen centuries. Spiritual experience does not make historical criticism unnecessary. Equally, however, historical criticism cannot erase the fact that people have had those experiences. If Shiite believers receive a saying as coming from an Imam, to understand that saying is to understand *how it comes from the Imam for those believers*. That is the question that the study of religious experience must ask, because only then can it encounter the experience as it is lived.

Historical criticism may begin by arguing, on its own grounds, that a particular text cannot genuinely come from the Imam. It has every right to do so within its own method.

But if it starts there, it can never reach the spiritual fact we are trying to understand: it has already set aside the relation to the Imam that gives the text its meaning for the believer. It is precisely that spiritual reality that we want to grasp when we study Shiite ways of reading the Qur'an.

We would therefore be mistaken to decide in advance that *ta'wil*, the search for hidden meaning, is nothing but a made-up technique or a flight of fancy. Literal interpretation is not the only approach that demands care and discipline. Discipline does not rule out inspiration: there can be *inspired rigour* and *rigorous inspiration*. As Sayyed Kazem Reshti writes:

> God allows these levels and degrees of understanding (*maqamat*) to be explained only on condition that they remain secret within hearts, wrapped in the veils of mysteries. For created beings must first pass through the second ascent and then through the stage of coagulation.[^EII1-190] The stages we are speaking about lie beyond these: the stage of union through fusion, and the vision of things through the secret of the heart, through awareness beyond ordinary consciousness.

> Where are the Pleiades, that a human hand could reach them? If we tried to explain these stages using the language of people who accept only the visible evidence of material worlds, we would never even reach the questions involved. For here we are dealing with the secret that only a secret can teach—the very words of the saying quoted earlier (p. 189).[^EII1-191]

As long as we confuse a symbol with an allegory, and assume that the realities in question could simply be known in some other way, we shall miss the point. The four lights of the Throne are not an allegory. They are a *ramz*: a sign in code that we can go on deciphering without ever reaching the end. It both reveals and conceals a truth that the human mind can receive only in symbolic form. People who regard spiritual worlds as nothing but abstractions will reject that truth.

Yet, in the language of this tradition, only prophets can restore sight to hearts that are blind.

It is understandable that scholars interpreting ancient texts should be fascinated by the remarkable archaeological discoveries of our day, discoveries that no one could have expected a generation ago.

But there is no conflict between archaeology and the interpretation of hidden spiritual meanings. Nor does the first make the second unnecessary. They ask different questions because they work at different levels of understanding: their *maqam*, or standpoint, is different. A document that provides decisive evidence for a historian may be, for a believer seeking inner meaning, another coded sign still waiting to be understood.

What the study of spiritual meaning is looking for cannot be reached simply by going ever farther back in time—not even into the immense timescales used by prehistory and the study of ancient life. Events from the earliest stages of earthly history are not, simply for that reason, events *beyond history*. Such events do not belong to the past tense of our ordinary speech. They unfold in worlds that can be approached only through the “secret of the heart.” This journey reaches towards the deepest horizon, where the secret of God's oneness (*tawhid*) appears as the secret of being itself: being eternally brought forth by its own Command, the “Be!” (*Esto*, KN) through which existence first appears in the First Being, the Light of Lights, shining in the fourteen radiant forms of the Immaculate Ones.

Human intelligence can reach only this Manifestation, where being has already been brought into existence as *something that exists*. The solitary divine source that commands being into existence remains beyond the existence it creates.

We can approach that source only through the manifestation that is its very Command, where being receives within itself the act that brings it into existence (*amr maf'uli*). This is the secret of the Imam expressed in the two-part saying quoted at the start of this chapter (p. 188).

The Twelve Imams, united in their essence as the “place of the prophetic message,” form, in their complete existence beyond time, the point where the active Command and the Command received coincide: the transcendent “Be!” (*KN*) and being (*wujud*) as it is present in an existing thing (*mawjud*). Shiite spirituality therefore teaches that without the Imam a human being could not truly affirm God's oneness (*tawhid*). The attempt would either lose God in empty abstraction (*ta'til*) or dissolve the difference between God and creation in the intoxication of likening them to one another (*tashbih*), perhaps going so far as to speak as God in the first person: *Ana'l-Haqq*—“I am God!”

The Imam is both the farthest horizon of the first divine manifestation and the form through which God becomes personally known: an inner companion, an unseen personal guide. We shall try to explain this more fully in Chapter VII.

The primordial Muhammadan Reality appears level by level as a descent of both the “Book of Being” and the “revealed Holy Book.” In that descent, the Word becomes a Book. When it reaches our earthly world, the cycle of prophecy begins with Adam and continues until the appearance of the one called the “Seal of Prophecy.” The end of the prophetic cycle is also the beginning of the cycle of *walayat*, spiritual guardianship, which will last until the return of the Imam who is now hidden. These brief reflections on being and on the primordial Muhammadan Reality—the complete spiritual company of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones—are therefore a necessary introduction to understanding Shiite teachings about the prophets and the Imams.

### CHAPTER VI

#### Prophecy and the Imams

##### I. Why Prophets Are Necessary—and Why Imams Are Necessary

We may now be in a better position to explore the Shiite teaching about prophets and Imams in detail, and to fill out the brief outline given earlier in Chapter II. So far, we have considered these matters in their full reality: in their *polar* dimension, where they have an unchanging source at the summit of the world of *jabarut*, the spiritual realm of divine power, and where everything exists together in an eternal present.

Now we must consider how these same realities appear one after another in the earthly world. To borrow the language of Qazi Sa'id Qummi, we are moving from the order of “subtle time” to that of “opaque time.”

We saw earlier, in broad terms, that the Shiite understanding of the Imams tries to answer a particular question: what does it mean, and what follows from it, to say that there will be no more prophets? We can understand the Shiite answer only if we first explore what prophecy itself means.

What makes someone a prophet? What kind of spiritual life and knowledge does a prophet possess? There are several possible answers, corresponding to different kinds of prophets. And those differences will reveal something important: prophecy is a wider calling than the particular mission of bringing a new religious law. A prophet—a *nabi*—is not necessarily, in the strict sense, a messenger sent with such a mission (a *nabi mursal*, or, in the fullest sense, a *rasul*).

Shiite teaching places *walayat* at the source of the prophetic calling, known as *nubuwwat*. The Persian word for *walayat* is *dusti*, friendship. We have already encountered the term. It refers especially to the divine love and friendship granted to the Twelve Imams from before the beginning of time. This gift makes them the “Friends of God,” or the “Beloved of God” (*awliya Allah*).

But *walayat* is not only the source of the prophetic mission. It also describes the spiritual state underlying prophecy in its broader sense, beyond the special mission of prophets who bring a new law.

A prophet who brings a law has an additional gift: he is sent by God to reveal a Book and a new sacred law (*sharia*). That law-giving mission belongs to a particular period of history. *Walayat*, by contrast, is eternal. It is what underlies the spiritual state of prophets as such.

Yet we must not confuse the terms. Once the law-giving prophet who is the “Seal of the Prophets” has appeared, there can be no further prophecy, even of the kind that introduces no new law, because there can be no new *sharia*. Before Islam, the simple word *prophecy* (*nubuwwat*) could cover prophets who did not bring a law; no separate term such as *walayat* was needed.

After the final Prophet, only *walayat* remains an appropriate name for this continuing spiritual gift. The gift itself, however, was present from the very beginning of the “cycle of prophecy.” With that cycle now closed, *walayat* emerges as the spiritual inheritance that prophecy has left to humanity.

Two questions follow. What exactly have the prophets left behind? And who inherits it? The Imams' own teachings answer both. The idea that prophecy has an eternal reality gives rise to the idea of someone on earth who inherits it spiritually: the Imam. Outside the wider picture established in the previous chapter, this answer may sound strange, even misplaced, to ordinary opinion, within Islam and beyond it. That is because it approaches the question from a different standpoint altogether.

Nevertheless, the answer was given from Islam's earliest days by people who traced their earthly descent from the Prophet through Fatima. Their family relationship was understood to reflect an eternal relationship within the complete company of heavenly beings, the *pleroma*. Fatima was called the “meeting place of the two lights” (*majma' al-nurayn*): the light of prophecy and the light of *walayat*. Whether people accepted or rejected the Imams' teaching has therefore shaped—and continues to shape—the spiritual destiny of Islam as a prophetic religion.

In the Shiite view, humanity's religious story did not end when prophecy came to an end. The very structure of our age or world-cycle, our *Aeon*, passes through the cycle of prophecy and then the cycle of *walayat*. It follows that further events still await us—not simply events of ordinary history, but events of sacred history.

To understand the Imam as the Prophet's spiritual heir, then, we need to look more closely at prophecy itself. Our first source is the body of traditions—the *hadith* and *akhbar*—handed down from the Imams. Many of them appear in the great collection assembled by Muhammad ibn Ya'qub Kulayni, a courageous Iranian Shiite theologian of the fourth Islamic century (tenth century CE), who died in 329 AH (940 CE). Kulayni lived long enough to know the last representatives (*na'ib*) of the Hidden Imam.

Indeed, his death came at roughly the time when the Imam's “Greater Occultation,” his longer period of hiddenness, began.[^EII1-192]

Kulayni's work is the oldest surviving comprehensive collection covering the major subjects of Shiite religious thought.

But it did not appear out of nowhere. Long before him, close disciples of the successive Imams had assembled smaller collections directly from what they heard. Some survive. Sadly, many are known to us only by their titles, preserved in other writings.[^EII1-193] Their manuscripts vanished during the upheavals faced by Shiite communities, which had to live more or less in hiding until the end of Abbasid rule in 1258. It is not our purpose here to recount those hardships, or the political unrest for which Shiite ideas could serve as a pretext.

The Imams' teachings, spread across thousands of pages, are religious teachings: they concern interpretation of scripture, moral life, worship, theology, and divine wisdom. They are never presented as a “political programme.” Shiite religious thought was preserved and developed not by politicians or agitators, but by the small circles of “faithful people whose hearts had been tested” who gathered around each Imam, even in the hardest circumstances.[^EII1-194]

As we stressed in the previous chapter, Shiite philosophical and religious thought—and what Shiites understand as its “history”—cannot be understood, still less lived, merely by standing outside it and explaining it in terms of external circumstances. The Imams saw this history as a spiritual history unfolding in the souls of their followers. It is made up of those followers' testimony, and the Imams themselves are the source from which their followers learn. That is why this “history” does not simply *develop* or *evolve* in the ordinary sense of those words.

Nor can we separate the Imams' teaching from the commentaries of those who lived it, reflected on it, and drew out its meaning because they believed in it. Their writings bear witness to their faith; their faith, in turn, made it possible for them to recognize everything contained in the teaching.

Here we meet again a principle we have had to affirm throughout this book. The historical reality of faith is not just a neutral sequence of external events that we can divide into equal stretches of chronological time. It is also the reality of faith itself, as each believer encounters what faith is directed towards, in the depth of the heart.

That is why our best guides to the holy Imams are the teachers who have commented on their words. They received those words as coming from the Imams and, because of their content, could understand them only in that way. The faith, thought, and writings of these teachers are themselves where the religious reality of Shiism—the reality of devotion to the Imams—comes alive in history.

Of course, this is not the kind of historical reality that ordinary historical criticism tries to establish when its main concern is to show that a particular Imam could not have spoken a particular saying. Such criticism may begin by destroying the object in which it does not believe. But once it has declared that object nonexistent, nothing remains for it to discuss.

We cannot regard a method that begins by destroying its own subject as a remarkable victory. I hope this book has shown why our study of religious experience tries instead to reach the religious reality *as religious reality*: to preserve the object of faith as it actually appears to the faith that encounters it. And no amount of historical criticism can alter this fact: for Shiite believers over thirteen centuries, a particular *hadith* has truly been spoken by a particular Imam, because its very content is understood as the Imam's own utterance.

So it should not be surprising that we have preferred, and will continue to prefer, the company of teachers who lived within the historical reality of Shiite faith. We have already met Haydar Amuli, Mulla Sadra Shirazi, Qazi Sa'id Qummi, and many others who sustained Shiite spiritual life. Mulla Sadra left us an immense commentary on the traditions collected by Kulayni.[^EII1-195]

When we are dealing with the realities of faith, the number of centuries separating two thinkers is not decisive. What matters is their closeness in intention and understanding: a kind of *being together across time*. We have already seen how this closeness makes possible philosophical reflection that never cuts itself off from spiritual practice. It also helps us understand why traditional Islamic philosophy continued to flourish in Shiite circles down to our own day.

If, then, we study with these Shiite teachers the sections of the great tradition collections devoted to prophecy and the Imams, we find that the teaching about prophecy gives especially clear expression to a central Islamic conviction: human beings need a guide to lead them along the “straight path” (*sirat mustaqim*) of their return to God. This is the path on which they remain faithful to the timeless covenant made with God before entering earthly life, as we saw in Chapter II. As far as the historical evidence allows us to trace the idea of prophecy and the special spiritual gift of the prophets, we cannot go back beyond the teachings of the Shiite Imams.

The question first takes shape through them, and Islamic thinking about prophecy grows from their teaching. There is a striking agreement between their arguments for the necessity of prophets and those later offered by philosophers such as al-Farabi, Avicenna, and Suhrawardi. They approach this necessity from two directions: from the human side and from the divine side.

For the philosophers who followed Avicenna, the *aql*—the intellect, or *nous*—remains only a potential ability in most people. Only in a few does the full human possibility become a living reality.[^EII1-196] These thinkers do not imagine a state of innocence in which people, simply following their natural impulses, could have built a society on their own.[^EII1-197][^EII1-198][^EII1-199] What passes for “natural law” would be what we call the law of the jungle. Avicenna and Biruni therefore hold that a divinely sent messenger, a prophet, is needed to establish law and justice.

Yet these philosophical arguments repeat what we find in the teachings of the Shiite Imams—for example, in the words of the Sixth Imam, Ja'far Sadiq (d. 148 AH/765 CE), preserved by Kulayni. Left entirely to themselves, people cannot find their way. They must come together in communities; but to do so they need someone who stands above the rest and shows them what is necessary both for safety in this life and for the life that continues beyond it.

The philosophers say that the fourth level of intellect—intellect fully at work—is reached by only a few individuals. Similarly, the Imams speak of five levels of Spirit (*ruh*), the highest of which, the Holy Spirit (*ruh al-quds*), is granted especially to the prophets.

For Imam Ja'far, however, the reason for this human inability is explained more directly from God's side. God, being beyond everything created, is inaccessible and invisible. No one has ever seen God or ever will. On this point Shiism differs from certain other Islamic schools: the Karramiyya allowed that God could be seen in this world and the next, and so conceived the vision in terms of space and dimensions; the Ash'arites allowed for vision in the next world, but without a face-to-face encounter or any spatial dimensions. After a long explanation of why no one can see or “touch” God, the Imam concludes:

> It follows that there must be people who can command and forbid in the name of the All-Wise, All-Knowing One, and speak on His behalf. These are the people we call prophets (*anbiya*). They are the chosen ones among His creatures: sages (*hukama*) who have been taught by Wisdom (*hikmat*)[^EII1-200] and sent on their mission by Wisdom itself. They share with other human beings the fact of being created and the possession of a physical body. Apart from this, however, they do not share the same ways of being and acting as other people, because the All-Wise, All-Knowing One supports them and inspires them through Wisdom.
>
> Such guidance remains available in every age and every period through the signs and proofs brought by the messengers and prophets. In this way God's earth is never left without a witness who stands as His proof (*hujjat*)[^EII1-201]—someone with a Sign (*alam*, a symbol) that shows the truth of what he says and the constancy of his justice.

This statement by Imam Ja'far raises three groups of questions.

**1. The prophets as mediators.** First, the prophets have a special qualification given by God that enables them to act as mediators. Following a long tradition, Mulla Sadra explains that prophetic existence has two sides. One faces divine transcendence and holiness (*taqaddus*); the other faces material reality and the human condition (*tajassum*). That is why a prophet can be called “a human being of divine standing” or “a divine lord in human form” (*insan rabbani am rabb insani*).

Both expressions are striking. They show that, from the beginning, Islamic thinking about prophecy and the Imams faced a problem similar to the one that divided the Nestorians and Jacobites in Eastern Christian debates about Christ.

Yet in Islamic prophecy, the divine qualification belongs only to the eternal prophetic reality—the *Muhammadan Reality* (*haqiqat muhammadiya*)—and not to the Prophet's earthly humanity (*bashariyat*). The Qur'an confirms his humanity in the words: “I am a human being like you, but divine revelation has come to me” (18:111). His divine reality, on the other hand, is suggested by another verse: “It was not you who threw when you threw; it was God who threw” (8:17).

**2. How can God be seen?** Second, as we have just read, the argument that prophets are necessary rests partly on the claim that God cannot be seen. The Imams' conversations with their close followers return to three related ideas: seeing God is impossible; God can be described only by the attributes God gives Himself; and God can be known only through God.

Yet, in the end, a certain kind of vision does prove possible. What kind of vision can that be?

**a)** Someone once wrote to the Eleventh Imam, Hasan Askari (d. 260 AH/874 CE), referring to a famous saying attributed to the Prophet—the *hadith of the vision*: “I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms.”[^EII1-202][^EII1-203] The writer asked: “How could anyone worship a God whom he does not see?” The Imam replied: “Truly, God—blessed and exalted be He—made visible to the heart of His Messenger that light of His sublime majesty which the Messenger loved.”

This answer takes us into the territory of mystical experience. It introduces inner vision: seeing with the heart. It is love that makes vision possible—and love is itself the one being guided. What love sees is the very object it loves. The depth of the vision depends on the depth of the love. Mulla Sadra makes the point clearly. Most people see only through their bodily senses; their intellect (*aql*) never rises beyond a latent possibility. The “holy intellect” (*intellectus sanctus*, *aql qudsi*), which is the spiritual heart, is free from the limits of physical time and space.

**b)** A visitor, a Kharijite, once asked the Fifth Imam, Muhammad Baqir (d. 115 AH/733 CE): “What do you worship? God Most High? Have you seen Him?” The Imam answered:

> No. Eyes do not see Him with their bodily power of sight, but hearts see Him through the realities (*haqa'iq*) of faith. He cannot be known by comparison (*qiyas*), whether by logical reasoning or analogy, and He cannot be grasped by the senses. His Signs (*ayat*) reveal how He may be described, and His symbols (*alamat*) make Him known. There is no violence in His judgments. Such is God, the God of whom we say: there is no god but *Huwa*—He.[^EII1-204]

**c)** The Sixth Imam, Ja'far Sadiq, also relates an answer given by the First Imam, the Commander of the Faithful, to a learned man who asked: “Commander of the Faithful, do you see your Lord when you worship Him?” The Imam replied: “Take care! I would never worship a God whom I did not see.” The man asked in return: “Then how do you see Him?” “Take care,” said the Imam. “Eyes do not see Him through physical sight. Hearts see Him through the realities of faith.”[^EII1-205][^EII1-206][^EII1-207]

The Imams' answers preserve a paradox. On one side stands the refusal given to Moses: “You shall not see Me” (*lan tarani*, 7:139). On the other stands the prophetic testimony: “I saw my God in the most beautiful of forms.”

Indeed, as we shall see in Chapter VII, the Imams' teaching led their followers towards a doctrine that agrees with Ibn Arabi's: a manifestation of God can be seen only in a form suited to the spiritual capacity of the person who sees it (*mutajalla lahu*). That person sees only his or her own form in the mirror of God; the Guide takes the form of the person being guided.

Vision of the heart, knowledge of the heart (*ma'rifat qalbiya*): these ideas appear repeatedly in the Imams' teaching. They do not belong exclusively to Sufism and were not invented by al-Ghazali (d. 505 AH/1111 CE). It is important to remember this whenever we ask about the relationship between Shiism and Sufism, or between the teaching about the Imams and mystical experience.[^EII1-208]

Let us turn to a remarkable passage from Mulla Sadra to see how fruitful this theme became for Shiite philosophers. It will keep returning throughout our study of prophets and Imams. Sadra asks us to think carefully about what we mean each time we use the word *vision*.

Among the followers of the later Imams, people often repeated a remark attributed to Hisham ibn al-Hakam, a famous young follower of the Sixth Imam. His argument bears a striking resemblance to certain ideas in Stoic physics: God, he said, must somehow be a *body* (*jism*). Otherwise God would be an *act* (*fi'l*, a verb)—something unreal that would only acquire concrete existence through the subject performing the action.[^EII1-209][^EII1-210] What looks like a contradiction does not trouble Mulla Sadra greatly.

Unlike many earlier philosophers, he is concerned not primarily with the fixed essences of things but with their *act of existing*, and here his thinking too has affinities with Stoicism. One and the same essence can exist on different levels. That is true of what we call a “body,” from a body made of physical elements to a spiritual body. It is also true of the human being, whom Sadra understands in three parts. (A threefold understanding of the human being was abandoned in the West at the Council of Constantinople in 869.)

Here is that threefold picture. First comes the **physical human being**, with an organic body and the senses through which we perceive the physical world.

Second comes the **psychic human being**, whose “psychic body” has no parts that can be located within the dimensions of this world, because it does not belong to this world. Its way of perceiving depends on imagination and imaginative awareness, whose theory Mulla Sadra developed in particular depth.

Third comes the **spiritual human being**, with a “spiritual body” that possesses spiritual senses (*hawass ruhaniya aqliya*): spiritual sight, spiritual hearing, and so on.

That is why certain Qur'anic verses and *hadiths* must be understood at a spiritual level if we are to grasp them at the level where they actually speak—in what is, for that level, their true *literal* meaning. If the essence we call “body” can exist in different ways, on levels that differ in dignity and density, we can even imagine, at the furthest limit, something like a “divine body” (*jism ilahi*).

But we must immediately remember the Qur'anic words: “Nothing is like Him” (42:9).

The home of these spiritual senses is the **heart**. It is the heart that makes prophetic knowledge possible. For prophetic revelation and mystical experience belong to the same kind of spiritual reality,[^EII1-211] as Mulla Sadra explains:

> The source of all mystical unveilings (*mukashafat*) is the human heart, through its very nature and its understanding[^EII1-212] of light, using the spiritual senses. For the heart has eyes, ears, and all the other senses. Many passages in the classical *hadith* collections confirm this. These spiritual senses are the source (*asl*) from which our bodily senses arise.
>
> When the veil between the spiritual senses and outward reality is lifted, the source—the spiritual sense—and what comes from it—the bodily sense—are joined. What bodily senses perceive is then contemplated through the spiritual senses themselves. The Spirit (*ruh*) contemplates all this through its own power, because at its level all realities (*haqa'iq*) form a unity, just as they do for the Active Intelligence.[^EII1-213]

The heart therefore brings together every form and every level of the teaching about prophets and Imams.

**3. Why the Imam must always be present.** Third, this same idea of the heart leads us from the necessity of prophets to the necessity of the Imam. This is the last group of questions raised by the Sixth Imam's statement quoted earlier, where he insists that the earth can never be without someone who stands as God's witness or proof (*hujjat*). The idea is essential to Shiite teaching about the Imams.

From it comes the image of the “pole of the world,” even the “pole of poles,” without whom earthly existence could not continue for another instant. The image is familiar even in non-Shiite Sufism. We have already learned that the Imam, the pole, may be visible and known, or may be hidden, unknown to people, and beyond the reach of their bodily senses. According to the tradition, the latter is our own situation: the age of occultation (*ghaybat*), the age of the Hidden Imam.

How was this idea established in the first place? We have already seen its foundation. The prophet's task was to reveal the outward wording of the sacred law (*sharia*). The task of another was to teach its inner spiritual meaning (*ta'wil*). That other person is the Imam, the “Guardian of the Book” (*qayyim al-Qur'an*), who keeps its meaning alive.

The Sixth Imam's *hadith* brings us to this conclusion: God must send prophets, because the great human task is to find the way to live faithfully by the timeless covenant made with God. “Am I not your Lord?” (*a-lastu bi-rabbikum?*), God asks in the Qur'an (7:171). People cannot find that way without a guide, and that guide is the prophet.

But what happens when the prophet is no longer there? More urgently still, what happens when the prophet who has departed was the **final** Prophet?

A follower named Mansur ibn Hazim once told Imam Ja'far about his conversations with Muslims who were not Shiites. He would ask them the crucial question: “Now that God's Messenger is no longer here, who will stand before humanity as the witness, the one who can give the decisive answer (*hujjat*)?” Usually they replied: “The Qur'an.”

But Mansur had studied the Qur'an himself. He knew how fiercely people disagreed about what its words meant. So he had concluded that the Qur'an alone could not serve as the decisive witness without a guardian (*qayyim*), an interpreter (*mufassir*), who knew its full inner truth (*haqiqat*).[^EII1-214] This guardian is the Imam: the Guide.

Mulla Sadra, for his part, argues that this central Shiite teaching follows directly from the fact that God is beyond everything else.[^EII1-215] Philosophy teaches, he says, that whatever has no cause—the uncaused ground, the *Abgrund*—cannot have its essence defined or be proved by appealing to something else. All other proofs begin from it. We know things that have causes through those causes.

But how can we know the One who causes all causes (*musabbib al-asbab*) and makes every cause knowable? That is the meaning of the First Imam's saying: “I have never known anything without knowing God before it.” A mystic echoes the same thought: “I know my God only through my God.”

To “know one's God” is to know God's attributes.

But how could we reach such knowledge without either a divine message brought by an angel (*wahy*) or divine inspiration (*ilham*)? Those who know about the “origin” and the “return” (*mabda'* and *ma'ad*) have received one of these two gifts. The prophets receive the message through an angel. The Imams and the Friends of God receive inspiration, whether in dreams or while awake. This kind of inspired knowledge is what we call *sacred knowledge* or *hierognosis*. Everyone who has received neither kind must turn to God's messengers, the prophets.

Yet the question immediately returns: whom are we to seek when there is no longer a prophet?

We now have the basis of the argument. A living witness (*hujjat*) must always be present, because the Qur'an by itself cannot perform that role. The Qur'an has an outward meaning and an inward meaning (*batin*)—indeed, tradition speaks of as many as seven inner depths. It is a book of symbols, whose meanings are not immediately visible. Mulla Sadra declares:

> The Qur'an is not a book that can be understood through the ordinary knowledge of philosophers. Most educated people already find it difficult to understand the philosophers' books, whether those of the ancients, such as Plato and Aristotle, or those of more recent writers, such as al-Farabi and Avicenna. How, then, could they understand the Qur'an—the divine speech that comes from God and descended into the heart of His Prophet?
>
> Who could guide people through its many hidden meanings, unless that person possessed an inward sight (*basirat*) illuminated by God, and a spiritual hearing (*sama' aqli*) able to hear from God and His angels—even without seeing an angel's form or hearing the sound of its speech, as the Prophet himself saw and heard through these two spiritual senses?

As we shall see, the difference between prophets on the one hand and Imams and Friends of God on the other does not lie in whether they possess this sacred knowledge. It lies in the way they receive it and the degree to which they possess it.

Anyone who possesses this double power of spiritual sight and hearing—even if it does not equal that of a prophet-messenger—is therefore capable, after the Prophet, of guarding the Book in the fullness of its meaning.
