All the divine knowledge inherited from the prophets—knowledge that is, in this sense, direct spiritual knowledge—brings us back to the experience in which the person being guided discovers the Guide and recognizes himself in that Guide. This idea of a spiritual inheritance from the prophets also governs the succession of two great ages: the “cycle of prophecy” followed by the “cycle of *walayat*.” It places the spiritual seeker in an interval between the age of the “Seal of Prophecy” and the future appearing of the “Seal of Muhammadan *walayat*.” The two cycles are essential to Shiite understandings of prophecy and the Imams.

##### 5. The Cycle of Prophecy and the Cycle of *Walayat*

The two cycles correspond to one another. Each is the other's mirror image. Together they suggest an enduring pattern running through sacred history. This pattern belongs to the history of spiritual meaning, not to history understood simply as a study of recorded events. *Walayat* is the hidden mystery of the Imamate: the inner truth into which the Imams initiate their followers. It is both what spiritual initiation reveals and the act of initiation itself.

When a believer inwardly professes the threefold testimony of faith, that person enters the special relationship of love and closeness to God enjoyed by God's Friends. The cycle of *walayat*—the age of God's Friends following the age of God's Messengers, or prophets—can therefore also be called the cycle of spiritual initiation.

The two cycles are held together by the figures each calls its “Seal.” The Seal of Prophecy (*Khatim al-nobowwat*), also called the Seal of the Prophets (*Khatim al-Anbiya*), is Muhammad. He closes the cycle in which prophets bring sacred laws. That cycle began with Adam and continued through successive ages, each named for its lawgiving prophet: Adam, Noah, Abraham, Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad.

But we also know that, from prophet to prophet, the hidden dimension of the eternal prophetic Reality was secretly present, accompanying each one.

Finally, during Muhammad's mission, it became openly manifest in the person of the Imam. The end of the cycle of prophecy thus marks the beginning of *walayat* in its own right. This new age does not prepare for another prophet bringing a new Law. It prepares for the coming of the One who will reveal the hidden meaning of all earlier revelations and thereby remove every restriction imposed by their merely outward forms.

*Walayat* endures; the mission of prophets who bring sacred laws is temporary. This distinction also lies behind the idea of universal or absolute *walayat* (*motlaqa*): a spiritual reality independent of the features of any one prophetic age, because it is present in all of them. The Seal of this absolute *walayat* is the First Imam, since the Muhammadan Imamate embodies the inner meaning of every earlier prophetic revelation. *Walayat* then takes the particular form of Muhammadan *walayat* (*khassa*). Its Seal is the one who completes the full company of the Twelve Imams: the Twelfth Imam, now the “Hidden Imam.” In this sense, the Imamate as a whole is the Seal of *walayat*.

This is a grand and coherent vision. Shiite writers, especially Haydar Amoli, could not understand how Ibn Arabi, the great mystical thinker, had broken its pattern by making Jesus the Seal of absolute *walayat*. In their view, Jesus, as the last prophet before Muhammad, is the Seal of *Adamic walayat*—the form of *walayat* associated with the successive lawgiving prophets from Adam onward.

But precisely because he is a prophet, he cannot be the Seal of absolute *walayat*. Perhaps, working in a Sunni environment, Ibn Arabi felt obliged to conceal part of his belief, a practice known as *ketman*. Haydar Amoli spent many pages debating who should be called the Seal of *walayat*. We have already noted the question and need not pursue it further here (see note 247 and Book Four, Chapter One, below).

The correspondence—or, more exactly, the symmetry—between the cycles also depends on the titles given to two figures. The Prophet Muhammad is the final Seal of the prophets and of prophecy. The Twelfth Imam, who also bears the name Muhammad, is the future Seal of Muhammadan *walayat* and of God's Friends.

In him, Shiism expresses a profound conviction about its place in the future: it sees itself as the final spiritual fulfillment of the enduring prophetic religion shared by humanity. Accordingly, every person initiated into the cycle of *walayat* stands in relation to the Twelfth Imam—“now hidden from the senses, but present in the hearts of his followers”—as each prophet in the earlier cycle stood in relation to Muhammad, the Seal of Prophecy.

We have already seen that the idea of the “Seal of Prophecy” grows out of a teaching about prophecy that closely resembles that of the Jewish-Christian Ebionites. It recalls the *Verus Propheta*, the True Prophet, who passes from one prophet to another, “hastening toward the place of his rest.” There is, of course, an important difference. In the Islamic account, the final prophet—the one in whom all earlier prophets find their rest and fulfillment—is not Christ. It is Muhammad, who came after Christ and whom, according to an interpretation shared throughout Muslim Qur'anic commentary, Christ himself foretold.[^EII1-259]

We can picture these relationships in several ways. Imagine a circle divided into two halves. One half may be the arc of descent (*qaws al-nozul*): revelation coming down, the giving of scripture (*tanzil*), and prophecy. The other is the arc of ascent (*qaws al-so'ud*): the discovery of deeper meaning (*ta'wil*), the Imamate, and *walayat*. Or imagine the circle the other way around.

First comes the upward arc, rising toward the noon of prophecy in its fullest revelation. Then comes the downward arc, entering the night of hidden spiritual meaning until the dawn of spiritual Resurrection and the appearance of the Twelfth Imam. In either picture, the prophets and God's Friends (*awliya*) stand opposite their counterparts on the two arcs.

Alternatively, we can picture two complete, separate circles: one for the “cycle of prophecy” (*da'irat al-nobowwat*), the other for the “cycle of *walayat*” (*da'irat al-walayat*). Here too the corresponding positions of prophets and God's Friends are clear. Shamsoddin Lahiji (died 912 AH/1506 CE) suggests both diagrams in his great commentary on *The Rose Garden of Mystery*, by the celebrated mystic Mahmud Shabestari of Azerbaijan (died 720 AH/1317 CE). In one version, the circles face each other; in the other, a single circle has two arcs symbolizing a cosmic “Day” and “Night”—a full cycle of day and night in the life of the world.

In this image, the sequence of prophets traces a circle (*da'ira*, *khatt mostadir*) whose points are the prophets themselves. Adam's life marks the first point of the “cycle of prophecy” in our world. To say that prophecy first appeared (*zohur*) with Adam is to say that he was the first earthly manifestation of its eternal reality (*haqiqat*). Every prophet (*nabi*) who followed manifested that same eternal prophetic Reality in a particular form. The cycle reaches completion in Muhammad. Coming last, he manifests in his earthly person every perfection that the earlier prophets had revealed separately. He gathers them all together (*jami'iyat*, or *anakephalaiosis*): in him the original prophetic Reality appears in its fullness.

Once the cycle of prophecy ends, the cycle of spiritual initiation begins. It is now for the Imams, God's Friends and Beloved, to initiate their own friends and followers into prophecy's inner meaning. Certainly prophecy and initiation are both present in the Prophet himself.

Indeed, his *walayat*—his divinely given spiritual authority and closeness to God—is the very source of his prophetic mission, his *nobowwat* (see the diagram above, p. 259). But because he has been sent as a prophet, and specifically as a prophet who brings a sacred Law, his prophetic office and message (*nobowwat* and *risalat*) do not include a mission to reveal the hidden meaning of the religion whose outward wording he proclaims.

That is why prophecy and initiation are assigned to two persons: the Prophet and the Imam. As we already know, this distinction lies at the heart of Twelver Shiite teaching about the Imamate, whose full reality appears in the twelve persons of the Imams.

We must also remember what makes the cycle of initiation following the Seal of the Prophets unique. Before Muhammad, every prophetic age prepared for the arrival of another prophet. Now that prophecy has closed, the cycle of *walayat* will not end with a new prophet or a new established religion. It prepares instead for the appearing of the Hidden Imam. With him will come the unveiling of what has remained concealed in all earlier revelations. The cycle of initiation that follows the cycle of prophecy is therefore initiation in its pure form—*walayat mahz*, spiritual knowledge no longer preparing for a new outward Law. This is the basis of the correspondence between the two cycles.[^EII1-260]

We have already described this correspondence briefly. Just as the prophets before the Seal of Prophecy each manifested the same eternal prophetic Reality (*haqiqat-e nobowwat*), so the Friends of God, who guide and initiate others, manifest an eternal *walayat*: initiation into the inner meaning of prophecy. And just as the cycle of prophecy reached its completion in the Seal of the Prophets (*Khatim al-Anbiya*), so the cycle of initiation reaches its fulfillment in the Seal of the Initiated, the Seal of God's Friends (*Khatim al-Awliya*).

Two ideas give this Shiite vision of the last things its distinctive character. First, traditions traced back to the Prophet identify the Seal of God's Friends with the Hidden Imam, the Twelfth Imam, child of Imam Hasan Askari and Princess Narkes (see Book Seven below).

Second, the future appearing of the now-hidden Imam will reveal the divine truths and secrets (*haqa'iq*, *asrar-e ilahi*) concealed within the wording of earlier revelations and the commands of outward religion. His appearance will usher in the reign of *ta'wil*, the uncovering of inner meaning. It will free people from every form of bondage and torment imposed by the Law. Spiritual knowledge and divine wisdom prepare for, and already anticipate, this appearance whenever they uncover the hidden meaning. They will reach their fullest development when the Imam and Guide, the Mahdi, appears and brings the cycle of initiation to its close.

This also points to the spiritual meaning we should give to the “events of the end.” Shiite books describe them in their chapters on the last things with dramatic scenes and the “return” (*raj'at*) of great figures from earlier ages. We should read those accounts in this light. Consider, for example, the saying in which the Prophet announces the last Imam's coming:

> Those who dwell in Heaven and those who dwell on Earth will recognize him. Heaven will hold back not a drop of its water, but will pour it out in life-giving rain. Earth will keep back not a single growing thing, but will make it sprout and flourish, until those then alive will wish for the dead to rise again.

And the very power of this wish will bring about that resurrection. The Imam and his companions will prepare it together; indeed, he has already begun the work through those who, generation after generation, are the “companions of the Hidden Imam.” As Lahiji says, the resurrection of the dead—the awakening of dead souls—is what makes it possible for the purpose and fruit of existence finally to be fulfilled. People will attain perfect knowledge and become true knowers of spiritual reality (*arifan-e haqiqi*). The Imam's reign will prepare the way for this magnificent new beginning.

Our writers know that philosophy allows for the possibility that the world might be destroyed. But their understanding of the Imam enables them to challenge that possibility. Iran's vision of the final destiny of the world has shown a striking continuity, both before and after Islam. In Zoroastrian teaching, salvation and the end of history center on *frashkart*: the transformation or renewal of the world through the Saoshyant and his companions, preparing for the final restoration of all things.

Shiite teaching about the last things is centered on the Resurrector (*Qa'im*) and his companions. It looks toward a new beginning (*isti'naf*), a new age, an *apokatastasis*: the restoration of all things to their original state of light. It does not separate the “lesser resurrection,” an individual's departure from the perishable body, from the “greater resurrection,” the coming of that new age.[^EII1-261]

Let us now look more closely at how the two Seals correspond, and how each relates to those who manifest its reality. Our authors explain that just as the Seal of the Prophets gathered into himself all the earlier prophets who had manifested the eternal prophetic Reality, the Seal of the Initiated gathers into himself every initiate, every Friend of God. The perfection present as a possibility throughout the cycle of initiation becomes fully real in his person.

All are related to him as members of a single mystical body (*corpus mysticum*). This is why the Sufi understanding of *walayat* would be left without a foundation if we removed the Shiite understanding of the Imam. It is not enough to say that the Prophet himself was the first bearer of *walayat*. In him, this *walayat* remains—and must remain—hidden. It can become openly active only through the Imam's work of spiritual initiation, embodied in the Imam himself.

We can ask another question. The title “Friends” or “Beloved of God” (*awliya*) belongs in a special sense to the Twelve Imams. How can their followers share in it? To understand this, we must picture a relationship like that between the prophet's mission and the Imam's work of initiation. Prophecy springs from *walayat* itself and is like the sun; the Imam's *walayat* draws its light from that sun, just as the moon draws its light from the sun.

The word *wali* can mean both the one who loves and the one who is loved. With this double meaning in mind, our authors call the initiatory role of the “Seal of the Initiated” a solar *walayat* (*shamsiya*). The *walayat* of every other initiate or Friend of God—from the *Afrad* to the *Noqaba*, different ranks among the spiritual guides—is lunar (*qamariya*).

The Twelfth Imam, as Seal of the Initiated, possesses and reveals the eternal reality of *walayat* (*haqiqat-e walayat*):

> Absolute initiation, in the fullness of all its perfections, appears in his person. He is the Whole. All the other Initiated manifest only one of initiation's perfect qualities, and so are like parts in relation to the Seal of the Initiated. Because he is with all of them, he is with each one.[^EII1-262]

This becomes understandable only through the intimate relationship between the Seal of the Prophets and the Seal of the Initiated. And, for our authors, that relationship can be understood in its full depth only through Shiite teaching.

We can distinguish three ways in which one person may be another's child (*farzandi*): descent through the body, the bond of affection through the heart, and a spiritual relationship that is essential and true. Shiite writers argue that all three come together completely in the Twelfth Imam, and only in him. Because he embodies this threefold relationship, they can say:

> In truth, the Seal of the Initiated is the real inner truth (*haqiqat*), the hidden perfection, of the Seal of the Prophets. … Just as the Seal of the Prophets, as the form in which the divine Name “the Merciful” becomes visible, brought Mercy to both worlds and gathered into himself all the diverse figures of the cycle of prophecy, so the Seal of the Initiated becomes the form in which universal Compassion appears.

> For the child is the secret of his father—in other words, the Twelfth Imam is the Prophet's secret. The Seal of the Initiated therefore gathers into himself all the diverse figures of the cycle of initiation. The happiness of both worlds will lie in following him. … For he will not destroy the many different things that exist. He will overcome their divisions by revealing the hidden laws of their unity.[^EII1-263]

If the Seal of the Initiated, the Seal of Muhammadan *walayat*, reveals the inner meaning of the Seal of the Prophets—or, more precisely, is himself the inner meaning of the last Prophet's mission—then the two must share a single, underlying reality. With the cycle of initiation, the greater cycle, which contains both cycles, comes full circle.

Yet its end is also its beginning: the eternal Muhammadan Reality (*haqiqat-e mohammadi*).[^EII1-264] Lahiji tries to picture this relationship in a diagram inspired by the very words of *The Rose Garden of Mystery*, on which he is commenting. In this diagram, the whole cycle of prophecy and initiation corresponds to one cosmic day and night.

The image of a cosmic Day and Night, unfolding with the revolution of the highest heavenly sphere, follows naturally when we consider the eternal Muhammadan Reality. It is the first definite reality to emerge from what has no determinate form at all (see Chapter Five above). It is the supreme Spirit, the universal Intelligence, a subtle fullness of primordial praise, also called the Muhammadan Light (*Nur mohammadi*). Each divine Name has its own form of manifestation and its own worshipper. In the same way, the eternal Muhammadan Reality corresponds to the supreme Name: the divine Name that gathers all the other Names into itself.[^EII1-265]

As Sadoddin Hamuyeh explains, precisely because it bears this supreme Name, the eternal Reality must appear in two distinct forms (*mazhar*). One is prophecy, embodied in the Seal of the Prophets. The other is initiation, embodied in the Twelfth Imam, the invisible master of the present age. Hamuyeh's disciple Aziz Nasafi puts it this way:

> Thousands of prophets who came before contributed, one after another, to establishing the form in which prophecy appears; Muhammad brought it to completion. Now the time has come for initiation to appear, and to reveal the inner realities. And the Initiator in whom initiation takes visible form is the Imam, the lord of this age.[^EII1-266]

These are the two manifestations of the highest world. Each has its own nature, and together they correspond to the phases of day and night in the world we can see.

While the sun is beneath the Earth, night covers the Earth. When the sun rises toward the eastern horizon, still unseen, the darkness caused by the Earth standing in the way of its light begins to lift from things. Dawn has come, though the full brightness of morning has not. The horizon is the circle that divides the visible part of the sky from the invisible part, as seen from where we stand. It is in relation to this circle that we speak of sunrise and sunset.

From its rising point in the east, the sun climbs through successive heights until it reaches the zenith. Once it has crossed the meridian, the movement of the highest heavenly sphere begins to carry it downward; the decisive moment is marked by the midday prayer (*namaz-e pishin*). At last, when a lengthening shadow begins to give each thing a second outline, evening advances and the sun returns to hiding, until another morning comes.

This is a faithful image of what happens beyond the world of the senses in the complete cycle of prophecy and initiation. Prophecy is the sunrise of the Muhammadan Light, ascending from prophet to prophet until it reaches the meridian in the Seal of Prophecy. At that very point begins the cycle of initiation: the gradual descent into the night of hidden spiritual meaning, with all the trials that such a night brings in a hostile world.

Yet there is no other path. It is the necessary journey toward the morning of Resurrection, *Yawm al-Qiyamat*.[^EII1-267]

The prophets differed from one another as individual people, with their own lives and forms. Adam, Noah, Moses, and Jesus were not Muhammad; neither were the 124,000 *nabis* who were prophets without also being messengers entrusted with a new religious law.

Yet in the eternal reality of what they were (*haqiqat*, or *ousia*), all were forms in which the same Muhammadan Light appeared. Until the cycle of prophecy finally ended, that Light—like the Ebionites' *Verus Propheta*, the True Prophet—revealed itself through each earlier prophet, beginning with Adam, who was its eastern horizon, its sunrise.

We must therefore read the story of the prophets as the rise of prophetic consciousness: the successive heights reached by this sun on its way to the meridian. Each prophet revealed one particular perfection of the eternal Muhammadan Reality. At sunrise, a person's shadow is long. As the sun rises, the shadow grows shorter. At the zenith, the people and figures beneath it cast no shadow. In the same way, in each age and generation, the sun of the Muhammadan Reality revealed the form and shadow of a Perfect One (*kamil*). Those shadows marked the successive stages of the sun's ascent. When the light of prophecy reached its zenith with the appearance of the last prophet, it was noon: every shadow had vanished.[^EII1-268]

Once the Seal of the Prophets had brought this light to its zenith, humanity stood beneath it like people living on the equator at noon. Our authors explain this image in several ways. Each brings us back to a problem that their spiritual theology must constantly confront: how to avoid two opposite extremes.

We might say, for example, that the Seal of Prophecy stands at the point of perfect balance—an equinoctial line—between the day of unity and the night of multiplicity. On one side lies the danger of an abstract and all-embracing monotheism that cannot recognize the many ways God's Names become visible. On the other lies a polytheism that sees the many forms but misses the unity within them.

This is a vision that unites by distinguishing, and distinguishes by uniting. It also gives perfect balance to outward and inner meaning, and therefore to prophecy and initiation. As we have seen, keeping that balance is a central concern of Twelver Shiite thinkers when they explain the relationship between the Prophet and the Imams. They also seek balance between *tashbih* and *tanzih*: on one side, the tendency of literal-minded believers to imagine God in human form; on the other, the effort of some philosophers and theologians to preserve God's utter transcendence by stripping away every positive description. In taking this second path, they risk reducing God to an abstraction.

Shiite divine wisdom finds a path between these dangers through the idea of *theophany*: a manifestation of God (*zohur*, *tajalli*). This preserves both unity and multiplicity. God can appear in a human form as an image appears in a mirror, without becoming embodied in that form any more than the reflected person actually enters the glass. The same principle applies to the visions of God's Friends, whether they occur in dreams or while awake (see above, p. 269). It also applies when these Friends themselves are called manifestations of the eternal Muhammadan Reality. Lahiji gives us further striking images to make the point.[^EII1-269]

The idea of divine manifestation avoids two traps at once. We need not conclude, as a strict rationalism might, that God cannot be known at all. Nor need we make the divine into a material thing, subject to the ordinary facts studied by sociology and history. The unknowable God appears through forms of manifestation. Only through these forms does God become knowable, yet God always remains beyond them. In one sense, the form that reveals God is truly one with what it reveals (*zahir* and *mazhar*). Seen in its true spiritual reality (*haqiqat*), it is entirely light.

But seen as a particular, limited form, it is also shadow—the boundary that any manifestation must have if it is to appear at all.

That is why the author of *The Rose Garden of Mystery* cries out, “O Light of God, divine Shadow!” His words express one of the great themes developed by several Sufi masters: the shining Night, the “midnight sun,” the black Light, and the dark Noon. This, too, is a way to describe the position of the Seal of the Prophets at the point of balance. The image leads naturally to another set of symbols: the cosmic North, the direction of the heavenly Earth, the world of real spiritual images called the *imaginal world* (*mundus imaginalis*, *alam al-mithal*).

Thus the *qibla*—the direction of prayer—of the Seal of the Prophets is said to face neither East nor West, but to lie between them. It is equally distant from purely inner and purely outward religion, and equally distant from abstract monotheism and the claim that God becomes physically embodied in the world.[^EII1-270]

And so the sun of the prophetic Reality has reached the full light of noon. It emerged from hiding in the Land of Mystery and rose through the successive levels of divine manifestation, each represented by the life of a prophet. Now it has reached its zenith. The point occupied by the Seal of Prophecy both separates and joins the arc of prophecy to the arc of initiation. It is the *barzakh*, the meeting place or threshold between them. Together, these two arcs form the complete Cycle.

As the sun begins to descend from the zenith toward the west, shadows return and lengthen. The world necessarily enters the night of hidden spiritual meaning. The final, complete manifestation has taken place, and humanity can expect no further prophet. As we have already observed, Shiism responds to this teaching about the end of prophecy with a feeling that is less triumphant than deeply moving, even sorrowful. The Imam who completes the company of Twelve is no longer visible to ordinary human eyes.

The cycle of initiation is now the age of the Imam's concealment. He is the master of this age (*sahib al-zaman*) precisely because he is its sign. In the darkness, hostile powers threaten the vulnerable human lives of God's Friends, the pilgrims who must make their way through the night. It is the “Night of Destiny,” lasting until the dawn of Resurrection—the Imam's appearance. No one can avoid this night. And there is only one way to pass through it unharmed.[^EII1-271]

One conviction guides the Shiite believer through the night. The cycle of initiation, the cycle of *walayat* that forms prophecy's inner meaning, corresponds exactly to the cycle of prophecy. This is because prophecy is itself the outward face of *walayat*, or initiation. Every stage in the ascent of Day, along the eastern half of the circle, has its counterpart in the descent of Night, along the western half.

Each prophet, as one particular manifestation of the original Muhammadan Reality, revealed a quality that the Seal of Prophecy eventually gathered into a single fullness. Similarly, each initiate (*wali*), each Friend of God, reveals in a particular way one aspect of the perfection of the Perfect Human Being: the Seal of God's Friends, the Seal of the Initiated, the Hidden Imam of this age.

Facing each prophet on the opposite arc stands one or more of God's Friends: each eastern point has a western counterpart. Lahiji writes:

> On the ascending arc and the descending arc, a figure from among the prophets and a figure from among God's Friends face one another. In the same way, every point on the western side of a circle faces and corresponds to a point on the eastern side.[^EII1-272]

This correspondence explains why Shiite authors take particular care to show the parallel between Christ, who came immediately before the Seal of the Prophets, and the First Imam of the Muhammadan age, Ali ibn Abi Talib, who came immediately after the last Prophet.[^EII1-273]

We will have reason to examine these parallels between ideas about Christ and Shiite teachings about the Imams. One especially striking illustration seems to occur in a dream of Princess Narkes, the mother of the Twelfth Imam (see Book Seven below).

That first conviction leads to a second, which gives inner strength to every believer facing the trials of this age. From one generation to the next, the hidden order of God's Friends forms a kind of spiritual knighthood, a community invisible to physical sight. At its summit stands the small company of immediate companions of the Hidden Imam (see Chapter Three, section 4, above). Very few people know of their existence, or recognize them.

Yet without them, the rest of humanity could not even continue to exist. Through them, generation after generation, there is a continual selection of “superhuman” beings: an ascent from the humanity of Adam toward the angelic humanity represented by the supreme spiritual Pole, the Hidden Imam.

Their names are the Imam's secret: “My Friends dwell beneath my tabernacles; no one knows them but me.”

Yet *walayat* calls each believer to make this relationship real within the hidden depths of his or her own being. The believer's relationship to the Imam, the Seal of God's Friends, should mirror that of the prophets to the Seal of Prophecy. To live that relationship personally is to move through the Night with confidence—and to bring the Night itself nearer to the dawn of the Resurrector, the *Qa'im*.

We have already seen what it means to establish such a relationship: to know the Imam “of one's own age.” And there can be no knowledge of the Imam without self-knowledge. Countless experiences reported across the centuries testify to this connection and to the mysterious presence of the figure at the heart of Shiite devotion: the Twelfth Imam, the “Expected Imam,” “hidden from the senses but present in the hearts of his faithful.” His name is never spoken without the ritual blessing: “May God hasten for us the joy of his coming!”

The theme of the Hidden Imam, with which this work will conclude in Book Seven, truly crowns Shiite teaching about the Imams. As we have already seen, the sense that a permanent prophetic religion still lives in this world leads certain Shiite writers, among them Haydar Amoli, to identify the Twelfth Imam, the “Expected Imam,” with the Paraclete promised by Jesus in the Gospel of John.

The Paraclete—the Comforter, the Defender—thus takes on a prophetic radiance within this Shiite understanding, a significance that the scholarly study of religion has so far overlooked. This identification of the Imam with the Paraclete gives us a final and especially powerful example of what the sayings of the Imams teach about Shiism as a lived spiritual experience. It is a religion of *walayat*, and therefore a religion of love. For it is only through the particular form of a person's love that genuine self-knowledge becomes possible. A person comes to know himself by knowing his Imam, the “soul of his soul.” Through that knowledge he discovers himself in the form of his love—and that love is the very form of his being.[^EII1-274]

### CHAPTER VII

#### *What the Imam Means in Shiite Spiritual Life*

##### 1. *Shiism as a Religion of Spiritual Love and a Path to Self-Knowledge*

The preceding pages, especially the end of the last chapter, have already shown us where to look for the meaning of the Imam in Shiite spiritual life. One word has appeared again and again: *walayat*. We have seen that Shiism is, at heart, a religion of *walayat*. We have also begun to see why no single word in a European language can fully express it. It describes a distinctly Shiite relationship with many sides.

Yet the settings in which we have met the term tell us something essential. So does its usual Persian equivalent, *dusti*, and the Arabic words that sometimes accompany or replace it—*hibb*, *mahabbat*, and *mawaddat*. All point towards the same basic meaning: a religion of spiritual love.

Our authors often make the connection explicit. *Walayat*, they say, is *mahabbat*: devoted love. A *wali* is a *muhibb*: a friend, someone who loves. We lose that direct and deeply felt meaning when we routinely translate *wali* as “saint.” There are certainly points of overlap.

But *wali* and *walayat* reach well beyond what European languages usually mean by “saint” and “sainthood,” whether in everyday speech or in formal religious usage. Perhaps it is no surprise, then, that the heart of Shiism has so often been misunderstood. *Walayat* is its central idea. Its different meanings extend across the whole of the Shiite view of the world, and we must begin by understanding what lies at its core.[^EII1-275][^EII1-276]

The Imams themselves taught their followers to understand Shiism as devotion grounded in love. I want to draw together what that means, and how it shapes the Shiite understanding of human life and destiny. When Islam is understood as a religion of love, the Imam is not an optional addition: his place becomes essential.

At the same time, we encounter the central question of Sufism—and find it raised, confronted, and answered without yet having to speak of Sufism at all. This, as I have suggested, is the key to a spiritual situation that has received too little attention. Ultimately, the Imam's meaning for the individual believer is found within *walayat* itself. Loving the Imam becomes a path through which the believer is led towards self-knowledge. Once that knowledge begins to open, the believer understands why love of God cannot be separated from love of the Imam.

The saying “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord” becomes something that can be discovered and tested through the experience of love. Then the many descriptions of the Imams in the traditions take on their full meaning. They guide the believer towards the “Soul of the soul” (*jan-e jan*): the Imam. I have discussed elsewhere how this understanding of the Imam becomes a lived spiritual experience in Ismailism. Here I will focus on Twelver Shiism.

Let us begin with an important point. To describe Islam as a religion of love is hardly what many people expect, especially when they think of Sunni Islam as a religion centred on religious law and the observance of the *sharia*. People are generally willing to speak of love in Islam when they are speaking of Sufism.

Yet Shiite Islam itself, without any special appeal to Sufism, presents itself as the religion of *walayat*. Evidence for this fills Shiite literature. It is brought together with particular care in a monumental work we have already encountered: *Prolegomena to the Shiite Interpretation of the Qur'an*, written in seventeenth-century Isfahan by Abu'l-Hasan Sharif Isfahani, a student of the great theologian Muhammad Baqir Majlisi.[^EII1-277] This work contains an extensive collection of sayings of the Prophet and the Imams, together with commentaries on them. They present *walayat* as the inward, hidden meaning (*batin*) of the Qur'anic revelation. *Walayat* certainly helps explain the unfolding of sacred history.

But it also shapes the believer's inner life. According to Shiite teaching, a religious act has true value only when it springs from an intention of love.

Consider the well-known tradition we have already quoted several times. One Imam after another says that upholding their cause is so demanding that only an angel close to God, a prophet sent by God, or a believer whose heart God has tested for faith can bear it. Our author stresses what this and similar sayings mean: the threefold declaration of faith—God's oneness, the Prophet's revelation, and the spiritual guidance of the Imams—cannot be fully accepted without intense longing (*shawq*), wholehearted assent, and perfect love (*mahabbat kamila*) for the complete purity (*ismat*) of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones.[^EII1-278]

Indeed, the commitment to this love, to *walayat*, takes precedence over every obligation of the *sharia*. Love is what makes the fulfilment of those obligations spiritually valid; and when a person falls short, love can make up for that failure. Many sayings of the Imams make this point. One declares: “The first thing a person is asked about after death is his love for Us. If he held fast to this love (*walayat*) and died holding fast to it, then God accepts his prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and pilgrimage.

“But if he did not have this love, God accepts none of his deeds.”[^EII1-279]

In Shiite ethics, then, actions must arise from the innermost self—from the *batin*. Prayer, good deeds, and religious duties must grow out of love, or they are empty formalities. Abu'l-Hasan Sharif writes: “Our shaykh”—meaning Muhammad Baqir Majlisi—“states this explicitly in his *Bihar al-Anwar*: all the Imamis agree that deeds have spiritual validity and are accepted by God only on condition of faith (*iman*). And an essential part of faith is love for the Twelve Imams and recognition of their spiritual authority.”

Nothing could be further from a religion defined solely by its laws. The implications for Shiite Islam's place in the world reach very far. We therefore need to understand exactly why the Imam is the focus of this love. And when we speak simply of “the Imam,” the name can mean each of the Twelve or all Fourteen Immaculate Ones together. Because they share one essential reality, each is, in this sense, also all the others.

Let me explain more fully, building on what we have seen so far. Whatever we know of God is, necessarily, knowledge of God as it is given to human beings. This is true of what we discover through our own efforts, but just as true of what the hidden God (*Deus absconditus*) reveals of himself as the revealed God (*Deus revelatus*). Even revelations given to prophets reach us as knowledge intended for human understanding. The saying “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord” expresses this human dimension of our knowledge of God.

But how can we move from knowing ourselves to knowing our Lord? According to the teaching we are examining, we can do so only because the Imam is the form in which self-knowledge becomes possible: the point of connection between the human person and the hidden God. The saying becomes true through an inward realization of the teaching about the Imam. The Imam gives human form to what a human being can know of God.

And recognizing the Imam—not merely one of the Twelve, but each and all of them in their eternal reality and their role as manifestations of God—protects our belief in divine oneness (*tawhid*) from two opposite errors. One is *ta'til*, denying that God can be known through any of the qualities we speak of. The other is *tashbih*, making God resemble the things we know. Simple believers and sophisticated theologians alike can fall into either trap without realizing it.

We have already met the first danger, *ta'til*. To avoid speaking of God in merely human terms, it places the divine reality altogether beyond human language and understanding. Shiism also teaches that God transcends every name and quality that human language can express.

But if we stop there, we are left with no knowledge of God at all. We have lost the personal relationship between God and humanity that faith requires. The opposite error is to treat God's utterly transcendent essence as though it possessed the very names and qualities we give it. That is *tashbih*: describing God too much in our own image. Someone might object: “Why do I need the Imam? God is enough for me. I need no one between God and myself.”

But the speaker forgets something basic. The God of whom we speak directly is always God as revealed to us—God as known through the form in which God makes himself known. Even when we describe God as beyond all personal identity, we speak on the basis of what is shown to us, or withheld from us.

Without some form of manifestation—a *mazhar*, a form through which God appears—we could not speak of God at all. This manifestation is what is called the “Face” of God. We have already seen how important this idea is in Shiism, and have been told that the Imam is this Face. Later we shall see that the Imam is also described as the one “placed before” the believer, the one who “walks ahead of his very being” (*moqaddam ala wujudi-hi*).

If we lose this understanding of the Imam, we also lose the grounds on which our human knowledge of God—or God's revelation to humanity—can be trusted. Then we are caught between the same two mistakes. We may dismiss that knowledge as merely human and end up unable to say anything about God (*ta'til*). Or we may accept our human descriptions without recognizing what they really are, and turn them into images of God that we mistake for God himself (*tashbih*).

Only the Imam, understood as the person through whom God is revealed, protects the truth in our human knowledge while carrying us beyond its merely human limits. This helps explain why certain Sufi masters outside Shiism wrestled so intensely with the tension between these two dangers. They were trying to preserve *tawhid*: the recognition that God is One.

Yet the mystery of God's oneness is the mystery of divine solitude—“God alone is alone.” We are not speaking of the number one standing above countless other separate beings. We are speaking of the mystery by which each unique being is unique: the One appearing in endlessly many ways without ceasing to be the One.

The Face of God that remains uniquely present for each unique being is, in this teaching, the Imam. That is what the Imams express through the many names and descriptions they give themselves in their sayings. Shiite prayers draw on these names throughout a complex religious calendar. A commentary on a single prayer can therefore become an entire study of the Imam and what he means. We have already seen one such example.[^EII1-280]

The love directed towards the Imam is universal. So too is the Imam's role in making God's revelation meaningful to human beings. Without him, there could be no authentic understanding of divine oneness. Together, these ideas explain what we might call the universal outlook of Shiism: its belief that all the prophets, and everyone who has truly followed them, belong to one continuing religion of love. It embraces the spiritual descendants of Abraham throughout humanity's sacred history.

Every prophet and every true follower has professed this same *walayat*. They make up one vast spiritual body—the *corpus mysticum*. Ismaili writers, for their part, speak of the “Temple of Light” of the Imamate. To reject this bond of love would, in this understanding, also be to reject the prophetic revelations that came before Islam.

The Second Imam, Hasan ibn Ali, declares: “Whoever denies the supreme standing of the Commander of the Faithful [Ali, the First Imam] contradicts the Torah, the Gospel, the Psalms, the writings of Abraham, and every other Book that God has sent down from heaven. For after the witness to God's oneness (*tawhid*) and to the mission of the prophets, the most important testimony in all these Books is the recognition of *walayat* towards Ali and the Imams.”[^EII1-281]

This follows from another saying we already know. The Prophet declares that the Imam was sent secretly with every earlier prophet, but was sent openly with him, the Seal of the Prophets. *Walayat*—the divine love given to the full company of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones—is the inward secret of every revelation entrusted to the prophets. It is the secret of the Hidden Treasure that longs to be known. The Imam is that Treasure becoming knowable and capable of being loved. Christian theologians have asked how people living before the historical event of Redemption could have been saved, given that Redemption took place at a particular moment in history.

But we are beginning to see why the question cannot be framed in quite that way within a prophetic religion understood as continuous from Adam to the final Imam.

Long before the Seal of the Prophets, earlier prophets brought humanity the same message. They called people to the same religion of love for the divine Face revealed to each of them. Acceptance of that love was their paradise; refusal was their hell. In a long conversation with his disciple Mufaddal, the Sixth Imam explains that the Imam is the one who separates those destined for paradise from those destined for hell. He does not even have to judge them: their love or hatred of the Imam already constitutes their paradise or hell.

In this sense, Ridwan, the angel of paradise, and Malik, the guardian of hell, may be understood as proceeding from the Imam's command.[^EII1-282] It has been this way since the first prophetic missions, and will remain so throughout the cycle of *walayat*. “The Shiites find salvation through an act of love for their Imam.” This saying brings to mind, in certain respects, the idea of salvation in Pure Land Buddhism.

As he introduces his disciple to the mystery of this universal religion of love, encompassing all believers, Imam Ja'far ends with a warning: “Mufaddal, keep all this carefully. It is a treasure of secret, hidden knowledge. Show it only to those worthy of receiving it.”

Why must the Treasure remain hidden? Because only someone who can see from a much wider spiritual horizon is ready for it. We have already approached that horizon in the mystery of the primordial Muhammadan Reality and the existence of pure spiritual beings before their earthly lives. There, in the world of Spirit, everything takes place before earthly creatures and individual human histories come into being. Every prophet, in this understanding, proclaimed the same eternal Imam, the one who is, as we saw in Chapter V, the “place” where the mission and message of the prophets become manifest. This is what Imam Ja'far is trying to explain.

At first Mufaddal cannot understand. How could prophets who lived earlier have loved the Imam? How could their followers or opponents have found paradise or hell in loving or rejecting him? Ja'far answers: “Do you not know that God Most High sent his Messenger—that is, a Spirit, the prophetic Word—to the prophets, who were themselves spirits created two thousand years before the creation of earthly beings? Do you not know that this Spirit called them to the threefold declaration of faith?”

Once again, Shiite spiritual philosophy places sacred history within a reality beyond historical time, where what exists before earthly life and what exists after it are present together. The number used to express the precedence of the spiritual world can vary; it measures a different kind of time, a “subtle time.”

The distinction between before and after, and the rule that time cannot run backwards, belong to the order of events in our ordinary historical time—the “dense” or “opaque” time (*zaman kathif*). They do not apply in the same way to events that remain present together in the world of Spirit. In the Imam's explanation there is no mistaken chronology, nor an impossible placing of one historical event before another. There is a complete togetherness of events that we can understand only from the spiritual horizon opened by the teaching about the Imam.

This same understanding lies behind the idea of a single spiritual body formed by everyone who has ever followed, or now follows, this eternal religion of *walayat*. The source of that love is God himself, revealing himself through those who are the objects of his love. And because God loves them, they possess a special claim—one that was invoked even before their earthly lifetimes. This is already an answer to Mufaddal's question.

In a tradition about the Prophet's ascent to heaven, at the moment when he was “at the distance of two bows” mentioned in the Surah of the Star (53:9), the Prophet tells Ali that he heard God say: “I wrote your Name and his Name upon my Throne before I created any creatures, out of my love for you both. Whoever loves you and takes you as friends is counted among those brought near to Me. Whoever rejects your *walayat* and turns away from you is counted among the ungodly who break faith.”

This tradition has several versions and has been pondered endlessly in Shiism.[^EII1-283] It points to the very source of *walayat*: God's own love, the love of the Hidden Treasure for the primordial Light that comes from it and reveals it to created beings. That divine love, in turn, is the source of the love (*walayat* and *mahabbat*) that believers feel for the Fourteen primordial Figures of Light who first received it. It is also the foundation of Shiite ethical life.

Two familiar Persian terms express the principle: *tawalla wa tabarra*. One must take God's friends and the friends of those friends as one's own, and turn away from their enemies. From the very beginning, moreover, God's special love gives those whom he has loved from eternity a kind of claim (*haqq*) upon him.

This explains a striking expression often used in Shiite prayers. It sounds almost like a final, irresistible appeal: by invoking the claim that God himself has granted his friends, the person praying seems to invoke a promise whose fulfilment is already assured. The Imams themselves used the words *bi-haqqina*: “by the right granted to us,” or “in the name of our cause.”

In some passages, this appeal to the Imams' “right” also answers Mufaddal's question. Because the right has its origin beyond historical time, prophets could invoke it long before the Imams appeared in their earthly lives. The way events become present together here may seem bewildering from the standpoint of ordinary history.

Yet it is the key to sacred history. Again and again, invoking this right—appealing “in the name of this cause”—brings each prophet's earthly trial to its resolution. It is for the sake of this cause that God “turned again to Adam” after his exile from paradise. And because the same cause is the secret behind the Qur'anic account of Christ being saved from death and raised up by God (4:156), its invocation by the prophets rules out even the possibility of killing God.

A tradition going back through the Eighth Imam, Ali Rida, to earlier Imams declares: “When Noah was in danger of drowning, he called upon God in the name of our cause [or our right], and God saved him from the waters. When Abraham was thrown into the fire, he called upon God in the name of our cause, and God made the fire cool and harmless.

“When Moses opened a path through the sea, he called upon God in the name of our cause, and God turned the sea into dry ground. And when the Jews sought to kill Jesus, he called upon God in the name of our cause; so God saved him from death and raised him up to himself [Qur'an 4:156].”[^EII1-284]

Another account, one among many, expresses the same idea: all the prophets belong to this single religion of *walayat*, and events that seem separated by centuries are joined at a deeper level. Here the Fifth Imam, Muhammad Baqir, speaks with his disciple Jabir al-Ju'fi. Their conversation belongs to a group of traditions offering Shiite interpretations of the Hebrew Bible. “I asked the Imam,” the disciple recalls, “whether Daniel's interpretation of dream visions was genuine. ‘Yes, it was genuine,’ he answered.

“‘Daniel truly received a revelation from God, because he was a prophet (*nabi*). He was among those whom God taught the hidden meaning of events (*ta'wil al-ahadith*). He was truthful and wise. And the divine religion he followed was the religion of love for us—the Prophet's Household (*Ahl al-Bayt*).’” This makes sense only within the vision of the primordial Muhammadan Reality.

Jabir does not yet see that. Surprised, he asks the same question that Mufaddal asked Ja'far: “Love for you? For the Prophet's Household?” The Imam replies: “Yes, by God! There has never been a prophet or an angel who did not follow the religion of love for us (*illa wa kana yadinu bi-mahabbatina*).”[^EII1-285]

The meaning could hardly be clearer. We are speaking of a “religion of love,” and the speaker is not a Sufi master but the Fifth Shiite Imam. In this understanding, the followers of every prophet have always belonged to that religion, because love for the divine Face revealed to them was the hidden heart of every prophetic message.

We have now reached the centre of our question. We have seen why *walayat* is understood as the enduring prophetic religion of humanity: “the Imam was sent secretly with each prophet.” We have also seen what the Imam means for sacred history—for the history of spiritual events that unfold in a kind of time different from the time of ordinary earthly history.

We can now begin to grasp his meaning for Shiite spiritual life itself. Shiism's universal outlook rests on the belief that love for the divine Face reaches across all times and peoples.

But to recognize this Face, each person must turn towards self-knowledge. Love is not simply added to faith; it is part of faith's very foundation. Through that love, Shiism sees all true believers as members of one enduring prophetic community, called to seek the Soul of their soul. The movement from the Imam's role in sacred history to his role in each person's innermost life is itself an example of the principle of Shiite interpretation that has guided our discussion throughout this book.

The sacred Book remains alive throughout our present age because its inner meaning—the meaning of *walayat*—continues to unfold in every new believer. From one period of the prophetic cycle to another, sacred history preserves an underlying pattern. The same kinds of people return, both those who carry the message and those who resist it. Faith kindles the same enthusiasm, and the same active refusal rises against it.

The names and the individual actors change, but the roles in the drama remain. This continuing pattern is expressed by the distinction between the prophets' missions, which come to an end, and *walayat*, which is eternal. It is also expressed in the relationship joining every prophet and every person of spiritual knowledge to the “Seal of the Prophets” and the “Seal of God's Friends.” Because *walayat* is the inward secret of the same message repeated from prophet to prophet until the final Prophet, it joins them and their followers in a single spiritual body, the *corpus mysticum*—the Temple of Light of the Imamate.

But what does it mean to belong to that body? How does love of the Imam make a believer—someone “whose heart God has tested”—a member of this spiritual community, ultimately described as the *Ahl al-Bayt*, the members of the holy Family, the prophetic “house” or “temple”? And how, in the First Imam's own words, does the believer whose heart has been tested discover that love within himself?

We already know that, without the Imamate, the hidden God (*Deus absconditus*) could be approached only through a theology of negation—the way of *tanzih*, which Christian tradition calls *apophatic* or “negative” theology. Only through God's revealed Face, the form in which he appears (*mazhar*), can the hidden God become someone we can know and love: *Deus revelatus*, God as revealed.

Yet to say that the Imam is this Face, this revealed form, is to say far more than something theoretical about God. It reaches directly into a believer's personal life. To accept it means entering into an actual relationship. And recognizing the Imam as the form through which God appears is, at the same time, the beginning of self-knowledge.

When the believer comes to know himself in this way, he becomes a form through which the Imam is revealed, just as the Imam is the form through which the hidden God is revealed. This is why the Fifth Imam could say: “We are God's treasurers and God's treasures in this world and the next”—we shall return to the fuller meaning of this statement—“and our Shiites are our treasurers and our treasures.” The Imamate contains, as a treasure, divine knowledge. And in every Shiite believer whose heart has been tested, some part of the knowledge of the Imam comes to life.

This theme is explored with remarkable depth in the writings of an important Iranian shaykh from the previous century, Hajj Muhammad Karim Khan Kermani (died 1870; see Book VI below). Unfortunately, I can give only the briefest account of his argument. In one chapter of a major work, he shows that love of God is realized through love of the Imams. More fundamentally still, there can be no love of God that is not, at the same time, love of them. The chapter develops a saying of the First Imam: “No person whose heart God has tested for faith has failed, in the end, to discover our love within that heart.”[^EII1-286]

What we most need to take from Kermani's demanding argument is a movement in two stages.

First, all knowledge and love of God prove to be knowledge and love of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones—or simply of the Imam, whose person gathers their whole company into one. Second, as the believer lives out that relationship, knowledge of the Imam becomes knowledge of the believer's own self.[^EII1-286]

**1.** We have said that the Imam gives human meaning to whatever human beings can know of God, whether through their own understanding or through divine revelation. As the one towards whom *walayat* is directed, the Imam also makes it possible for human beings to love God and gives that love its meaning. Muhammad Karim Khan Kermani examines this idea with exceptional care.

At the deepest level of the divine essence (*kunh al-dhat*)—the reality beyond every essence, which philosophers call *hyperousion* and which may be compared with Meister Eckhart's *Grund*—God is absolutely one, utterly alone, pure, and undivided. Nothing can be said of this reality. No name or description applies to it; it resembles nothing, and nothing resembles it. As such, it cannot be the object of one particular being's love, nor can its love be directed towards one particular being.

Love, after all, calls for some likeness or proportion between two beings, so that each can move towards the other and they can come together. The divine love that belongs to this highest, unknowable level—the love of the Hidden Treasure longing to be known—embraces everything that exists. It is what gives existence the weight that overcomes nonexistence. This is the meaning associated with the universal divine Will (*mashiat amma kawniya*), which is examined in the philosophy of existence.

Theologians, however, have another task: to reflect on a particular divine Will (*mashiat khassa shariya*), a Will that relates to distinct beings and things, loving some and rejecting others in their particularity. The place in which divine Will becomes manifest (*mahall*), in both the philosophical and the religious sense, is formed by the primordial Figures of Light: the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. Many traditions of the Imams describe them in this way.

Because they are where divine Will becomes manifest in both senses, their complete company forms the passage from what cannot be reached or described to what can be known and revealed. In a certain sense, then, they are that Will itself: the manifestation it wills to bring forth. They are God's Names, the bearers of attributes that cannot be ascribed to God's essence beyond all description. They are the *ma'ani*: the positive meanings through which the divine intentions are expressed in the Names and Attributes.[^EII1-287]

In short, they are the forms in which God can be known by human beings—what Kermani calls God's *knowability* (*marufiya*). A person whose deepest life comes to resemble theirs becomes capable of entering into the relationship with God, “because the Fourteen Immaculate Ones are themselves that relationship.”

To love them is therefore to love God. They are not only the way in which God can be known, but also the way in which God can be loved—God's *being an object of love* (*mahbubiya*). And whoever is loved by them is loved by God, because they are God's own love, the way in which God is the one who loves (*muhibbiya*). Notice how well classical Arabic serves this sort of philosophical thought: from a word meaning “the one who acts” or “the one acted upon,” it can form an abstract noun naming the corresponding state or quality.

A person who has come to share something of the Imams' spiritual nature, whose innermost life is shaped by their example and whose love for them reaches every part of his being, is drawn into union with their own souls—their very selves (*bi-anfusihim*). This is the complete and specially favoured believer (*mu'min khasis kamil*), who, like Salman the Persian, is taken into the holy Family (*Ahl al-Bayt*) in this world and the next.

The Shiite believer is said to be “created from the rays of their light.” That light is the very substance of the believer's being. The form it takes depends on how fully the person is able to receive it. This gives rise to different degrees of spiritual life, as we saw earlier (III, §4). Only through this likeness can a human being love God. Without it, the absolute difference between God and humanity would rule out a relationship of love.

God becomes knowable and lovable through the form in which God appears. In that revealed form, the lover, the beloved, and love itself are united. That form is the Imam. It safeguards the truth of divine oneness from both of the dangers we have examined. And here lies the secret of the Imam's life within every believer: he is the one who stands ahead of the believer's being, the centre from which everything begins and to which everything returns.

**2.** It is precisely because the Imam lives within the spiritual life of the believer that he can lead the believer towards self-knowledge. As the highest object of knowledge and love, he reveals the Self that is the Soul of one's soul. Every Shiite—and indeed every human being—has a highest thought, a furthest limit of understanding. No one can pass beyond that limit without losing the very form of his or her own being.

Yet the fact that this is our *highest* thought also tells us that something greater lies beyond it.

We cannot reach that further reality by simply breaking through the limit of what we are. Kermani explains that reaching the highest point *within* our being—the reality that stands “ahead of our being”—is what it means to “reach ourselves.” This is the *nafs*: the self understood as soul or heart, the most personal centre of life, the Self that is the Soul of the soul.

Hence the saying, “Whoever knows his own soul knows his God.” We are speaking, of course, about someone for whom this spiritual level has become a lasting state, not a momentary experience. At that highest point, what is otherwise beyond all reach becomes accessible in the only way it can. The person does not have to leave behind the limits of the self, make the transcendent God fit the self, or try to make the self fit an utterly transcendent God. Without the Imam, each of these attempts would endanger the very understanding of divine oneness it was meant to preserve.

The relation between knowing ourselves, knowing the Imam, and knowing God becomes clearer through what we might call Kermani's account of the Highest (*al-ali*, what is above) and the lowest (*al-dani*, what is below). The Highest cannot descend as it is, in such a way that the lowest could directly perceive and understand it. The absolute difference between them would remain, still making knowledge and love impossible. Nor can the Highest descend by changing its own essence, giving up its true nature so that it becomes like the lowest.

But there is another possibility. Kermani writes:

> If this descent takes place not by altering or emptying the Highest of its nature, but through a manifestation of God (*tajalli*), an appearance (*zuhur*), an attribute (*sifat*), a Light (*nur*), then we have found what we are looking for. For if this manifestation did not correspond to the faculties through which Shiite believers perceive (*masha'ir*), we would still face the same problem.

> But if it does correspond to them, the manifestation has something in common with the believers. It belongs to their own being, and they can reach it.

> What is present in the manifestation is also present within them. Otherwise, it would make no sense to require them to reach it.
>
> So the Highest makes itself known to the lowest through an attribute that the lowest can perceive, know, and understand. This is the highest level the lowest can reach, the furthest point of its thought. It is its own soul—its self (*nafs*)—and its heart. As the tradition says: “Whoever knows himself, his own soul, knows his Lord.” The Qur'an points towards the same truth: “And within yourselves are signs. Do you not see?” (51:21). And again: “We shall show them Our signs on the horizons and within their souls”—that is, within themselves (41:53).
>
> In this way, God makes himself known to Shiite believers through their own selves, their own souls. When they come to know themselves, they have fulfilled what is asked of them: they have reached the one who stands ahead of their being, their Imam [...]. They are manifestations of their Imam, just as the Imams are the manifestation and meaning of God. It is of them that the *Ziyarat al-Jami'a* says (see Chapter V above): “Peace be upon those whom, if you know them, you know God, and if you do not know them, you do not know God.”[^EII1-288]

Kermani's words, together with our discussion so far, lead to a clear conclusion. The Imam is the form in which God becomes manifest (*mazhar*). Through that form, God can be known and loved. To reach it is to reach knowledge of God, because it is the only form in which God can be known.

For the human being, it is therefore the highest possible level of existence, understanding, and love. Every manifestation of God creates a relationship between the one who reveals himself (*mutajalli*) and the one to whom he appears (*mutajalla lahu*). What appears must take a form suited to the person receiving it. Ibn Arabi had already insisted on this point.

But here the relationship is understood specifically through the teaching about the Imam. It is this teaching that makes the relationship possible without compromising God's oneness.

A manifestation of God (*tajalli*) is possible because the form in which God appears has something in common with the person who receives it. And because that manifestation is the highest reality that a person living in this lower world can reach, to arrive at its “place”—the believer's own mystical Mount Sinai—is to reach the summit, or the deepest centre, of one's being: the self, the soul (*nafs*). The form in which God appears there, the Face revealed at the summit of the soul, is the Imam. This is why knowing oneself, knowing one's soul and all that belongs to its world, means knowing one's Imam. And for each person, that is what knowing the Lord means.

The Imam is the form taken by the revealed God (*Deus revelatus*) when self-knowledge becomes knowledge of God. The Imam is the form through which I know and love God. When a believer comes to know the Imam, this knowledge reveals itself as the very form of the believer's love—and therefore as the secret of the believer's existence, because that existence is itself an act of love. That is why love of the Imam, the religion of *walayat*, is also an initiation into self-knowledge.

In the Shiite understanding, it embraces the whole of an eternal prophetic religion and the followers of every prophet. The Self it reveals is not an empty, impersonal Absolute. It is the Soul and Beloved of the soul (*jan-e jan*): a “you” at the centre of my “I,” the one who “walks ahead of me.” This is the Imam, in the original meaning of the word itself.

Shiite devotion and spiritual life thus reach their fullest expression in *walayat*, love directed towards the Imam as the form through which the hidden God reveals himself. It is through this form that the hidden God becomes someone who can be loved—God's *lovability* (*mahbubiya*). In that sense, every love of God, simply because it is love directed towards a God who can be loved, is *walayat* towards the Imam. Sufis outside Shiism struggled to find such a way forward, longing to escape what Ruzbihan calls the “madness of the unreachable.”

What matters here is that Shiism itself has already asked the question and answered it through the teaching about the Imam. This is the meaning of the many titles given to the Imam in Shiite prayers. The titles echo those the Imams use for themselves in their sayings: Guide, Pole, *A'raf*, Witness of God, and others. Each points back to the same central insight. To know oneself is to know the Imam; and knowing the Imam is knowing God, because no other knowledge of God is available to human beings.

We can explore only the titles I have just mentioned. To bring this account of Shiite spiritual life to a close, I want to show how they were understood by thinkers for whom philosophical reflection could never be separated from personal spiritual practice and experience. Above all, I shall turn again to Mulla Sadra Shirazi, whose work we have encountered so often already.

Along with Saleh Mazandarani, Mohsen Fayz, Qazi Sa'id Qummi, and others, Mulla Sadra belongs to a group of Shiite thinkers who produced immense works of commentary on the sayings of the Imams. Their writings help explain why their philosophy is sometimes called “prophetic and Imamic wisdom” (*hikmat nabawiya wa walawiya*, the second adjective coming from *wali*). At other times they call it “Yemeni divine wisdom” (*hikmat yamaniya*), a reference to the symbolic meaning of Yemen and the Yemeni corner of the Kaaba. The expression also recalls a saying that plays on the similar sounds of *iman*, meaning faith, and *Yaman*, meaning Yemen: “Faith comes from Yemen, and wisdom—divine wisdom—is Yemeni.”[^EII1-289][^EII1-290]

“Yemeni divine wisdom” and “Eastern divine wisdom”—the Illuminationist teaching (*Ishraq*) of Suhrawardi, an especially Iranian and Islamic form of Neoplatonism—draw their strength from the same sources. Both look to the traditions of *walayat* and to the Imam as a Figure of Light, the Face of God who reveals himself only by remaining veiled. From this comes the understanding of the Imam as the Witness of God. At the highest point of the believer's soul, the Imam is the believer's living awareness of God—the witness within who bears witness to a God otherwise beyond all reach.

In Mulla Sadra's work, to which we shall return particularly in these final pages, this becomes a philosophy of the witness and the act of witnessing. The person who contemplates and the reality contemplated become one. Existence itself is understood through *presence*: the soul's growing presence in more and more worlds. As it becomes present to those worlds, it is freed from confinement to this mortal world.

The understanding of the Imam as part of spiritual experience undoubtedly shaped Mulla Sadra's philosophy of existence. Rather than giving first place to the fixed natures of things, as older philosophy often did, he gives priority to *existing itself* (see Book V below).

But the journey towards self-knowledge requires the possibility of a transformation that reaches into the very substance of a being. Mulla Sadra calls this “substantial movement” (*harakat jawhariya*), and it is fundamental to his philosophy. It is also the key to the *Mabda'* and the *Ma'ad*—the beginning and the return—which open the possibility of sensing transformations that took place before we can remember, and future renewals of our existence. The two “arcs,” one of descent and one of return, enclose a vision of existence far wider than what the West has usually meant by evolution.

##### 2. The Imam as Guide and Spiritual Centre

Everything we have discussed so far has brought this central idea of prophetic philosophy into view. Here, we need only bring its essential points together. The first is the question we have put so directly: what happens after the Prophet is gone, when there will be no further prophet? The true meaning of his revelation cannot be found in the outward words alone.

Nor can anyone arrive at it simply by constructing an argument or drawing a series of conclusions. It can be revealed and passed on only by someone who *knows*. The Shiite traditions answer this question by joining the Imam and the Qur'an into a single, inseparable reality: the Qur'an is **the silent Imam**, and the Imam is **the speaking Qur'an**.

As the speaking Qur'an, the Imam is the guide who is always present: the one who leads people into the true meaning of Qur'anic revelation and keeps the Book alive as God's living word. We have already discussed sayings of the Fifth Imam that anticipate and overcome the danger of reducing revelation to the history of the time in which it appeared. The Sixth Imam, Ja'far al-Sadiq, makes the same point when he tests one of his disciples. “Abu Muhammad,” he asks, “the Prophet was the Warner, and Ali was the Guide.

“But is there a Guide (*hadi*) today?” His disciple replies, “Yes, may my life be given for yours! In your family, one guide has always followed another, down to you.” The Imam answers, “May God have mercy on you, Abu Muhammad! If a verse revealed on the occasion of a particular person's life were to die when that person died, the entire Book would be dead by now.

“But no! The Qur'an is alive. It will continue to find its fulfilment among people in the future, just as it did among those who lived in the past.”[^EII1-291][^EII1-292]

The meaning could hardly be clearer. If we could understand the sacred Book only by relating it to “its own time,” to the social and historical circumstances in which its verses first appeared, the Qur'an would have been dead for centuries. Without the continuing *walayat*—the spiritual bond and authority of God's Friends—in this world, the Book of God would have no future. The life of the Imam and the life of the sacred Book depend on each other.

The Imam and his companions must therefore remain present in the world. This was the subject of the First Imam's conversation with Komayl ibn Ziyad, quoted above (III, 3). We had already encountered the idea of a spiritual centre, or *pole*, without which the human world itself could not endure.[^EII1-293] Mulla Sadra echoes the First Imam when he writes: “The Earth can never be without an Imam, a guide for every age. Otherwise the Qur'an would have to die when those who sustain it die.

“But the Qur'an is alive and will never die before the Day of Resurrection. At every moment, until the final Hour, someone living guides people towards it.”[^EII1-294][^EII1-295][^EII1-296]

This is precisely what we find throughout the sayings collected in the chapter of Kolayni's great work devoted to the Imam as Guide and as God's witness and guarantor (*Hojjat*): the one who speaks for God before humanity. We should remember some of these sayings, in which the Imams show their unwavering awareness of who they are. The Fifth Imam, Muhammad Baqir, declares: “God is my witness!

“From the moment Adam's soul was taken—that is, from Adam's death—God has never allowed an earthly world to exist without an Imam to guide people towards Him. That Imam is God's witness before His servants, and the world is never left without an Imam who stands before humanity as that witness and guide.” The Tenth Imam, Ali Naqi, says: “Truly, the earthly world is never without a witness and guide. And God is my witness: at this moment, I am that person.”[^EII1-297]

Abu Hamza, a disciple of the Sixth Imam, recalls: “I asked Imam Ja'far, ‘Can the Earth remain without an Imam?’ He answered, ‘If the Earth were left without an Imam, it would sink away.’”[^EII1-298] The Fifth Imam also says: “If the Imam were taken away from the Earth for even an hour, the Earth would heave in waves, tossing its inhabitants as the sea tosses the creatures living within it.”[^EII1-299]

These declarations suggest a mysterious bond—almost a sacred bond—between the Imam's presence and the continuing existence of the human world. Several consequences follow.

First, the need for an Imam is plainly not just another political or social question. It concerns the unseen order and structure of reality itself. The Imam is the spiritual Pole, the Pole of poles (*qotb al-aqtab*), the centre on which the world depends.

Mulla Sadra explains this in a particularly dense passage. The need for an Imam expresses an inner law of existence: every higher level of being is the goal towards which the level below it moves. The lower level exists through the higher one, and can reach fulfilment only in it. The lower level therefore presupposes the higher; the reverse is not true. This is more than a law of development. It is a movement upwards towards a higher kind of being that already exists.

Humanity follows the same pattern. It can reach fulfilment only at the highest level of human perfection. This is what the Imamate means. “The degree of the Imamate,” Mulla Sadra explains, “means the Perfect Human Being (*al-insan al-kamil*, *anthropos teleios*), who is the king of the earthly world.”[^EII1-300]

But this kingship belongs to the Perfect Human Being as the very goal of existence. It does not arise from political circumstances, or depend on them. To treat the Imam simply as a rival to the Umayyads or Abbasids would place him on the wrong level altogether. We are dealing with something that social history alone cannot describe: a form of kingship that does not, by its nature, require political success in this world. Still less does it depend on the claim that majorities are always right because they are the ones who “make” history.

Another history is unfolding without their knowing it. It is the history of a hidden spiritual kingship over the visible world—something like the role played by the guardians of the Grail.

Other consequences follow immediately. As we have seen, the idea that the Imam might remain unknown was already present in the Prophet's declarations limiting the Imams of his own line to twelve. With a fixed number of Imams, the Imamate must eventually enter a state of concealment (*ghaybat*). The Shiite believer's present relationship with the Imam, as the spiritual centre of their own being, is therefore not a relationship with an institution in this world. It is a relationship with a world beyond what the physical senses can perceive. The Twelfth Imam appeared briefly in the earthly world, but his continuing presence is now invisible.

This means that his mode of existence transcends the ordinary biological conditions of earthly life. Such a presence can be experienced only in visions or through encounters in which his identity remains hidden.

Yet this invisible presence lies at the centre of Shiite devotion. Ordinary believers and scholars alike live in a sense of familiarity with the Imam (see Book Seven below). He need not be visible to the physical eye, any more than he needs to be known or recognised by the masses or by worldly rulers.

Being an Imam is intrinsic to what he is: the Perfect Human Being. Human ignorance or blindness cannot take that away from him. Here we reach the fundamental difference between the Shiite understanding of the Imam as guide and spiritual centre and the Sunni understanding of the Imam. The two concepts cannot be reduced to one another.
