We have already stressed this difference when discussing Mulla Sadra's treatment of a long account of the Imam by the Sunni theologian and philosopher Fakhr al-Din Razi.[^EII1-301] In the Shiite understanding, the Imam is the centre on which the coherence and unity of existence depend. His presence is necessary at the deepest level of reality. His task is to lead people into spiritual knowledge, and it opens towards the events of the last days, when the Twelfth Imam is to appear as the Mahdi. His role and its necessity belong to what he is. They do not change according to whether people recognise him.

In the Sunni account discussed here, by contrast, the Imam is the centre of social order, and there is no need to appeal to the hidden structure of reality to explain his role. He is necessary because of the requirements of life in this world. The concept is not sacred in the sense of giving the universe a sacred structure; it belongs to public and political life.

Neither the Imam's person nor his office requires the kind of spiritual necessity or end-time role found in the Shiite account. Consequently, this view does not require him to know the *ta'wil*, the inner meanings of the Qur'an; to possess knowledge inspired directly by God (*ilm laduni*); or to be protected from every impurity and failure (*isma*). Choosing him is therefore a matter of agreement among people: he is elected.

The Shiite reply is that people can elect a political leader or president, or appoint someone to religious office, but it makes no sense to speak of *electing* a prophet or an Imam. Their special calling is not created by human choice. More than that, most people cannot even perceive the quality that makes them what they are.

As the saying puts it: “My Friends (*awliya'i*) are hidden beneath My tents; no one knows them but Me.” And consider the saying we have just seen at the heart of Shiite spirituality: “Whoever dies without knowing the Imam of their time dies the death of those who know nothing.” To apply that saying to the Sunni idea of the Imam described here would not merely empty it of meaning. It would make it monstrous.

This brings us to an objection Sunnis have often raised against Shiites, and to the Shiite answer. The objection runs as follows: “You say the Imam is necessary because God has made him necessary. In that case his rule should never be interrupted; there should be no concealment (*ghaybat*).

“But you also call him a gift of divine grace. Either he is necessary, in which case he is not a gift of grace, or he is a gift of grace, in which case he is not necessary.”

The Shiite response is: “The Imam's existence remains a gift of divine grace, whether he exercises political power or not. As the Commander of the Faithful [the First Imam] said: ‘The earthly world is never left without someone who speaks for God, whether openly and with public recognition, or secretly and unknown to others.

“Otherwise the signs of God and His manifestation would disappear from the Earth.’ The Imam's freedom to exercise outward rule would be another gift of grace. The prophetic mission that brought religious law has reached its end and been sealed; but the Imamate, which is the inner meaning of prophecy, endures until the Day of Resurrection. This remains true whether people recognise the Imam or reject him.

“A messenger of God is still a messenger even if no one believes his message, as happened, for example, with Noah. In the same way, the Imam remains an Imam even if no human being recognises him. A doctor does not cease to be a doctor simply because no patient comes seeking treatment or healing. The same is true of the doctors of the soul, who treat spiritual sickness and the afflictions of the heart: the prophets and God's Friends.”[^EII1-302]

The answer is unmistakable: the Imam remains the Imam under all circumstances, even when he must carry out his mission in secret. Public opinion, official recognition, or the absence of recognition tells us nothing about whether his presence is necessary. The Imamate and the prophetic mission form a single reality in their deepest nature (*haqiqat wahida bi'l-dhat*).

The line of Imams therefore continues, whether openly or in concealment, in order to preserve the Prophet's spiritual inheritance—not to maintain any particular political order. In fact, apart from the First Imam, none of the Twelve exercised earthly political authority. Yet each was fully an Imam. This is central to Shiism and shapes its understanding of Islam.

We have been told that the Prophet and the Imam do not exist merely because human beings need them to manage their religious and worldly affairs. Of course, the proper conduct of those affairs presupposes their existence.

But the Earth continues to exist through the Imam for a deeper, spiritual reason: his level of being is that of the Perfect Human Being. Because the Perfect Human Being is the purpose and ultimate goal (*ghayat*, *telos*) of the earthly world, the human world could not even continue to exist without him.[^EII1-303]

This is precisely the meaning of the mysterious existence of the Twelfth Imam, “hidden from the senses but present in the hearts of his followers.” He is the spiritual Pole of existence, and that is what he remains. His Imamate does not depend on anyone recognising him. As we have said, the line of Imams is not just another dynasty among other dynasties. An Imam is not a *claimant* to the Imamate. He **is** the Imam. “We are like the Israelites among Pharaoh's people,” declared the Fourth Imam.[^EII1-304] The line of Imams has withdrawn into concealment, like the last guardian of the Grail.

Yet through this line there continues, without interruption until the Last Day, the *silsilat al-irfan*: the living succession of spiritual knowledge that the First Imam taught his disciple Komayl ibn Ziyad.[^EII1-305] The spiritual centre of this succession is the Twelfth Imam, the Imam now in concealment. Those who belong to it recognise and are recognised by the people who call themselves the people of the *A'raf*. This gives the Imam's role in Shiite spirituality an even deeper meaning: he guides us towards knowledge of ourselves.

##### 3. The Imam as the A'raf

The *A'raf* is the mysterious barrier mentioned in the Qur'an between Paradise and Hell. The seventh sura takes its name from it.[^EII1-306] In verses 44–45, we read: “On the A'raf stand people who recognise each person by their appearance” (7:44). A disciple relates an answer given by the Sixth Imam, who repeats a saying of the First Imam, when someone asks about the people of the A'raf:

> “It is we [the Imams] who stand upon the A'raf. We recognise our companions by their faces. And we ourselves are the A'raf, because God can be known only through knowing us. We are the A'raf because, on the Day of Resurrection, God knows us as the Way (*sirat*). No one enters Paradise except those who know us and whom we know. No one enters the Fire except those who deny us and whom we deny.

> “Had God Most High wished, He could have made Himself known to humanity directly. Instead, He made us His thresholds, His way, His path, the Face towards which people must turn. Whoever turns away from our *walayat*—refusing us the devotion of love—or prefers others to us, turns away from the Way.”[^EII1-307]

The Imam's answer moves through three stages, until the Imam and the A'raf are identified with one another. Mulla Sadra begins by showing how commentators concerned only with the outward meaning of scripture have largely missed the point. Even interpreters outside Shiism who seek hidden meanings have failed to grasp what is essential about the A'raf. He therefore follows the Imam's words one phrase at a time, looking for an interpretation rooted in the Imams' own teaching.[^EII1-308] The name *A'raf* comes from the Arabic root *'rf*, associated with knowing and recognising. Once we understand that connection, we can follow the three steps in the Imam's answer.

**1.** At the first level, the Imam says: “It is we [the Twelve Imams] who stand upon the A'raf.” This means that they stand at the summit of knowledge (*ma'rifat*), its highest point. The height is spiritual, not a location somewhere in physical space.

**2.** At the second level, something remarkable happens. The Imam no longer says simply that the Imams stand upon the A'raf; he says that **they are the A'raf itself**. In other words, all human knowledge of God passes through knowing them. They are not merely people who know, whose knowledge stands at the summit of all knowledge. They are also what makes this knowledge possible. They are the very reality reached by the highest knowledge—its object as well as its source.

Here a person's name, or the quality that defines that person, is used to name the thing itself: in this case, knowledge, of which the Imams are the source. At the first level of the answer, *A'raf* refers to knowledge or direct spiritual understanding (*ma'rifat*). “We stand at the summit of the A'raf” means: we stand at the highest point of that understanding.

At the second level, *A'raf* names the cause of this knowledge, the reality that makes it possible. “We are the A'raf” means: through us, human beings are able to know God. We are what human knowledge of God reaches, because we are the form in which God becomes manifest—a *theophany*.

To put it another way, knowledge of God (*ma'rifat Allah*) is possible only for the person who knows the Imams. We have already seen that the Imam is the form in which God reveals Himself. The Imam is the “Face” through which God is known, the form God necessarily takes in any human knowledge or experience of Him. Without that Face, God remains entirely hidden, the *Absconditum*. As the A'raf, the Imam is this supreme Face: the one through whom human knowledge of God becomes possible.

We recognise here the meaning of the Imam for Shiite spiritual life that we examined earlier. The Imams themselves teach the connection between two sayings. An Imam can say, “Whoever knows us knows their Lord.” And the spiritual teachers repeatedly say, “Whoever knows themselves—their own soul—knows their Lord.” The two sayings belong together because, in knowing one's deepest self, or soul (*anima*), one comes to know one's Imam. And whoever knows their Imam knows their Lord.

Thus the ideas of the Imam and the deepest Self meet: to know one's Imam is to know oneself; to know oneself is to know one's Imam—the Soul of one's soul—and therefore to know one's Lord.[^EII1-309]

What Shiite spirituality offers through the persons of the Twelve Imams, through their “forms of light,” is access to this self-knowledge without which there can be no knowledge of God. It is an awareness of the personal relationship through which God is present *as this particular God, appearing in this particular way*, to the person who worships Him.

This explains the importance of dreams in which the Imams appear. A believer who receives such a vision discovers their most intimate secret: the Imam as the Soul of their soul, the hidden meaning of their own knowledge of God. Earlier we spoke about the *human* meaning of knowing God.[^EII1-310] Now the Imam also reveals the *divine* meaning of this human knowledge.

**3.** At the third level, the Imam goes further still: “We are the A'raf because, on the Day of Resurrection, God knows us as the Way.” Here *A'raf* refers to what is known in its own essential nature, not to something known incidentally or from the outside.

What does this essential knowledge mean? At the second level, the Imam was the knowledge through which a person knows God. At the third, he is the divine knowledge through which God knows a person.

The Imam says that God knows someone who knows the Imams as a person of Paradise.

The second level tells us that a believer's knowledge of the Imams is their knowledge of God. The third tells us that God's knowledge of the believer is the believer's knowledge of the Imams. By knowing the Imams, a person knows themselves as someone belonging to Paradise, and this is also God's knowledge of them. Conversely, the person who rejects the Imams has a sense of self that is itself their hell.

“No one enters the Fire except those who deny us and whom we deny.” That denial is also the way God knows the person who rejects the Imams. It is the one who denies who drives God out of their own paradise; that is what hell means here. At the point where knowing the Imam and knowing oneself become one, the outward image of the A'raf as a barrier reveals its full meaning: the Imam truly is the boundary separating Paradise from Hell.

This teaching offers the philosopher endless possibilities for reflection. The Imam is the knowledge a human being has of God, and for that very reason he is also the knowledge God has of a human being. The two statements place the Imam at the level of the first manifestation of God, at the very dawn of God's becoming knowable.

We have already witnessed the rising of this dawn in other texts (above, pp. 296–297). There, a particular divine will emerged on the horizon of a universal, primordial Will. That dawn made possible the appearance of a form (*tajalli*) in which God could become the object of love—His *mahbubiya*, or being loved.

In that earlier account, the emphasis on divine will went with a view of existence found in a Shaykhi master such as Muhammad Karim Khan Kirmani. He refuses to include God's ineffable, indescribable Being within a single, unqualified unity of being (*wahdat al-wujud*). Here, with Mulla Sadra Shirazi, we encounter a thinker who accepts that unity. His account of reality begins instead with knowledge.

There is, first, an all-encompassing divine knowledge: perfect knowledge identical with the simple, undivided essence of God. It contains no multiplicity, because the divine Essence (*dhat*) is the source from which the existence of everything flows. When God knows Himself, He knows all things through the very act of knowing that is identical with His Essence. There is also God's knowledge of individual things. This can mean that the essences of things are present to Him as they exist concretely, or that their Ideas are made real in being “before” they exist in the concrete world.

Together these levels form an order of causes and effects. Mulla Sadra explains that its downward and upward movements mirror one another exactly. In the downward movement, angels act as causes that gradually bring creatures' potential existence into reality. In the upward movement, prophets, Imams and all God's Friends serve as causes and guides who awaken the potential angelic nature within human beings. They lift people beyond the merely animal level and bring their angelic possibilities into full reality, so that they become people of Paradise (*ahl al-jinnat*).

The same pattern applies to divine knowledge. In the order of creation, God knows the beings of this changing world through His knowledge of their angels—the intellectual and heavenly angels described in the philosophical system of Avicenna. That is why angels are called the “witnesses” (*shuhada*) of creation before God. In the order of the last things, God knows the faithfulness of believers through His knowledge of the prophets and God's Friends. They, in turn, are God's witnesses for humanity on the Day of Resurrection.

Through this idea of the witnesses, the Imam's words lead the philosopher to see the parallel between the role of angels in the origin and ordering of the world—the order of the *mabda'*, or Beginning—and the role of the Imams in the return of souls to their source—the order of the *ma'ad*, or Return.

The second concerns salvation and what awaits us at the end of earthly life.[^EII1-311] Both the teaching about angels and the teaching about the Imams have their deepest foundation in divine knowledge. Both reach their highest expression in the idea of the **Witness**.

In that idea, a philosophy of presence and a spiritual experience of presence come together. Everything in prophetic philosophy points towards it. The Imam is the meeting point where the Witness, the one who beholds (*shahid*)—the Imam standing upon the A'raf—is also the one beheld (*mashhud*), the Witness who is himself present to contemplation: the A'raf itself. He bears witness to the God he contemplates, speaking for God before humanity.

Yet he is also the one human beings behold when God reveals Himself to them. He is the eye through which God looks towards humanity and cares for it, because he is also the eye through which humanity looks towards God and turns towards Him.

We shall see this theme develop in Ruzbihan's mysticism (Book Three below).

The Imams are both the eyes through which God looks upon this world and the eyes through which human beings contemplate the divine attributes, since God's Essence itself is beyond their reach. The Imam is thus at once the one who contemplates and the one contemplated (*shahid–mashhud*), beheld by God and by humanity. He keeps us from both extremes: denying any meaningful manifestation of God's attributes (*ta'til*), and making God resemble created beings (*tashbih*). My knowledge of the Imam is therefore also God's knowledge of me. This is why the Imam is the barrier that separates the people of Paradise from the people of Hell.

As Mulla Sadra puts it: “God's knowledge of the spiritual condition of these two groups passes through His knowledge of the Witnesses in their twofold role: bearing witness to the Paradise of some and the Hell of others. This is the deeper understanding (*tahqiq*) of the prophets and Imams as God's Witnesses before humanity, and of the Qur'anic verse: ‘What will happen when We bring forth a witness from every community, and bring you forth as a witness against these people?’ (4:45).”

Now the full meaning of the Imam's three successive statements becomes clear. “We are the A'raf” means: in our very essence, we are those whom God knows (*ma'rufun bi'l-dhat*), those whom He contemplates (*mashhudun li'llah*), His direct witnesses in contemplation. We do not need intermediaries, because we ourselves serve as intermediaries for others. We are the highest stages of the Way (*sirat*) through which human beings must pass to reach the greatest possible closeness to God.[^EII1-312][^EII1-313]

The A'raf thus emerges as the summit, the protective boundary, of the philosophy of prophecy and the Imams. That philosophy offers the gift of the highest wisdom. The Imam Ja'far explains this to a disciple while commenting on a Qur'anic verse (2:272): “Whoever has been given wisdom has received an immense good” (compare Proverbs 3:13 and following). “This wisdom (*hikmat*),” he says, “is spiritual awareness, the direct knowledge (*ma'rifat*) of the Imam.”[^EII1-314]

Several ideas prepare us to understand what this wisdom means. The most important is that of the *Hojjat*, to which Sadra Shirazi returns repeatedly in his commentary on the Imams' sayings. There are two kinds of *Hojjat*: two kinds of witness, guide and guarantor. The first is the **outer guide**: the prophet who brings God's message to humanity, and, after the Prophet, the Imams for those who need a guide they can see.

But Twelver Shiism, living under the guidance of the Hidden Imam, naturally leads us towards the second: the **invisible inner guide**, the Imam within (*Hojjat batina*, *Imam dakhili*).

This inner guide is a radiant, holy light. It comes from the divine Throne and rises at the eastern horizon of the soul, at its highest point. It illuminates the “senses of the heart,” through which the prophetic message can be heard in its hidden meaning: the *walayat* of the Imams. It is a secret, inward prophecy (*nobowwat batiniya*) concerned with unseen worlds and the hidden life of the soul.[^EII1-315]

The idea of an inner guide does not make the teachings about prophecy or the Imams unnecessary. Quite the opposite: it brings them to fulfilment. This is where the teaching of the Imams is meant to lead. The inner guide reached through this process protects the mystic from the intoxication of a spiritual pride that would make them imagine themselves godlike.

Before entering the Way, the mystic is still the person addressed by the Fifth Imam's warning: “You know even less about the roads of Heaven than you do about the roads of Earth.” The Shiite believer's “search for the Imam” is therefore not a search for someone familiar with the physical spaces of the astronomical sky. It concerns another world entirely, one that “corresponds to inward, invisible forms, which cannot be perceived by our physical senses, but only by our spiritual senses.”[^EII1-315][^EII1-316]

So when the Imam speaks of wisdom, with its successive levels expressed as faith in God, His angels, His revealed books, His messengers and the Resurrection, Sadra reminds us that wisdom is twofold, just as the *Hojjat* or guide is twofold. There is **revealed wisdom** (*hikmat makshufa*) and **veiled wisdom** (*hikmat mastura*). Revealed wisdom is embodied in the visible persons of the sages: they are wisdom made present as living human beings.

Whoever sees one of them with the “eyes of the heart,” which reveal the sage's true nature, sees wisdom in personal form. For ordinary people, this is God's gift of wisdom, the “immense good” spoken of in the sacred text: the visible person of the Imam, who is wisdom itself (*nafs al-hikmat*).

Veiled wisdom, by contrast, is the wisdom within the hearts of God's Friends (*awliya*), the prophets and the Imams—the *hukama ilahiyun*, sages of God, or “theosophers” in the full original sense of lovers of divine wisdom. The Imams' teaching about the A'raf helps us understand why each Imam is a sage from one point of view, and wisdom itself from another.[^EII1-317]

A deep joy runs through Mulla Sadra's reflections at this point.[^EII1-318] He reaches the place where Shiite spirituality meets his own philosophy of being and knowledge, shaped by the tradition of illumination. Both come together in the spiritual awareness of the Shiite philosopher devoted to that tradition.

The union of the sage and wisdom, he tells us, is like what happens in the act of understanding: the person who understands (*'aqil*) and the intelligence actually at work (*'aql*) become one.[^EII1-319] This expresses the distinctive character of this form of Shiite spirituality, which we have already encountered: philosophical thought and spiritual fulfilment cannot be separated from one another. Each depends on the other (see also Book Two, on Suhrawardi, and Book Five).

The twofold *Hojjat* and the twofold wisdom are really two ways of describing the same thing. In the Imam, there is a wisdom made visible and a wisdom that remains hidden (*makhfiya*). The visible wisdom is the Imam's person, present before our eyes. The hidden wisdom is an inward light of spirit and understanding (*nur batini 'aqli*). This light is the Imam's spiritual life. Through it, the person he guides is able to see the world beyond death, together with the heavenly beings and forms within it. That illumination is the gift of wisdom.

When someone truly understands, the act of intelligence is not something added to them from outside. Their understanding is part of what they are at that moment. In the same way, the sage—the Imam—is wisdom itself. To know this sage through direct spiritual knowledge (*ma'rifat*) is to know the wisdom that he embodies.

But in that very act of knowing, the Imam's wisdom becomes the wisdom of the believer who follows him, just as intelligence becomes the living activity of the person who understands.

The believer then discovers that two sayings express the same truth from opposite sides: “Whoever knows their Imam knows their Lord,” and “Whoever knows themselves knows their Lord”—which here also means knowing their Imam. To be fully aware of one's Imam, one's personal and invisible inner guide, is to become someone in whom the wisdom embodied by the Imam has come to life. Such a person possesses the “inner Witness,” who is precisely the Imam himself as the Imam within (*Imam dakhili*), the “divine Face” that remains when everything else passes away.

We said earlier that the Imam is the form in which God appears. In the same way, the faithful believer becomes the form in which the Imam appears. This is the heart of spirituality centred on the Imams: the outer Imam leads us to the inner Imam, and knowing the Imam leads us to knowledge of ourselves.

We can now reflect on what each of the Shiite Imams, and all twelve together in their spiritual fullness, mean for Shiite life. The teaching of the A'raf reaches its highest point in a philosophy of the Witness (*shahid*) and of the presence experienced through witnessing (*shuhud*).

The Imam becomes, in a sense, the active awareness of the believer. This is how the *silsilat al-irfan*, the succession of spiritual knowledge, continues in the world. It is unknown to most people: the hidden line of those who play their part in the sacred history of the age of *walayat*, and who are truly “alive” in the fullest sense of that word.[^EII1-320]

This “community of the living” extends towards a shared spiritual faith that reaches across the whole history of prophecy. Its foundation is the same understanding of the inner meaning of religion. Earlier (§ 1), the idea of universal *walayat*, of which the Imam is the Seal, already brought us to this point. All the prophets of earlier ages, together with their believers, belong to the same eternal prophetic religion. Together they form a single spiritual body (*corpus mysticum*), the “Temple of Light” of the Imamate, as Ismaili writers call it.

Mulla Sadra writes: “This has been true in every age, and it will remain true in the future. All the sages of God (*'ulama rabbaniyun*, the *theosophoi*), all the prophets and all their Imams, together belong to one religion (*din wahid*) and one school (*madhhab wahid*). Or, better still, they form something like one complete spiritual person (*shakhs wahid kulli 'aqli*). In the same way, the believers who follow them, wherever and whenever they live, are like a single Soul. The school of every Imam is also the school of every other Imam, and at the same time the school of all the prophets and God's Friends.”[^EII1-321]

These words of Mulla Sadra could stand as the declaration of faith of Shiite inner spirituality: faith in an eternal *Ecclesia spiritualis*, a community joined together in spirit.

##### 4. The Imam as God's Witness and the Witness of Contemplation

The texts we have examined and discussed have, I believe, told us what matters most. Yet Mulla Sadra's final pages on Kolayni's *Kafi*—the pages he still had time to write before his death—add a number of illuminating refinements.

Sadly, they break off in full flight, with the same poignant abruptness as Bach's unfinished *Art of Fugue*. They end just as we are about to discover the Shiite thinker's deepest meditation on one of the high points of the Imams' own teaching about the Imam, a text he was explaining line by line. Here I can offer only a brief outline and paraphrase of these extraordinarily dense final pages.

The whole commentary on the Twelve Imams as the “Witnesses of God” (*shohadâ' Allah*)[^EII1-322][^EII1-323][^EII1-324] is guided by a single insight: the degree to which something exists—its very act of being (*wojûd*)—depends on, and is proportional to, its degree of presence (*hodûr*, *hozûr*). And presence is essential to what it means to be a witness (*shâhid*). Here Mulla Sadra's entire metaphysics of being rests upon the understanding of the Imam and is bound to its central theme.

Sadra begins with an extended discussion of two words, *shâhid* and *shahîd* (distinguished in our transliteration by the position of the circumflex). *Shâhid*, the one who witnesses, is the active form of *shohûd*—being present to something, witnessing it directly, seeing it with one's own eyes—and is related to *moshâhadat*, vision or contemplation. In mystical language, this means the visionary perception of worlds that the mystic beholds but that remain invisible to others.

All of this presupposes that one being can be present to another. The *shâhid*, the witness who contemplates something, is the one to whom, and within whom, the form or image of that thing is present. The *shahîd*, by contrast, is the Witnessing One—the “martyr” in the word's original sense of someone who bears witness. It is the faculty or power (*qowwat*) through which the witness's vision (*shohûd*) and presence (*hodûr*) become possible.

What, then, makes it possible for one being to be present to another—the very condition of witnessing? Many things, by their fundamental nature, cannot receive the presence of another thing or themselves become present to it. This is true of all material things situated in the perceptible space of our darkened world. None can be inwardly present to another, or present *for* another; and no other thing can be present in or for it.

We cannot say, for example, that the Earth, as a physical mass, exists as a “presence” for the starry heavens, or the reverse;[^EII1-325] nor that the element air is present to the element water, or the reverse. That is why this world is the dwelling place of unconsciousness and death.

Everything is immersed in darkness and unconsciousness to the degree that it belongs to this world and is remote from the world of Light, Knowledge, and Life—the world beyond, the dwelling place of the Living. Conversely, consciousness and presence grow in proportion to the light received from the *Malakut*, the spiritual world.[^EII1-326]

When Mulla Sadra says that the degree of existence is proportional to the degree of presence, his insight comes close to one expressed in language familiar today.

But we must be careful. For Sadra and the *Ishrâqîyûn*, the philosophers of illumination, this is a way of being *in* the present world fundamentally different from an existence irretrievably cast into it, abandoned to its “being-toward-death.” What the relation between existence and presence means for Sadra is this: the more intense one's presence becomes, the more one is present to other worlds—and the more one escapes the conditions of unconsciousness, death, and absence.

The more fully a human life becomes Presence, the more that person witnesses other worlds. Such a life becomes less a being-toward-death and more a being-toward-what-lies-beyond-death. A metaphysics of Presence thus unfolds into a metaphysics of vision, of the presence through which one witnesses (*shohûd*). This has already been announced in the teaching about the Imam and is realized as that teaching becomes an inner experience (*above*, § 3).[^EII1-327]

Presence must therefore have degrees of intensity. These are marked by stages of becoming immaterial (*tajarrod*) and correspond to different levels of perception and awareness: sensory perception, imaginative perception, and intellectual understanding. At every level, the principle of unity described earlier applies.

What we perceive through the senses, imagine, or understand is not the external material thing itself, but its form—sensory, imaginal, or intellectual—as it is present within us. An understood form is such a form only in relation to someone who understands it. The act of understanding is not something added to the person who understands: it is that person in the very act of understanding. The same holds for sensory and imaginal forms.

Thus, the form understood (*ma'qûla*) itself becomes, precisely as understood, an understanding form, an active form. The same is true of sensory and imaginal forms.[^EII1-328] Seen in this light, knowing proves to be the very source of spiritual life. This is the spiritual meaning of “oriental presence” (*hozûr ishrâqî*): presence is called *oriental* because it rises at the East of the soul, when the soul itself becomes the East, the dawning place, of its own knowing.[^EII1-329]

Here too lies the whole metaphysics of Witness and Witnessing. My spiritual awareness (*ma'rifat*) of the Imam brings about the Imam's presence within me. The Imam then becomes the “inner Imam,” the Witnessing One, the active consciousness present within me (*shahîd*). This is why we can say that every prophet, and every Imam after him, serves as the very faculty of knowing in each of his followers.

For the follower, precisely as a follower, can have neither knowledge (*'ilm*) nor testimony (*shahâdat*)—can neither be “present to” nor have something “present within”—except through the knowledge and testimony of the Imam.[^EII1-330] He becomes, as we said earlier, “the eye through which he sees.”

Let us draw the threads together. The Imam is God's Witness (*shâhid*).

But what does he witness? In discussing the *A'râf*, we encountered this declaration by an Imam: “We are what God knows; we are the essential object of divine knowledge.” The Imam as *shâhid*, the one who contemplates, is at the same time the *mashhûd*, the one contemplated: the object of God's contemplation and therefore the form and content of divine knowledge—the form in which that knowledge becomes known to us as human beings.

And if the Imam is the Witness of God for his follower, the form through which that follower knows God, then the Imam must at the same time be the one whom the follower contemplates, his *mashhûd*. He is Witness and Witnessed, Contemplator and Contemplated (*shâhid-mashhûd*): the Witness whom one contemplates, the Witness of contemplation.

In contemplating this Witness, the follower contemplates the very one whom God contemplates—the object of divine knowledge and contemplation—which the follower can contemplate nowhere except in this Witness. The act of contemplation makes the Witness present within the follower. This mystery of shared presence, of two beings present to one another, is what we mean by the Imam as the inner Witness (*Hojjat bâtina*). What the follower beholds and attests is what this Witness himself beholds and attests.

Indeed, the follower can see and contemplate it only by contemplating the Witness, because the Witness is necessarily the form in which the follower can know the God to whom the Witness bears testimony. Such knowledge means that the Witness is present within the follower; at the same time, it means that the follower is present to the Witness. And to be present to this Witness is already to be present to the One to whom he bears witness.

As we have said, the follower's knowledge of this Witness is therefore, in that very act, God's knowledge of the follower: God knows the follower in the one who bears witness to that follower before Him. The Imam is the Witness whom God beholds, through whom God is beheld, and through whom God beholds. It is through this inner Imam, the “Imam of one's own being,” that God knows the follower. “We are the essential object of divine knowledge,” said the Imam.

What God knows in this Witness is therefore every person to whom that Witness is present and who is present to him. We have already seen Mulla Sadra draw a fundamental parallel. Just as God knows the beings brought forth in the creation of the cosmos through their Angels, so He knows those making their Return to Him through the Imams and the *Awliyâ*, the friends of God.

Since the Imam is the essential object of divine knowledge, to know the Imam is, in that very act, to know God's knowledge of His follower. Once again we return to the saying we have repeated so often, because its meaning can never be exhausted: “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord.”

To know oneself—to know the Soul of one's soul—is to know one's Imam. And the Imam is precisely the object of divine knowledge: what God knows of the human being and within the human being. The follower's presence to God and God's answering presence to the follower—this is the Imam, the mutual presence established without either *ta'tîl* (denying God's attributes) or *tashbîh* (making God resemble His creatures).

The *ishrâqî* or “oriental” metaphysics of illumination thus reaches its summit in a metaphysics of the Imamate. At its heart stands a Shiite spiritual life centered on the Imam: God present to the Imam who is present to the human being; God present to the human being who is present to the Imam; the Imam present to the human being who is present to himself.

Through a similar deepening of spiritual understanding, we shall see Semnani use his interpretation of sacred texts to discover the “prophets of your being” (*below*, Book IV, Chapter IV). For the Sufi master Ruzbihan of Shiraz, every beautiful face—because its beauty testifies that its Creator is present to that beauty—becomes the *shâhid-mashhûd*, the Contemplator-Contemplated, the Witness of contemplation (*below*, Book III).

But we may ask whether this disclosure of the divine “Face” in a human face would have been possible, even in Sufism outside Shiism, without the mediation of Shiite teaching about the Imam: without the revelation of God's “Face” in the heavenly Anthropos, the luminous Forms of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones.

This mediation is indeed proclaimed in the Quranic verse: “We have made you a mediating community” (2:137). Imam Ja'far explains this verse at length to a disciple.[^EII1-331][^EII1-332] The community occupying this middle or mediating position is not the Arabs, as some interpretations concerned only with the outward meaning would have it.

No: it is the Imams. They mediate between two acts of testimony: they are witnesses for humanity, while the Prophet is a witness for them. As their initiator, the Prophet acts as their active faculty of knowledge and vision, just as each Imam does for his follower.[^EII1-333][^EII1-334]

We now come to the last description of the Imams that Mulla Sadra had time to examine before leaving this world. Just as the sage is also wisdom, and the one who contemplates is also the one contemplated, so the Keeper of the treasure of divine knowledge is the Treasure itself.

A disciple relates: “I heard Imam Ja'far declare: We are the guardians of the *res divina* (*amr ilâhî*, the divine affair), the Keepers of the treasure of divine knowledge, the Watchers over the secret of divine Revelation.” When the Imam says “we are the guardians,” he uses the word *hâfiz*.

Philosophers, meanwhile, give this name to the “faculty that preserves” (*qowwat hâfiza*) the forms of knowledge—the faculty that serves as their storehouse or treasure. They say that imagination is the treasury preserving the forms of sensory perception, while the Active Intelligence is the treasury of things understood by the intellect.

From here Mulla Sadra's meditation takes flight, but we cannot follow it to its destination: that destination would have appeared in the unfinished portion of his commentary. Even so, we can clearly discern the summit toward which his understanding of the Imam was leading.

On the one hand, the Treasures of divine knowledge can only be intellectual Essences, beings of light, free from any mixture with material substance and fully actual in their knowledge and understanding. They cannot, therefore, be forms impressed upon bodies, or even souls, since a soul still possesses only the potential for perfect intellectual understanding.

Mulla Sadra writes: “It is therefore established that there exist spiritual beings, intellectual Essences, in whom all existing things are fully actual in a spiritual and intellectual way. Through them souls are brought to perfection and become beings who understand in actuality, having formerly been receptive beings capable of understanding only in potential. These spiritual beings stand between God and humanity as intermediaries through whom spiritual blessings and influences are continually bestowed and descend.

“They are the Perfect Divine Words (*Kalimât tammât*), which have neither a beginning nor any possibility of passing away. They are known by many different names, depending on the many different ways of looking at them: the Words of God (*Kalimât Allah*), the World of the Divine Command (*'âlam al-Amr*), the Keys to the Divine Mystery (*Mafâtîh al-ghayb*). They are the Witnesses of God and of His existence. ‘There is nothing whose treasuries are not with Us’ (2:21).”[^EII1-335]

To call these “Perfect Words”—these Intelligences or beings of pure light—the Keepers of the treasure is also to say that they *are* the Treasures of divine knowledge. That is the identity expressed in the Imam's words.

From two different points of view, they are at once Keepers and Treasures. Their difference and their identity are the same, Mulla Sadra observes, as in the cases we have already considered: the person who understands and the act of understanding; the sage and wisdom. “This is true of every attribute of an essence that exists only through the existence of the essence to which it belongs.”

On the other hand—and this is where the highest point of his teaching about the Imam was coming into view—the *hadith* he is explaining gives the Imams themselves the title “Treasures and Keepers of the treasure of divine knowledge.” Everything just said about the cherubic Intelligences as “Perfect Words” must therefore apply, in one way or another, to the Imams as well.

Mulla Sadra is preparing to take a decisive step: “Now, to show that the persons of the Imams are the Treasures of God's knowledge—that is, that by being what God knows, in and through their act of knowing Him, they are both the Treasures and their Keepers—requires two higher sources, or rather, two sublime oceans from the ocean of knowledge disclosed in mystical divination ...”[^EII1-336] And here the flight is broken off. The sentence was never finished.

Yet we can glimpse the metaphysical summit toward which Mulla Sadra's understanding of the Imam was moving. Other Shiite philosophers of divine wisdom lived long enough to approach it and to say what can be said of it by following, step by step, the Imams' own allusions. Everything in the foregoing pages has sought to draw on their teaching.

Indeed, the Imams' own words about the *A'râf* already help us understand how what is said of the “Perfect Words” applies to the Imams too.

Our sketch of some essential features of Shiism can thus end, for the time being, where it began. All that has been said in these pages, compared with the great works of Shiite spiritual philosophy, is no more than a drop in the ocean. I have referred several times to a small private study circle in Tehran.

To bring this part of the book to a close, I want to recall one more evening there, a memorable evening in the autumn of 1964. Our discussion was devoted to the recurring theme of Shiite theology, the theme that has guided us throughout the preceding chapters: *Tawhîd*, the affirmation of God's oneness, and the Imam. How can *Tawhîd* be realized in its full truth—escaping the twin dangers of *ta'tîl* and *tashbîh*—except through the existence of the Imam?

At the end of the evening, we listened as the venerable Shaykh M. H. T., whose knowledge of Mulla Sadra's philosophy was exceptionally deep, brought his meditation aloud to something like a conclusion: “All the Names and Attributes we give to God—or rather, that God gives to Himself in revealing Himself to us—are made possible only by the figure of the eternal Imam, who gathers them all into himself.

“At the height of our spiritual states, these Names and Attributes may be absorbed into the inner human being. That person is no longer himself: the Imam becomes that person.

“But God in Himself remains unknowable and beyond our reach. The Imam is the living, eternal reality, a hidden immaterial splendor, our immaterial bond with the immaterial. He is that Face of God of which the Quranic verses (55:26–27) declare: Everything on earth is passing away, but the Face of your Lord endures, surrounded by splendor.”

To conclude, our shaykh recalled the famous final episode of the birds' pilgrimage in the great mystical epic by Farid al-Din Attar, *Mantiq al-Tayr* (*The Conference of the Birds*, twelfth century), one of the masterpieces of Persian mystical poetry. Thousands of birds set out as pilgrims. For years upon years they travel, crossing mountain heights and plunging into abysses.

Almost all are lost in the dramatic trials along the way. Only a few—thirty birds in all—reach the sublime goal and find themselves before the mysterious bird called *Sîmorgh*, symbol of the distant divinity. Its name goes back to the Avesta, the sacred book of Zoroastrian Persia, and it reappears in the heroic and mystical epics of medieval Persia (*below*, Book II).

In Persian, Attar's mystical genius brings a delicate play on words into its name: *Sîmorgh* can be read as *sî morgh*, “thirty birds.” And so, at the end of their long and painful quest, *Sîmorgh* becomes the mirror that reveals to the thirty survivors the mystery of their own being. When they look toward *Sîmorgh*, it is *Sîmorgh* they see.

When they contemplate themselves, what they see is again *sî morgh*, thirty birds. And when they look both ways at once, *Sîmorgh* and *sî morgh* are one and the same reality. There are, in a sense, two *Sîmorghs*, and yet *Sîmorgh* is one. Identity within difference; difference within identity.[^EII1-337] Meister Eckhart, for his part, said: “The gaze by which I know Him is the very gaze by which He knows me.”

When we reached the end of Attar's famous verses, I asked the shaykh, “That is the Imam, is it not?” “Certainly, that is it. And if there were no Imam, if this were not the Imam, nothing would remain but to sink into mystical intoxication, expressed in the famous cry of the Sufi al-Hallaj: *Anâ'l-Haqq!* ‘I am God!’ ...”

We have already seen how the experience of *walâyat*, the bond of spiritual love and guidance, makes Shiism, in its essence, a religion of love. Perhaps we can now sense again how the Imam keeps the mystic from losing his balance in an ecstasy whose paradoxical cry retains, despite every later recantation, a Luciferian echo.

What the mystic *can* say is what the believer says in the Gnostic *Acts of Peter*: *Talem eum vidi qualem capere potui*—“I saw Him as I was able to grasp Him.” He showed Himself to me in the form my own being had the capacity to receive.[^EII1-338] Nothing more and nothing less.

Yet this very correspondence, the immense grace of it, is precisely what the Shiite vision of the Imam means.

We can now understand why Shiite spirituality does not experience the gulf that has troubled so many speculative Christian mystics: the gulf between the idea of the eternal Christ and the historical reality of Christ, with the divinity's “self-emptying” (*exinanitio*)—extending even to the cry that “God is dead.” That same evening our shaykh said: “Glory be to God!

“In our Shiite Islam, the Imams have reflected the eternal Imam. They are his mirrors, his *mazâhir*, the forms in which he is revealed. Their task is not to awaken us to consciousness of this world. Their *walâyat* is not an institution belonging to this world. They are our spiritual bond with the spiritual universes. They open the way for us to ascend, so that the veils may fall—the very veils they themselves have deliberately kept in place, lest the weak misunderstand what is meant by their divine qualification.”

We shall need to remember all these teachings in the final book of this work, devoted to the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam. Some of our Shiite authors have recognized in him the *Saoshyant*, the saving hero of Zoroastrian Iran; others have recognized the Paraclete foretold in the Gospel of John.

## Henry Corbin

### Within Iranian Islam

*Spiritual and Philosophical Aspects*

★

**Twelver Shiism**

Within the Islamic community, the Iranian world has, from the beginning, formed a distinct whole. Its character and vocation can only be understood if we regard Iran's spiritual universe as a unity extending across the centuries before and after Islam. Islamic Iran has been, more than anywhere else, the homeland of some of Islam's greatest philosophers and mystics.

For them, speculative thought can never be separated from the fruit it bears and its practical consequences—not primarily in the social world, but in the concrete whole that a human being nourishes with his own substance beyond the limits of this life: his spiritual world.

The great work Henry Corbin presents here, in four volumes comprising seven books, is the result of more than twenty years of research carried out in Iran itself. His method is essentially phenomenological, though it belongs to no particular school. He seeks to encounter religious experience by allowing its object to reveal itself as it reveals itself to those who experience it.

The phenomenologist must therefore become the spiritual guest of those to whom that reality appears, and share with them the responsibility of receiving it. Historical considerations will consequently remain within the world of the religious object itself, rather than imposing an alien category from outside, whether dialectical or otherwise.

The first volume (Book I) sets out several essential aspects of Twelver Shiism, or Imamism, which was firmly established in Iran from early times and became the official religion in the sixteenth century. The inquiry begins with what the author has proposed to call “the phenomenon of the Revealed Book,” as it appears to those whom the Quran calls *Ahl al-Kitâb*, the “People of the Book,” embracing Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.

The second volume (Book II), published at the same time, examines Suhrawardi and the Platonists of Persia.

*In preparation:* Volume III: *The Faithful of Love* (Book III); *Shiism and Sufism* (Book IV); *The School of Isfahan* (Book V). Volume IV: *The Shaykhi School* (Book VI); *The Twelfth Imam and Spiritual Chivalry* (Book VII); general index.

The same teaching can be found in Haydar Âmolî a century earlier, and our authors invariably appeal to statements by the Imams themselves in its support. We must stress from the outset that, in a Shiite context, we consistently use the term *walâyat*, not *wilâyat*, the word commonly used in Sufism. In Western writing these terms are often confused and inadequately translated as “sainthood.” *Walâyat* describes the Imams as God's Friends, Beloved Ones, or those brought close to God (*walî Allâh*; plural *Awliyâ' Allâh*). One can immediately see why the mystery of this divine election and sanctification lies at the very heart of the prophetic mission (*nobowwat*): every prophet (*nabî*) is a *walî*, but not every *walî* is entrusted with prophecy. The fundamental meaning of *walâyat* is “friendship” (Persian *dûstî*), and the word is frequently paired with *mahabba* (love, devoted affection). It also names the love and devotion Shiites bear toward their twelve Imams. For the believer, *walâyat* toward the Imam is a participation in the Imam's eternal *walâyat*. In the metaphysical framework of the teaching about the Imams, *walâyat* has a cosmic meaning and function, revealing itself on different levels of the universe. *Wilâyat*, in the usual Sufi sense, refers essentially to the mystic's subjective spiritual states. To trace the move from *walâyat* to *wilâyat*, and to ask whether one can speak of *wilâyat* while remaining silent about *walâyat*, is to raise the whole question of the relationship between Shiism and non-Shiite Sufism. That question would require a book of its own (see vol. III, Book IV below). In any event, the question of prophecy raised here and throughout this book must be understood in terms of *nobowwat* and *walâyat*: *walâyat* is “the esoteric (*bâtin*), inward reality of prophecy.”

Panikkar writes from the standpoint of Catholic theology but senses that Melchizedek's priesthood embodies a universality capable of grounding a general theology of religions. Unfortunately, he seems unaware that Ismaili teachings on prophecy and divine wisdom had developed this idea centuries earlier. Nor does he seem to know that, within fifth-century Christianity itself, Melchizedek was, for the Melchizedekian Gnostics, the supreme figure in which the Logos appeared as divine—the Logos “apart from the flesh” (*asarkos*). This idea of divine manifestation provides a clue to the connection between the Melchizedek of Melchizedekian gnosis and that of Ismaili gnosis.

The *Ziyârat* brings together the attributes ascribed to the Imams in earlier *hadîth*. In Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î's profound, densely argued commentary (Tabriz edition, 1276/1860; see below, vol. IV, Book V), it becomes a complete exposition of the divine wisdom and spirituality associated with the Imams. On this work, see our report in the *Annuaire 1968–1969* of the Religious Sciences Section, pp. 151–154. The attributes by which the Imams appear to Shiite religious consciousness are, in themselves, the foundation for spiritual interpretation of the Qur'an.

Readers will understand why, to complete that latter work, we must first perform the thankless labour of editing texts, most of which still survive only as manuscripts. The article mentioned in this book's preface outlines the programme we have tried to pursue over the years in our teaching at the École des Hautes Études. Meanwhile our colleague Sayyed Jalâloddîn Ashtiyânî, professor at the University of Mashhad, is preparing an *Anthologie des philosophes iraniens* from the seventeenth century to the present, which is to include some fifty Shiite thinkers.


[^EII1-55]: This letter of Imam Ja'far is quoted at length in *Tafsîr Mir'at al-Anwâr* (above, p. 27, n. 4), pp. 12–14. The people criticized by the Imam are followers of Abû'l-Khattâb and, in the commentator's secondary application, the reformed Ismailis of Alamût. Certain *hadîth* make the strange assertion that “Prayer is a person,” “Fasting is a person,” and so on. Some followers have used these statements to claim that knowing this person releases them from actually observing religious practices. What lies behind the question, however, is a metaphysics of being that determines the relation between the name of an action (*nomen actionis*) and the name of its agent (*nomen agentis*). It concerns personal archetypes, not abstract essences. See our studies “Rituel sabéen et exégèse Ismaélienne du rituel” (*Eranos-Jahrbuch* XIX, pp. 229 ff.) and “Le Temps cyclique dans le mazdéisme et dans l'ismaélisme” (*Eranos-Jahrbuch* XX, pp. 208 ff.), which examine important passages from Nasîr Tûsî's *Tasawworât*. Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î, in his major commentary on the *Ziyârat al-Jâmi'a* (p. 378), resolves the issue admirably through the idea of *walâyat*: the faithful are created through a ray of the light that constitutes the being of their Imams.

A follower had come to speak with the Tenth Imam, 'Alî Naqî, whom the Abbasid authorities were holding prisoner in the military camp of Samarra. The long record of their conversation amounts to a complete statement of Imami Shiite faith. Qâzî Sa'îd repeatedly returns to the Imamate as a purely spiritual kingship. This matters because impoverished philosophies of history too often try to “explain” a turn toward the spiritual realm and hopes of the end times as compensation for political frustration. Quite apart from entirely missing the point, such explanations overlook the fact that Qâzî Sa'îd was writing at the height of the Safavid period, when Shiism could hardly be said to suffer political frustration. Just as the Imams in the *hadîth* always discuss religious matters with their disciples, our thinkers have always known that the Imamate's meaning transcends all worldly politics: its essential dimension concerns the ultimate destiny of humanity.


[^EII1-60]: The threefold *shahâdat*, or declaration of faith, that makes an ordinary *moslim* (Muslim) into a *mu'min* (a faithful Shiite believer) therefore comprises affirmation of divine oneness (*tawhîd*), affirmation of the prophetic mission (*nobowwat*), and affirmation of the Imams' *walâyat*. See, among others, *Tafsîr Mir'at al-Anwâr*, *Moqaddamât* I, *Maqâlat* II, pp. 23 ff.

This teaching assigns the Imams an “epiphanic function” (*mazharîya*): they make manifest not the divine Essence (*dhât*) itself, but God's action or “energy” (*fe'l*). See our paper “Imâmologie et philosophie” (Strasbourg conference, 1968; above, p. 65, n. 46). Negative theology is set out with complete rigour in a long sermon (*khotba*) delivered at Merv by the Eighth Imam, 'Alî Rezâ, and included in Ibn Bâbûyeh's *Kitâb al-Tawhîd*, Chapter II, second *hadîth*. Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî's commentary on this text is fundamental.

Abû Hanîfa asks the Imam to come to Kufa and forbid people to insult the memory of the Prophet's Companions. “The Imam: They would not accept what I told them. — Abû Hanîfa: How could they refuse to accept it from you, when you are a descendant of God's Messenger? — The Imam: You yourself are the first to disregard me. You entered my house without my permission. You sat down without my asking you to. You speak without consulting me. I hear you argue by syllogisms? — Abû Hanîfa: Yes. — The Imam: Beware, O No'mân! The first to make a syllogism was Iblîs [Satan], when he was ordered to bow before Adam. ‘You created me from fire,’ he said, ‘whereas you created him [Adam] from clay.’” (The Imam then asks Abû Hanîfa a series of questions about religious law, *fiqh*, and Qur'anic commentary, *tafsîr*. Every time Abû Hanîfa answers, the Imam asks, “Why, then … ?” until Abû Hanîfa's position becomes impossible to defend.) Haydar Âmolî continues with magnificent vehemence: “This is how that man [Abû Hanîfa] spoke to the Pole of poles during his lifetime. Yet this is the very man whom the gnostic [*'ârif*, Dâwûd Qaysarî] counts among the most eminent Friends of God [*Awliyâ*]! I call God to witness: it is an enormous imposture. Truly, the hostility toward Shiites and toward certain other Sufis arises from absurdities of this kind. If I were not afraid of making this too long, I would explain some of their principles [*osûl*] and their derivative rulings [*forû'*], which would allow us to judge their position. But it is better to be silent.”

It begins with a long *hadîth* of the Sixth Imam on the secret of the Black Stone (see our “La Configuration du Temple de la Ka'ba comme secret de la vie spirituelle,” *Eranos-Jahrbuch* XXXIV, pp. 129 ff.). Qâzî Sa'îd writes: “What comes to mind in trying to explain this mysterious account is that the best explanation is that the covenant [*mîthâq*] was received in several successive dwellings or levels, as the thing descended from the higher heavens to the lower heavens” (fol. 183). *Tafsîr Mir'at al-Anwâr* draws the same teaching from a long *hadîth* of the Sixth Imam, which says, among other things: “Then He created the angels, revealed Himself to them, and received from them the covenant [*mîthâq*]: toward Himself with respect to divine lordship [*robûbîyat*], toward Mohammad with respect to prophecy [*nobowwat*], and toward 'Alî with respect to *walâyat*” (p. 29). There was therefore a covenant before the one required of Adam, ancestor of earthly humanity (Qur'an 7:171). We shall also have occasion to note that the angels ordered to bow before Adam (Qur'an 2:28) were only the lower angels (*malâ'ika*), not the four angels supporting the Throne (*'arsh*), nor those called *al-'âlûna* (“the Sublime Ones”). These latter are the Veils, the Lights of the *Haqîqat mohamma-dîya* (the eternal Muhammadan Reality) of which the Throne is composed; it was precisely before these Lights shining within Adam that the lower angels bowed. Nor did the command concern the *Karûbîyûn* (Cherubim), called the “angels of the Veils.” See Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î, commentary on *Ziyârat al-Jâmi'a* (above, n. 48), p. 117. Like Ismaili teachings about Adam, Imami teachings recognize Adam on several levels: *Adam al-akbar*, the greater or cosmic Adam; *Adam al-asghar*, the lesser or little Adam; and so forth.


[^EII1-79]: We must mention here one of Mollâ Sadrâ's most powerful passages, commenting on Qur'an 7:171 in his great commentary on Kolaynî, *Sharh al-Osûl min al-Kâfî*, Tehran, n.d., p. 321. Sadrâ speaks of the different levels on which souls become manifest: the world of Intelligences, the *Malakût* (spiritual kingdom), the *mundus imaginalis* or *barzakh* (intermediate imaginal world), and finally the physical world. He invokes Plato's teaching on the pre-existence of souls and finds it entirely consonant with Qur'an 7:171. Yet he believes that “pre-existence” alone is not enough: one must recognize that “there” souls have another mode of being and another way of appearing. The *zohûr* referred to in the verse, the “loins” that contained Adam's descendants, were precisely the Intelligences, the *'Aqûl*, regarded as their “fathers” in their pre-existence on the level of the world of Intellect. We shall return to this interpretation in a book devoted specifically to Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî. For now, let us simply note that Mollâ Sadrâ was not the first to find an agreement between Platonism and Shiism concerning the pre-existence of souls. Seven centuries earlier, Ibn Bâbûyeh had already taught pre-existence, in language with striking Platonic echoes, in his *Kitâb al-I'tiqâdât* (*Book of Beliefs*), a fundamental work of Shiite thought.

[^EII1-140]: Qur'an 4:156 states: “They say: ‘We put the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, God's Messenger, to death,’ whereas they did not kill him and did not crucify him; it only appeared so to them […] Rather, God raised him to Himself.” Because this verse approaches the teaching of the *Acts of John* (cited above, n. 127), we must emphasize that this teaching is much subtler than the usual, straightforward conception of Docetism—or, at least, the oversimplified account commonly given of it—as the belief that Christ had only a semblance of a body and suffered only in appearance. In truth, the “Docetism” of the *Acts of John* is, above all, a theological critique of knowledge itself. Recall C. G. Jung's words: “Historical facts are real, certainly, but they reveal only what impresses the man of the senses and what he can conceive. For the person who knows the divine mysteries, however, the event of the crucifixion is more than this: it is a *Mysterium*—a symbol expressing a parallel psychic event that takes place within the contemplative person. In Platonic terms, it is an event in a heavenly place: on a mountain and in a cave where a Cross of Light stands [*Acts of John* 97 ff.], a cross with many synonyms—that is, many aspects and meanings. It expresses the unknowable nature of the ‘Lord’ […]. Understood in this way, the Docetism of the *Acts of John* appears rather as a fulfilment of the historical fact, far from diminishing its value” (*Von den Wurzeln des Bewusstseins*, Zurich, 1954, p. 331). We would add that Docetism simply gives voice to the experience reported in the *Acts of Peter*: “I saw him as I was able to grasp him” (*Eum vidi qualem capere potui*). Each divine appearance, or theophany, is measured by the “dimension of the soul”: by its capacity to allow a divine Figure to appear to it. Ultimately, the soul does not witness an event outside itself; it is the place where the event happens. Likewise, in our phenomenology, knowledge is not knowledge *about* Being: it is Being knowing itself.

    


[^EII1-141]: See Ernst Benz's article cited above, p. 157, n. 128, and the new edition of his major work *Ecclesia spiritualis*, Stuttgart, 1964. It would be highly worthwhile to bring out certain shared features of Joachim of Fiore's interpretation through corresponding biblical figures and events, and the spiritual interpretation practiced in Shiite theosophy. Just as there is a correspondence between events and figures in the Old and New Testaments, so too there is a correspondence between different periods in the complete cycle of prophecy, with the same protagonists appearing on a continuing plane of sacred history. There is also a correspondence between the cycle of the prophetic mission (*nobowwat*) and the cycle of the Imams' *walâyat*. As the Old and New Testaments stand to the “Spiritual Gospel,” so the Torah and Gospel stand to the Qur'an. Since the Imam was secretly commissioned alongside every prophet, Shiite esotericism understands itself as gathering together all earlier inward teachings and bringing them to the flowering of their truth. Some Shiite writers themselves have identified the Paraclete—the reign of the Spirit—with the Twelfth Imam. There is an affinity between the “archetype of the Book” (*Omm al-Kitâb*) and the *Evangelium aeternum*, or Eternal Gospel. On both sides, spiritual interpretation takes a prophetic form. We have occasionally used the phrase *Ecclesia spiritualis* (“spiritual church”) above for the hidden hierarchies of the Shiite community. There is nevertheless a difference. Given the Twelfth Imam's present concealment (*ghaybat*), the Shiite community cannot cross that boundary; whereas devout enthusiasts tried to bring Joachim of Fiore's *Ecclesia spiritualis* “into history,” and tragedies ensued.

See Piotr Hendrix's penetrating analysis, “Der ‘Garten’ und der ‘Morgen’ als Ort und Zeit für das Mysterium Paschale in der Orthodoxen Kirche,” *Eranos-Jahrbuch* XXXII, Zurich, 1964, p. 151.

(around 1860), quarto, 352 pages. [^EII1-167]: For simplicity, both *korsî* and *'arsh* have been translated here as “throne,” although the terms refer to two distinct metaphysical realities. Their relationship resembles that between the empyrean heaven (corresponding to *'arsh*) and the *firmamentum*, the heaven of the fixed stars (corresponding to *korsî*). Note, too, a difference in the use of “Light of Lights” (*Nûr al-anwâr*). Among the *Ishrâqîyûn* (philosophers of illumination), the term means the First Being, which is also the supreme Being (*Ens supremum*) and the source of emanation. Here, the “Light of Lights” is the First Being understood as the first *created* being (*protoktistos*), because the creative Principle transcends being, including the first being it brings into existence. Imami and Ismaili gnosis agree on this metaphysics of being, which calls for a rigorous “first philosophy.” See above, p. 200, n. 159, and *Pénétrations*, pp. 235–236.

The Throne motif—corresponding in Islamic gnosis to the *Merkabah* (divine chariot or throne) in Jewish Kabbalah—has a constant fourfold structure, though the symbolic lights and the names of the four higher archangels (Seraphiel, Michael, Gabriel, Azrael) are assigned in somewhat different ways. See our book on Ibn 'Arabî, pp. 270–271. All our theosophical authors discuss this motif; coordinating the details would require a whole book. Above this archangelic group of four stand the four *Malâ'ika al-a'lûn*, or *Angeli Sublimes* (“Sublime Angels”). Two are the Spirit of the divine Command; the other two have charge of the angels of the Veils (the Cherubim, *Karûbîyûn*). See Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î, *Ziyârat*, p. 117.

Here, what we know of God is the knowledge God has of His Creation and of Himself within the *Haqîqat mohammadîya* (the eternal Muhammadan Reality). It is remarkable that a kind of *kathenotheistic* conception—each divine figure appearing in turn as supreme—is already found in a proto-Ismaili text such as *Omm al-Kitâb*, edited by W. Ivanow in *Der Islam*, vol. 23, Leipzig, 1936. An Italian translation was recently published by Pio Filippani-Ronconi, Naples: Istituto universitario orientale, 1966. The master ('Abdallâh Sabbâh) ceases to see the young Imam (Moh. Bâqir) and instead sees the Prophet transfigured, his face encircled by a halo of luminous hair: “I am the Lord, pure and beyond every attribute and description.” He then sees 'Alî and, after him, Fâtima. Dressed in silk and gold brocade, with a green veil over her hair, she declares: “There is no God but me, no God in divinity or humanity, in the heavens or on earth, except me, Fâtima the Creator [in the masculine: Fâtima-Fâtir]. It is I who created the spirits of the True Believers.” Finally, Imam Hasan appears, then Imam Hosayn, who declares: “I am Hosayn ibn 'Alî, I am Hasan ibn 'Alî, I am Fâtima the Radiant [Fâtima al-Zahrâ]; I am 'Alî al-A'lâ [the Most Exalted]; I am Mohammad the Chosen” (manuscript fols. 19b–22; see Italian translation, pp. 18–20).

[^EII1-192]: We have often referred to Kolaynî's great work, *al-Kâfî* (above, p. 29, n. 15, and p. 57, n. 31), which systematically organizes the teachings of the Imams. Mohammad ibn Ya'qûb ibn Ishaq Kolaynî Râzî came from a prominent family in Ray (ancient Rhages, roughly twelve kilometres south of Tehran), where he became the shaykh and *pîshvâ* (spiritual guide) of the Shiites. Leaving behind that distinguished position and the relative advantages Shiism enjoyed in Ray, he moved to Baghdad (around 309/921), seat of the Abbasid caliphate and an inhospitable city for Shiites. He had the courage to do so because of his great undertaking: to move closer to the sources and assemble the extensive corpus of traditions that would sustain his fellow believers for centuries. He lived long enough to know at least the last *nâ'ib*, or representative, of the Twelfth Imam: 'Alî al-Samarrî, whose death in 329/940, only months apart from Kolaynî's own death in Baghdad, also marked the beginning of the “Great Occultation” (*al-ghaybat al-kobrâ*; see Book VII below).


[^EII1-193]: One can appreciate the scale of this literature by leafing through the newest bibliographical inventory of Shiite writings: Shaykh Aghâ Bozorg Tehrânî, *Dharî'at ilâ tasânîf al-shî'a*, published in Tehran and Najaf. Eighteen volumes had appeared by 1968, listing titles only as far as the end of the Arabic letter *lâm*.


[^EII1-194]: Conditions were particularly difficult for the Ninth, Tenth, and Eleventh Imams. The last two, Imam 'Alî Naqî and Imam Hasan 'Askarî, were kept under more or less continuous detention by the Abbasid authorities in the military camp of Samarra, about a hundred kilometres north of Baghdad. But we must remember that if the Fifth and Sixth Imams, Mohammad Bâqir and Ja'far Sâdiq, seem more prominent than the others because of the extent and importance of their teaching, it is not because they were “greater.” All twelve Imams share the same essence and are equal. Rather, the decline and fall of the Umayyads and the rise of the Abbasids (751) briefly made conditions less difficult for the Fifth and Sixth Imams. That is why Imam Ja'far could have so many pupils. One may judge the wider situation from the records of conversations preserved by Ibn Bâbûyeh in his *'Oyûn akhbâr al-Imâm al-Rezâ*.

A moment later he turned to me and said: ‘Are you Hishâm ibn al-Hakam?’ I said: ‘No!’ — ‘Then are you one of his companions?’ — ‘No!’ — ‘Where are you from, then?’ — ‘I am from Kufa,’ I replied. — ‘Then you *are* Hishâm!’ He drew me into his arms, seated me in his own place, and said nothing more until I stood to leave. When Imam Ja'far heard this story, he laughed and asked: ‘O Hishâm! Who taught you all this?’ — ‘It is something I learned from you yourself,’ said Hishâm, ‘and then put together afresh.’ The Imam replied: ‘God is my witness! The truth of what you have said is written in the Books of Abraham and Moses’ [Qur'an 87:19].” We hope to return elsewhere to the engaging figure of Hishâm ibn al-Hakam. As for the Mu'tazilite master 'Amrû ibn 'Obayd (d. 144/761), once a pupil of Hasan Basrî, see Mâmâqânî, *Tanqîh al-Maqâl*, vol. II, p. 334, no. 8729; and *Rayhânat al-adab*, under “Abû 'Othmân 'Amrû,” vol. V, p. 131, no. 225. It has become customary to emphasize certain points of agreement between Mu'tazilism and Shiism. Hishâm's encounter shows how far the two are from being in general agreement. Their spiritual tone differs. Even where they agree on points of *kalâm* (doctrinal theology), Shiite thought is not confined to *kalâm*: its fullest expression lies in *hikmat ilâhîya* (divine wisdom) and *'irfân* (spiritual knowledge).


[^EII1-218]: On the symbolism of Sinai and the olive tree, see *Trilogie ismaélienne*, third part, pp. 102–122. Compare Ibn 'Arabî's idea of the Imam of the microcosm during ritual prayer; see our *Soufisme d'Ibn 'Arabî* (above, n. 149), pp. 193 ff.


[^EII1-219]: Mulla Sadra, *Sharh*, p. 441. Compare the important discussion on pp. 261–262 (on *Tawhid*, chapter IX, seventh *hadith*, p. 178). Beyond sunlight, the brightest light in our world, there are other hidden, spiritual lights (*anwar batiniya*) that cannot be perceived by bodily sight: the more intense a light is, the less visible it becomes. These lights beyond the senses (*malakutiya*) form a hierarchy. At the lowest level is the life-giving, animating soul (*nafs haywaniya*), which the Qur'an (6:125) calls the *sadr*, the chest or breast (*pectus*). Above it is the thinking soul (*nafs natiqa*), called the heart (*qalb*) in religious language. Higher still is the contemplative intellect (*aql nazari*), which religious language calls the Spirit (*ruh*). Finally comes what the mystics (*urafa*) call the *sirr*, a level of awareness beyond ordinary consciousness, and what philosophers call the Active Intelligence (*aql fa''al*). All these correspondences deserve closer study. The last two lights may be compared to Fire and Air in our world of physical elements. Because they are so exalted, they have no outward form of manifestation (*mazhar*) in our world and no connection to a body of any kind, whether heavenly or earthly. The first two, being closer to our world, do have forms in which they become visible. The “animating souls” manifest in living earthly bodies and in the *sadr* (chest) of the human world in miniature. The greatest of these manifestations is also the greatest individual expression of the Soul of the World: it is the heaven of the firmament (*Kursi*). The thinking soul, by contrast, is the spiritual heart (*qalb ma'nawi*). Its earthly manifestations (*mazahir*) are human hearts—at least those of people “who have a heart” (50:36), that is, an Imam. “The greatest of all these forms is the Throne (*arsh*), the heart of the greater world. It is the place where the Light of Thought appears, and this Light is the seat of the name *al-Rahman* (the Merciful), the form in which God's hidden secret (*sirr*) becomes manifest...”

Anything heard from outside [*masmû'*] is entirely useless when inborn intelligence is absent, just as sunlight is useless when the eye's power of sight is paralysed” (*Sharh*, p. 445).

Mollâ Sadrâ quotes several Qur'anic verses in support. “We showed Abraham the *Malakût* of the heavens and the earth” (6:75); clearly this is not an outward perception. “The heart did not deny what it saw” (53:11, concerning the Prophet's first visionary experience): the heart's perception (*idrâk al-qalb*) is explicitly called vision (*ru'ya*). The opposite of knowledge is therefore blindness. Hence the verse: “It is not their eyes that are blind; it is their hearts, within their breasts, that are blind” (22:45).
