Râzî presents the Shiite understanding of the Imam as fairly as he can in his great Qur'anic commentary *Mafâtîh al-ghayb* (Constantinople edition, vol. I, pp. 71 ff.), but remains entirely unaware of *walâyat* as the inward reality of prophecy. See above, p. 187, n. 150, and below, p. 306, n. 295. On the qualifications required for the Imamate in the Shiite sense, see also Shaykh Mofîd, *Awâ'il al-maqâlât*, Tehran edition, 1371 (1951), pp. 7 ff.


[^EII1-228]: *Osûl*, *Hojjat*, Chapter III, first *hadîth*, pp. 329–330. Here Mollâ Sadrâ (*Sharh*, pp. 449–452) develops an extensive account of “prophetic philosophy.” He begins with scientific preliminaries of extraordinary interest, linking every recognized form of sacred, revealed knowledge (*hierognosis*) with the understanding of mind and bodily life commonly accepted in Islamic esotericism. His theory of knowledge is especially well suited to explaining such experiences because it begins from the principle that “every sensory perception, every perception possessing reality, does not at all mean that the soul sees a form existing in external matter. That external form is not the object of sensory perception, nor is it what becomes present to the perceiving soul. Rather, the essential object of sensory perception consists of the forms the soul sees with the eye of imaginative consciousness. External forms are causes that bring before imaginative consciousness a form corresponding to them symbolically [*yomâthilo-hâ*]. Thus what is truly perceived by the senses is the symbolic form shaped within representation, while what is external is called perceptible in another sense.” Mollâ Sadrâ can therefore readily explain that the symbolic or representative form (*sûrat motamaththila*) arises before imaginative consciousness in fundamentally the same way whether it is occasioned from outside and approached through the sense organs, or occasioned from within and brought into presence through the imaginative faculty's power to make spiritual realities knowable. In both cases there is vision. The point of this theory of knowledge is therefore *not* to place the “imaginary,” as something unreal, on one side and sensible objects, as the sole objects of true perception, on the other. It begins by recognizing the priority of the imaginative faculty, then distinguishes the processes leading to true vision from the disturbances or disorders producing hallucinations (or what we might call schizophrenia). All this is extraordinarily important. Mollâ Sadrâ takes the only critical position compatible with a prophetic theory of knowledge. We should also stress how Avicenna's theory of knowledge bore fruit through Suhrawardî's philosophy of Illumination (*Ishrâq*).


[^EII1-229]: Ibid., second *hadîth*, p. 330. Mollâ Sadrâ's pages on this *hadîth* and the next (*Sharh*, pp. 452 ff.) could form the basis of a substantial study of the archangel Gabriel's role in Islamic spirituality. Our authors know the derivation of his name (the names ending in *-el*). “Gabriel is the one called the Holy Spirit, the Initiator of mighty strength [an allusion to Qur'an 53:5], who gives aid by casting divine revelation into the prophets, inspiration into the Friends of God [*Awliyâ*], and truthful dream-visions into spiritual people. He is the Faithful Spirit, the Noble Messenger, whose virtues are countless and whose received gift is universal, as the verse says: ‘The Qur'an is the word of the Noble Messenger, who has power before the Master of the Throne and is firm, obeyed, faithful’ [81:19–21].” “When we speak of the Angel's speech [*taklîm*] and the account he gives [*tahdîth*], we mean something that happens in the innermost depth of consciousness [*fî bâtin al-sirr*], as spiritual speech [*kalâm 'aqlî*] and spiritual communication [*hadîth rûhânî*]. That is why Gabriel is called the Holy Spirit [*Rûh al-Qods*]: in himself he is a sacred essence, so long as he has not descended from the heaven of his transcendence and nearness to God. When he descends from that rank of divine nearness, he takes on a figure and assumes a particular form corresponding to the person upon whom he descends” (*Sharh*, p. 453).


[^EII1-230]: *Sharh*, p. 452. On this central theme in Mollâ Sadrâ's work, see Book V, Chapter II below. Prophetic knowledge forms a coherent whole: the reality of the *mundus imaginalis* (*'âlam al-mithâl*), the capacity of imaginative perception to convey knowledge, and its spiritual nature, independent of the physical body and constituting something like the soul's subtle body.


[^EII1-231]: See n. 222 above.

The received Qur'anic text, that is, the edition of 'Othmân, is held to have been purged of passages favourable to Shiism. This seems to offer a particularly clear indication. Note also that the concept and title of the “Seal” (*khâtim*) of prophecy explicitly occur in the Imams' teachings.

Or, to put it more precisely: the dimension [*jihat*] of prophecy [*nobowwat*] in a *rasûl* is higher than the dimension of his *risâlat* [the prophetic mission directed toward others], because the former is the perfection of the contemplative intellect, while the latter is the perfection of the practical intellect” (*Sharh*, p. 449). The couplets introducing that chapter do nothing less than reproduce—without saying so—the teaching of traditions from the Fifth, Sixth, and Eighth Imams. The very idea that prophecy continues under the name *walâyat* cannot deny its Shiite origins. Then comes the rupture: the teachings about the Shiite Imams are made to disappear, at least apparently. Here lies a large part of the problem of Sufism. We shall see below how deeply Haydar Âmolî was troubled by this. On *walâyat* and *wilâyat*, see n. 20 above.

[^EII1-244]: Here Ibn 'Arabî adopts a position that appears profoundly mistaken to Haydar Âmolî and to all Shiites. His entire teaching on prophecy and *walâyat* proceeds from Shiite premises (above, p. 250, n. 234). Yet he maintains that the Seal of absolute, universal *walâyat* is not the First Imam but Jesus. As for the Seal of Muhammadan *walâyat*, it would be Ibn 'Arabî himself. (On this latter point, we suspect that his commentator Dâwûd Qaysarî exaggerated the importance of a famous dream by transferring it to the plane of sacred history.) It would therefore be worth studying how the commentators on the *Fosûs* take positions on this issue. Haydar Âmolî holds Ibn 'Arabî in immense, admiring respect—he wrote his own commentary on the *Fosûs*—but cannot compromise on this point. Ibn 'Arabî's thesis breaks apart the whole understanding of prophecy: a Messenger who came before the Seal of prophecy cannot be made the “Seal of *walâyat*.” An entire chapter of Book II of *Jâmi' al-Asrâr* (pp. 355–448 of our edition) is devoted to refuting Ibn 'Arabî through theological tradition, philosophy, and theosophy. Haydar Âmolî returns at length to the issue in the introduction to his commentary on the *Fosûs*. We cannot explore this dispute in detail here, although it deserves close analysis. It shows precisely where Shiism recognizes something of its own in Ibn 'Arabî, and where it has to part company with him, for reasons reaching back to the still rather obscure early relationship between Shiism and Sufism. An anonymous annotator (p. 443, note) suspects a case of *taqîyeh* (prudential concealment of belief) on Ibn 'Arabî's part: “I have often observed,” he says, “that mystics use the name Jesus while meaning the Holy Spirit and the *res divina* [divine reality]; both refer to the Commander of the Faithful [the First Imam].” Ibn 'Arabî's apparent “error” thus highlights the relationship between the teaching about the Imams and the understanding of Christ. We shall discuss it again below, vol. III, Book IV, Chapter I.

Among the great Iranian Sufis known as *Owaysîs*—those guided spiritually without physically meeting their guide—was Abû'l-Hasan Kharraqânî (d. 425/1034), whose guide was the spiritual being, or angel (*rûhânîya*), of Abû Yazîd Bastâmî. Another was 'Attâr of Nishapur (around 617/1220), guided by the angel or being of light of Hallâj. Sunni Sufism thus brings about a kind of secularization of *walâyat*. Sa'doddîn Hamûyeh (or Hamûyî) was a pupil and one of the *kholafâ'* (successors) of Najmoddîn Kobrâ. He taught 'Azîz Nasafî, was a friend of Sadr oddîn Qonawî, and corresponded with Ibn 'Arabî. After travelling for twenty-five years through Syria, Iraq, and Khwarezm, he settled in his native Khorasan, where he died in 650/1252. See *Rayhânat*, II, p. 193, no. 409. As already noted, he was distinguished by his personal relationship with the Twelfth Imam. In Haydar Âmolî's view, Dâwûd Qaysarî bears the chief responsibility for distorting Ibn 'Arabî's teaching about the person of the Mahdî. (Other commentators, Kamâl Kâshânî for example, have no doubt that the Seal of the Muhammadan Friends of God [*Awliyâ*], the Twelfth Imam, is the Mahdî.) Dâwûd so confuses the issue that it is no longer clear whether he means the Seal of universal *walâyat* or of Muhammadan *walâyat*. Haydar judges him harshly: “If Dâwûd Qaysarî opposes the eminent masters [*mashâyekh*], even his own shaykh and teacher, he does so only as a display of Sunnism [*tasannon*] combined with Sufism, to raise his standing in the eyes of the multitude” (op. cit., p. 436).

Spiritual sciences cannot be approached by “anyone lacking the faculty to taste them [*dhawq*], however intelligent or experienced that person may be […]. Someone who has tasted them cannot make them known to someone who has never tasted them. One sign of the higher rank of spiritual sciences and of the scholars of the other world is that it is entirely possible to acquire other kinds of knowledge while loving this world and betraying the essential realities of pure religious feeling. Love of this world may even help someone acquire them […]. Scholars then undergo all sorts of difficulties because they know that gaining knowledge [*bi-hosûl al-'ilm*] will advance their careers and social standing [*rif'a*]. Spiritual sciences, by contrast, cannot coexist with worldly ambitions. They are revealed only when one sets passions aside, resolutely avoids the company of people intent on keeping up with their age, and shuns their easy or corrupt ways to devote oneself entirely to the spiritual life.” On Mollâ Sadrâ's personal ethics, see also vol. IV, Book V, Chapter II below.

The author of *Tarâ'iq al-Haqâ'iq* (I, p. 258) even names the leading Sufi shaykhs in this “dynasty,” drawing on 'Alâoddawleh Semnânî's *Kitâb al-'orwat al-wothqâ* (on Semnânî, see vol. III, Book IV, Chapter IV). This is a point of tension between Shiism and Sufism. It fails to grasp what is meant by the Twelfth Imam's presence in both past and future, his time lying “between times,” between the past and what is to come. No one can therefore “succeed” the Twelfth Imam or even publicly “represent” him. Because he is concealed, his *Bâb* (“Gate” or threshold) is also concealed. From the Shiite perspective, anyone claiming such a status must be betraying the truth or acting as an impostor.

Likewise, the death of knowledge means nothing other than the death of the scholar, as we showed earlier in the ‘Book of Intelligence and Knowledge’ [*Kitâb al-'Aql*, the first book of the *Osûl*]. But God does not take knowledge away; He causes it to descend from one scholar to another. A scholar dies and takes with him what he knows, for a book is only knowledge written on pages.” This is why the “Sustainer of the Book” continues to exist until the Day of Resurrection.


[^EII1-295]: The whole of Chapter V of the *Kitâb al-Hojjat* in Kolaynî's *Osûl* concerns this (*Sharh*, pp. 457 ff.).


[^EII1-296]: Ibid., eighth *hadîth*, Arabic–Persian edition, I, p. 333; Sadrâ, *Sharh*, p. 461.


[^EII1-297]: Ibid., ninth *hadîth*. Sadrâ emphasizes that the Tenth Imam, 'Alî Naqî, knew himself to be the *Hojjat*—God's proof, the Guide and the one answerable for the people of his time—through two sources: “The first was his inward awareness [*wijdân*, sacred knowing], the perfect mystical insight [*al-kashf al-tâmm*] by which one knows oneself [*hâl nafsihi*, the state of one's own soul]. The Imam knew that inspiration [*ilhâm*] had come to him from God, bringing knowledge of things beyond the capacity of created intellects to perceive […]. He was conscious of divine support [*ta'yîd*] in his spiritual struggle […]. The other source was the investiture [*nass*] granted by his father and, through him, by his ancestors and predecessors” (*Sharh*, p. 461).


[^EII1-298]: Ibid., tenth *hadîth*.


[^EII1-299]: Ibid., twelfth *hadîth*.


[^EII1-300]: Mollâ Sadrâ, *Sharh*, p. 461, commentary on the *hadîth*. The meeting between the Shiite understanding of the Imam and the Hermetic idea of the “Perfect Human Being” (*Anthropos teleios*, *al-Insân al-kâmil*) is a keystone of Imami theosophy.


[^EII1-301]: We referred earlier to these decisive passages of Mollâ Sadrâ (above, p. 187, n. 150, and p. 240, n. 221). After carefully analysing and criticizing Fakhroddîn Râzî's teaching about the Imamate (*Sharh*, pp. 447–448), Mollâ Sadrâ examines the views generally held by Sunnis and by most Mu'tazilites (*Sharh*, pp. 457–459), then the views of Jâhiz, al-Ka'bî, and Abû'l-Hasan Basrî. Finally he sets against them the Shiite teaching about the Imam and the Imamate. These pages are so illuminating that they deserve translation in full; unfortunately, we cannot undertake that here.


[^EII1-302]: Sadrâ, *Sharh*, p. 459, commentary on the first *hadîth* of Chapter V of the *Kitâb al-Hojjat*.


[^EII1-303]: *Sharh*, p. 464.


[^EII1-304]: *Sharh*, p. 462: “Al-Minhâl ibn 'Amrû relates: ‘I went,’ he said, ‘to see 'Alî ibn al-Hosayn [the Fourth Imam]. I asked him, “How are you this morning, O son of the daughter of God's Messenger?”’ (Notice the reference to Fâtima in the greeting.) ‘The Imam replied: “This morning, I call God to witness, we are in the same position as the Israelites among Pharaoh's people, who slaughtered their sons and dishonoured their women. And now the best of creatures after God's Messenger is cursed from the pulpits, while anyone who loves us is deprived of his rights because of that love.”’”


[^EII1-305]: On the conversations of Komayl ibn Ziyâd with the Imam, see above, pp. 81 ff., nn. 83 and 85. Mollâ Sadrâ refers to those who have tried to evade the question of the succession of Imams by claiming that the “twelve” foretold by the Prophet were the first twelve caliphs, including the Umayyads. He shows the absurdities to which this thesis leads. He quotes the *hadîth* of the Prophet's nightmare (above, n. 22), in which he saw a band of monkeys climbing his pulpit and forcing the faithful to retreat. He calls on the commentaries as witnesses—those of Sunni authors such as Zamakhsharî, Fakhr Râzî, and Taftazânî, as well as that of the Shiite theologian Abû 'Alî Tabarsî. Finally he summarizes the introduction to Shahrastânî's *Kitâb al-milal*, in which Shahrastânî analyses the first dispute to shake the Islamic religion. Shahrastânî traces it back to Iblîs's revolt against Adam's investiture. That revolt spread through creation in seven successive disputes. They are mentioned in the commentary on the four Gospels (*sic*) and in the Torah (in fact the apocryphal *Vita Adae et Evae*, *Life of Adam and Eve*), and all were brought together in the form of manifestation (*mazhar*) taken by the first dispute in Islam. Shahrastânî, a Sunni scholar, is sufficiently allusive that a Shiite thinker like Sadrâ can invoke his text. Sadrâ ends this long discussion by quoting the Prophet: “Rulers will come after me. Those who gather around them, accept their falsehoods, and support their violence do not belong to me, nor do I belong to them. But those who refuse to take their side and refuse to accept their falsehoods belong to me, and I belong to them.” Sadrâ then shows that the numerous authentic reports (*riwâyât*) can refer only to the succession of the Twelve Immaculate Ones, with no other spiritual interpretation (*ta'wîl*) possible: those who know God and His Signs through mystical unveiling (*kashf*) and visionary witnessing (*shohûd*). The succession of the Imamate is unbroken. It perpetuates the line begun with Noah and Abraham, because the Imamate has the same essence as prophecy, of which it is the inward reality. The spiritual meaning of prophecy must endure. The saying must prove true: “Whoever dies without knowing the Imam of his time dies the death of those who remain unaware.” How could anyone dare maintain that this spiritual meaning and this knowledge have anything to do with one of the rulers the Prophet glimpsed in his nightmare? *Sharh*, pp. 462–464. We have already noted an idea that runs almost like a refrain through Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî's thought: the Prophet chose to be a servant-prophet, not a king-prophet, and could therefore bequeath to the Imams only a spiritual kingship (*saltanat ma'nawîya*). See n. 54 above.


[^EII1-306]: On the *A'râf* (the Heights), see the texts translated in our *Terre céleste*, pp. 235 ff. and 237 ff.


[^EII1-307]: *Kitâb al-Hojjat*, Chapter VII, ninth *hadîth*; *Sharh*, p. 473. This *hadîth*, which expresses the Imams' awareness that they are the source of gnosis, ends with these words: “It is no small matter for people to turn toward muddy springs that pour into one another. But the person who turns toward us turns toward pure springs flowing at their Lord's command. They never run dry; they never cease.” On Water as a symbol of knowledge, see n. 302 below.


[^EII1-308]: For what follows, see *Sharh*, pp. 475 ff. Mollâ Sadrâ first analyses the meaning of the *A'râf* and the *Ahl al-A'râf* (“people of the Heights”) among the outward-looking Sunni commentators, including Jobbâ'î and Bâqillânî, before developing the Imams' teaching at great length.


[^EII1-309]: See our translation of Mollâ Sadrâ, *Le Livre des pénétrations métaphysiques*, pp. 186–187.


[^EII1-310]: These visions are not limited to mental or dream appearances involving personal dialogue: they extend across the entire field of symbolic perception. Later (vol. III, Book IV, Chapter I), we shall quote a vision of Haydar Âmolî in which he perceived fourteen symbolic circles of lapis lazuli, with golden inscriptions, in the sky above Baghdad. See also, in our *Trilogie Ismaélienne*, the themes of the Imam as the “Soul of the soul” and the olive tree on the summit of mystical Sinai.


[^EII1-311]: *Sharh*, p. 466.


[^EII1-312]: *Sharh*, p. 475. Mollâ Sadrâ fully understands that he is opening a new way of spiritual interpretation for the philosopher to contemplate: “Make the most of all this,” he writes, “for you will find it in no book other than this one.”


[^EII1-313]: This extensive commentary on the ninth *hadîth* of Chapter VII thus follows the structure of the *hadîth* itself: the Imams are the *A'râf*, the Heights, and they are the pure springs (see above, p. 311, n. 301), opposed to the muddy springs.


[^EII1-314]: Ibid., Chapter VII, eleventh *hadîth* (from the Sixth Imam); *Sharh*, p. 476: “Just as the *Hojjat* [the guarantor or witness] is twofold, outward and inward, so too is wisdom twofold. There is a veiled wisdom and an unveiled wisdom. Veiled wisdom is what lives within the hearts of the prophets and the Friends of God [*Awliyâ*], the theosophers [*hokamâ' ilâhîyûn*, sages of divine wisdom]. Each of them is a sage in one respect, and wisdom itself in another.” This accords with what we have established about the unity of understanding (*'aql*), what is understood (*ma'qûl*), and the one who understands (*'âqil*). In the “metaphysics of witnessing,” that unity becomes the unity of testimony (*shahâdat*), witness (*shâhid*), and what is witnessed (*mashhûd*). See also below, p. 318, nn. 311 and 313.


[^EII1-315]: On the “inner Guide,” the Messenger of the inner world, and inner prophecy, see *Sharh*, p. 456 (commentary on Chapter IV, first *hadîth*).


[^EII1-316]: See ibid., Chapter VII, tenth *hadîth* (from the Fifth Imam). Mollâ Sadrâ's entire commentary could be studied as a gradual approach to the hidden *Hojjat*, an encounter with the inward Guide or Imam. He returns to the theme whenever the Imams' sayings invite him to. We shall briefly note some stages for future research. (1) Chapter IV, first *hadîth* (above, n. 309). (2) Chapter VI, third *hadîth*, *Sharh*, p. 465: a human being begins as little more than an upright biped. Then the soul slowly awakens from unawareness through a twofold Guide: the outward Messenger, who may be a *nabî* (prophet) or someone acting in his place; and the inner Imam (*Imâm dâkhilî*, *Hojjat bâtina*). (3) Chapter VII, seventh *hadîth*, *Sharh*, p. 472: the Sixth Imam's saying that “for every science God has established a door.” Only the person who knows that door knows the science: there is an outward door and an inward, esoteric door. Similarly, God's *Hojjat* is twofold, an inner witness and an outer witness. The first belongs to prophets and those like them; the second to ordinary people. (4) Ibid., eighth *hadîth*, *Sharh*, p. 472. (5) Ibid., eleventh *hadîth*, *Sharh*, p. 476 (above, p. 316, n. 308). (6) Ibid., thirteenth *hadîth*, *Sharh*, p. 476 (below, p. 318, n. 311): the outward Imam initiates the believer into the inward Imam; knowledge of the Imam initiates one into self-knowledge. This sums up Imami spirituality. (7) Chapter VIII, seventeenth *hadîth*, *Sharh*, p. 484: there is the door of the heart and the door of outward hearing; see also below, pp. 319 ff., nn. 314 and 315. (8) *Sharh*, pp. 484–485: in the long introduction to Chapter IX of Book VII, Mollâ Sadrâ examines witness and testimony and establishes the foundations for an Imami metaphysics as a “metaphysics of witnessing” (below, § 3 and p. 323, n. 324). (9) Chapter IX, second *hadîth*, *Sharh*, p. 485: the Imam as both outward and inward Witness. (10) Chapter XI, first *hadîth*, *Sharh*, p. 491: the Imams are both the Keepers of the Treasure and the Treasure itself; and so on.


[^EII1-317]: Chapter VII, eleventh *hadîth*, *Sharh*, p. 476; see n. 308 above. Veiled wisdom is the wisdom within the hearts of God's sages, the theosophers. “Unveiled wisdom, by contrast, consists of their very persons, for they are wisdom embodied [*ashkhâs al-hikmat*]. Whoever sees one of them sees the form and person of wisdom. It is for this reason that wisdom is given to them as a gift of immense good on behalf of humanity at large. For whoever knows his Imam and pledges allegiance to him pledges allegiance to God, and receives wisdom and an immense good—that is, the Imam himself, because the Imam is wisdom in person.”


[^EII1-318]: Ibid., pp. 476–477, commentary on the eleventh and thirteenth *hadîth*.


[^EII1-319]: Mollâ Sadrâ speaks of this union—a teaching also found in al-Fârâbî—as an event in his own inner life, an inspiration whose date he carefully recorded: sunrise on Friday, 7 Jomadâ I, 1037 AH (= 14 January 1628). See our introduction to *Le Livre des pénétrations métaphysiques*, pp. 2 ff., 185 ff., and the index under “ittihâd”; see also n. 308 above.


[^EII1-320]: Ibid., thirteenth *hadîth*, *Sharh*, p. 481: “In relation to the Second Life, human beings fall into two groups: the dead and the living. Among the living are those whose life is essential and personal, and those whose life follows from the life of another.” The Imam is the one who possesses essential life, infused directly by God. Yet through *ittihâd* (union; see above, pp. 316 ff., nn. 308 and 313) as it flowers into spiritual experience, whoever attains complete knowledge of the Imam thereby reaches the level of the Imam's inner light; that light becomes, in turn, the believer's own inner light. See also below, p. 323, n. 324, and the seventeenth *hadîth*, *Sharh*, p. 484, which recalls three groups of human beings: the *'âlim* (the initiator, the sage), who is the Imam; the *mota'allimûn*, those who receive wisdom from the sage—the Imam's disciples or initiates; and, alas, the foam swept away by the torrent (*ghothâ*). Or, in Qur'anic terms: those brought close to God (*moqarrabûn*), the companions of the right, and the companions of the left.


[^EII1-321]: Ibid. On the unity of prophetic religion across successive periods, see also Chapter IX, first and second *hadîth*, *Sharh*, p. 485: “The Witness belonging to each community of prophets and Messengers—all the Witnesses [*shohadâ*]—is part of us [the Imams] and of our own company: members of the Family of prophecy and certainty, of direct witnessing [*shohûd*] and knowledge. They and we together constitute, in the true sense, the community of Mohammad. All the others who follow them also belong to Mohammad's community. Thus we and they are witnesses for the peoples and their followers, and Mohammad is witness for us. That is the meaning of Qur'an 4:45. Therefore, my friend, you must not reinterpret the Imam's words to make this verse refer exclusively to Mohammad's community, excluding the other prophets and their respective communities.” In understanding Mohammad's community this way, Mollâ Sadrâ gave voice to a Shiite “ecumenism,” an embracing of the unity of prophetic religion. Moreover, in the second *hadîth* of this Chapter IX, Imam Ja'far states that the Imams were expressly named in the holy Books revealed earlier, beginning with Abraham's Book (*Sharh*, p. 486).
